The cypress thinned out around midmorning, and the river opened up in front of him, brown and wide and slow, and the levee ran along its eastern bank like a long low wall of grass.

He tied Felix to a willow at the foot of the bank and climbed up with his iron rod in his hand and his notebook in his coat. From the top of the levee he could see the bend, the long lazy curve of the river, the dark line of cypress on the far side, and on his own side a stretch of low pasture that ran back maybe a quarter mile to the wall of the swamp. In the middle of that pasture stood a house. He had not expected a house.

It was a planter's house, two stories, white once but mostly gray now, with a wraparound porch and a sagging center and a row of empty windows on the upper floor that did not catch the light the way windows should. The roof was half gone. The chimneys leaned. A fig tree had grown up through one corner of the porch and shouldered the boards apart.

There was a smell coming off it, faint at that distance, that was something like wet stone and something like old leather and something like nothing he could put a name to. The parish board had not told him about a house. He stood on the levee for a while and looked at it. He looked at the ground around it.

The ground was wrong. It was hard to say at first what was wrong about it. The pasture should have been flat. It had been pasture once.

But around the house, for maybe two hundred yards in every direction, the ground bowed inward, not all at once, in a long slow dish, as if the earth were exhaling under the house, and had been exhaling for a long time, and would keep exhaling until the house went under. He took out his notebook. He wrote, "Residence present at coordinates not previously recorded. " He wrote, "Structure approximately seven decades old, advanced decay.

" He wrote, "Ground subsidence in radial pattern, depth indeterminate, estimated dish 30 feet across by 2 feet deep at center. " He stopped writing. He looked at the house again. He had the strong sense that the house was looking back, not with the windows, with something behind the windows.

He had felt the same thing once at a wake in his cousin's house in Huma, where the coffin had been at the far end of a long parlor, and he had been at the other end with his back to a wall. And every time he had turned away from the coffin, he had felt the eyes of his dead cousin on the back of his neck. And every time he had turned back, the coffin had been a coffin, and nothing more. The house felt like the coffin.

He climbed down off the levee and walked across the pasture toward it. The closer he got, the more the smell took on a shape. It was the smell of river water that had been standing in a closed room. It was the smell of a thing that had been wet a long time and had never been allowed to dry.

He pulled the cloth bag out of his shirt pocket and held it against his nose without thinking about it, and the dry sweet smell of the herbs cut through the wet smell of the house, and he was grateful for old Augustine's mother for a moment without knowing why. He noticed, walking across the pasture, that there were no insects. There should have been insects. It was March in Louisiana.

The grass should have been alive with grasshoppers and small things skipping out of his boots with every step. There was nothing. The grass parted around his boots and closed behind him, and that was all. He noticed halfway across that there were no birds.

He stopped. He looked up. The sky was a clean spring blue with thin clouds moving slowly to the southeast. There were no birds in it.

Not high, not low, not on the cypress at the edge of the swamp, not on the levee behind him. He had not seen a bird since he came over the rise. He started walking again. He kept the herb bag against his face.

He stood in front of the porch. He pushed the iron rod into the ground at the foot of the steps. The rod went in. It went in the way a rod goes into soft mud, which is the way it should have gone in if the ground was saturated, but it kept going in.

He had brought a six-foot rod. He had used it for nine years. He had never lost a six-foot rod into soft ground in his life. He lost it.

The rod slid out of his hand and was gone, and the ground closed quietly over it, and he stood there with his empty hand still curled around the memory of the grip, and he heard himself say out loud in his own voice, "That's not possible. " The house creaked. It was not the wind. There was no wind.

He took two steps back from the porch. He took out his notebook. His hand was steady. That surprised him later.

His hand was perfectly steady. He wrote down, "Ground at base of structure, saturated to depth exceeding 6 feet. Possible sinkhole. Recommend evacuation of pasture.

" He looked at what he had written. He thought about what to write next. He could not think of what to write next. He looked up.

There was a woman on the porch. She had not been there a moment before. He was sure of that. He had been looking at the porch when he pushed the rod in.

The porch had been empty. Now she was standing in the doorway of the house with her hand resting on the frame, and she was looking at him the way you look at something you have been waiting on for a long time. She was not a young woman. She was not an old woman.

She was somewhere in between, in that long gentle country where a woman can stay for thirty years if her life is kind to her. She wore a gray dress that might have been white once. Her hair was dark. Her feet were bare.

Her hand on the doorframe was a hand that had worked. Her face was the face of a woman who had decided something a long time ago and never gone back on it. She said, "Are you the one they sent? " Her voice was low and clear.

It carried across the pasture as if there were no air between them. Octave remembered very faintly, like a hand laid on his shoulder, what Augustine had told him. "You answer them once, civil. You do not answer them twice.

" He said, "I'm with the parish board. " She said, "I know. " She did not move. She stood in the doorway with her hand on the frame, and the house creaked again behind her, and Octave realized that the creak had a rhythm, that it had been creaking the whole time he had been standing there in a slow, regular rhythm, the way a porch swing creaks, or a rocking chair, or a chest rising and falling.

He said nothing. He let her speak again. She said, "The parish records don't show a residence at this location. You will have noticed that.

" She said it the way a teacher prompts a student. He thought, "That's one. I have answered her once. I will not answer her again until I must.

" She tilted her head a little, as if she had heard the thought. She said, "You are a careful man. " She said it almost approvingly, the way a woman compliments a horse for not bolting. She said, "The careful ones live longer.

" The smell of wet stone moved around them like a slow current. Somewhere out in the swamp, a frog called once and then was quiet. She said, "You should leave. " She said it more softly now, the way you say the important thing in a long conversation.

"You should leave now. "

Octave did not leave. He told me later that he wished he had. He told me that for the rest of his life, when he was alone in a quiet room, he could hear that woman saying "You should leave now" in that low patient voice, and he could feel the cloth bag pressed against his chest, and he could feel the way the air had thickened on the porch, the way it slowed in his lungs, the way it tasted of stone, and he would think, "Why did I stay?

Why did I stay? " The answer was that he was thirty-one years old, and he had a baby coming that was not yet a baby, and he had a work order in his coat pocket signed by a man who paid him every Friday, and you do not walk away from such things in the spring of 1928. He tipped his hat to her because he had been raised to tip his hat to women. And he walked the perimeter of the house with his notebook in his hand and a hollow place where his iron rod should have been.

He walked the south side first. He kept his eyes on the ground and on the foundation, and he wrote down what he saw, which was that the foundation had no foundation. The house was resting on the dish of the earth. Where there should have been brick piers, there were only the rotted stumps of brick piers, and the house was sitting on those stumps the way a man sits on a chair he is too tired to fall out of.

He wrote, "Structure unsupported. " He wrote, "Will not survive next high water. " He wrote, "Occupant present, single woman, refuses identification. "

He walked the east side.

The fig tree had pushed up through the porch boards and into the eaves, and there were small, dark things growing in the bark that he did not look at closely. He smelled them anyway. They smelled of wet stone, like everything else, only stronger. He moved past quickly.

He walked the north side. On the north side there was a well. It was a brick well, old, with a low stone lip and a wooden cover laid loose across the top. The cover was crooked.

He could see down into the well between the boards and the lip. The well was full of water. The water was very still and very dark, and even at noon, with the sun directly overhead, the surface of it did not catch the light. He had been a levee man for nine years.

He had looked into a lot of water. This water was wrong. He could not have told you in what way. He told me when he finally told me that the water looked the way a closed eye looks.

He told me that it looked patient. He told me that he stood there for what might have been a full minute with his notebook open in his hand and the pencil resting against the page, and he did not write anything, and he did not move, and somewhere behind him the house creaked in its slow rhythm and the porch creaked under no weight at all. He noticed after a while that the well cover had carvings on it. They were not the sort of carvings you would notice from across the pasture.

They had been cut shallow into the wood and then weathered down by rain and sun and the dragging of the cover back and forth across the lip. But up close, with his eyes adjusted to the green half-shade of the fig tree, he could see them. They were not letters. They were not anything he recognized.

They were small, careful marks made in a steady hand, in a pattern that went around the rim of the cover in a circle. He counted them without meaning to. There were sixty-three of them. He thought, "My God, somebody has been counting.

" Then he heard the small sound from the well. It was the sound a hand makes when it touches water from underneath. Soft. Once.

He stepped back. He stepped back two paces and three. And he turned around, and the woman was standing behind him on the grass. He had not heard her cross the pasture.

He had not heard her come down the steps. She was standing about four feet from him, and her bare feet were on the grass, and her hand was at her side now, and her face had not changed. She said, "I told you to leave. " He said, "Ma'am, what is in this well?

" He had answered her twice now. He knew he had. He had felt the moment the second answer left his mouth, the way a man feels the moment a coin leaves his hand into a fountain, gone and not coming back. He had broken Augustine's one rule.

He had broken it because he could not stand not knowing what the sound under the cover had been. The woman closed her eyes for a long moment, the way a person closes their eyes when they hear a piece of bad news they have been expecting. She opened them. She said, "You have a wife.

" He said, "I do. " She said, "She is carrying. " He said, "Yes. " She said, "You should not have answered me twice.

" She said it with great gentleness, the way a doctor tells a man that the leg cannot be saved. She said, "But it is done now. So I will tell you what is in the well, because you have made yourself a man who needs to know. And a man who needs to know cannot leave until he does.

"

She said, "My husband put them there a long time ago, before the war, before his war, before any war you would remember. " She said it the way you say something you have said in your own head every day for so many years that the words have worn smooth and they come out of your mouth without effort, the way a coin comes out of a pocket. She said his name was Etienne Rocheblave. He came to this country from Santo Domingo when he was a young man after the troubles there, with a great deal of money and a smaller amount of God.

He built this house. He planted indigo in the pasture and then sugar in the pasture and then nothing at all in the pasture, because by the time he stopped planting things he had stopped wanting things to grow. She said he became interested in his middle age in a question. She said the question was: what is the most a man can take from another man without taking his life?

She said it without any change in her voice. Octave felt the cloth bag against his chest. He pressed his hand to it. The herbs had gone warm.

She said he tried to answer his question over a period of about eleven years. He kept careful records. He was a careful man. "I was his wife.

I knew what he was doing. I did not stop him because I was a woman of my time, and there were no doors in my life that I could open by myself, and the door to that particular room was the most closed of all. I have lived with that for sixty years. I will live with it for as long as he requires me to.

" She said, "When he died in the year 1868, he asked me one last thing. He asked me to keep the lid on the well. He had put them in the well one at a time over the eleven years after he was done with his question. He had put them in alive because his question required it.

He had put the cover on after the last one. He had made the marks. And he had told me on his deathbed that they would not stay still, that they would push, that the cover would have to be sat upon and prayed over and kept. " She said, "He made me promise, and I promised.

I have kept the lid on for sixty years. "

Octave looked at her. He looked at her bare feet on the grass. He looked at her gray dress.

He looked at her hand, which had returned to her side and which now hung very still. He said, "Ma'am, are you alive? " She said, "That is the third question you have asked me, and that is the one I will not answer. " She said, "I will tell you only this.

The ground has been giving way under us for sixty years. The house is sinking. The well is sinking with it. When the well goes under, what is in it will come out into the river, and the river will carry it past your city, and your city will drink it.

Do you understand me? " He did not. He understood the shape of it. He did not understand the thing inside the shape.

He said, "Ma'am, I have to make a report. " She said, "You will make no report. " He said, "The parish board. " She said, "The parish board has sent men out here before.

Three of them in the year my husband died, and again twelve years later, and again seven years after that. None of them made a report. You will not make a report either. " He felt the cloth bag against his chest.

It was warm now, almost hot, the way a stone is warm after a long day in the sun. He said, "What happened to those men? " She said, "They listened to me. I told them to leave.

They left. But you have asked me twice, and now I have told you what is in the well, and the well has heard you ask. The well remembers voices. My husband taught it to.

You spoke into it when you spoke to me, because I am near it, and what is near it is part of it. The well knows your voice now. There is only one way I can keep it from knowing more. " He said, "What way?

" She said, "You have to leave now. Right now. You have to walk away from this porch and you have to not look back. You have to ride to old Augustine's house and you have to ask him to give you the second bag.

And you have to wear the second bag for the rest of your life. And you have to never come back to this bend. And you have to never speak my name aloud. And you have to never speak my husband's name aloud.

And you have to never, ever speak the name of this place aloud. If you can do all of those things, the well will forget. Eventually. " She said, "Please.

"

That word almost undid him. There was no please in her voice the way there is please in most voices. There was a please in her voice the way there is please in the voice of a person who has been carrying a heavy door for sixty years and is not asking you to help her, only asking you not to push. He said, "I will leave.

" She said, "Thank you. " He said, "But I have to come back with the board. " She said, "They will send other men. I know.

And I will tell them what I told you. And some of them will listen, and some of them will not. And the ones who do not listen will go into the well, and I will put the lid back on, and the ground will keep sinking, and one day the lid will not hold. But that is not your day.

Your day is this: you can walk back across that pasture to your mule, and you can ride back up the road to your wife, and you can let the baby that is coming be born, and you can grow old somewhere away from this bend in the river. That is your day. If you take it. "

He took it.

He did not run. A man who runs in a place like that calls attention to himself the way a child calls attention to himself by holding still in a game. He walked. He walked back across the pasture the way he had come, with the notebook closed under his arm and the cloth bag pressed against his shirt by his hand.

He walked over the long, slow dish of the sinking ground. He could feel the dish beneath him now in a way he had not felt it before. He could feel the slight inward tilt of every step. He could feel the ground listening.

He climbed the levee. He untied Felix. He mounted. He rode.

He did not look back until he was a mile up the road. And when he did look back, he could see the levee, and he could see the cypress on the far side of the river. And where the house had stood, he could see only pasture, and a faint silver dish in the green, and a single dark spot in the middle of the dish that might have been a stone, or a well, or nothing at all. He rode hard for an hour.

Then Felix stopped. Not lame exactly. Felix stopped. He stopped in the middle of the road in a stretch of cypress where the light was green and the cicadas were doing their work, and he would not move.

Octave clucked at him. He pulled the reins. He dismounted and checked the hooves. There was nothing in the hooves.

There was no thorn. There was no stone. He led Felix by the bridle, and Felix walked. But the moment Octave tried to mount Felix again, Felix went still as a wall.

Octave looked at the mule for a long time. He said, "All right. " He led Felix the rest of the way to Augustine Pellerine's on foot, in the slow heat of the early afternoon. It took him four hours.

He did not run. He walked the way the woman had told him to walk, with his hand on the bag against his chest and his eyes on the road and his mouth closed. He thought the whole way about the mule. He thought about it because it was something to think about that was not the well.

He thought, "The mule knows. The mule knows something about my voice that I do not know yet. The mule knows I am carrying something. The mule does not want it on his back.

"

He arrived at Augustine's at sundown. The old man was on the dock smoking. The dog Mister was at his feet. The dog had not moved.

The old man did not turn around when Octave came up the path on foot leading the mule. He said only, "You come back early. " Octave said, "Yes. " Augustine said, "You got your rod.

" Octave said, "No. " The old man nodded. He said, "You talked. " Octave said, "Twice.

" The old man closed his eyes for a moment. He opened them. He said, "All right. Come inside.

"

He took Octave inside. He sat him at the small wooden table. He went to a shelf and he took down a tin box. He opened the box.

Inside the box was a row of small cloth bags, neatly tied, each about the size of the one Octave was already carrying. He counted them. There were nine. He picked one up.

He weighed it in his palm. He set it down. He picked up another. He weighed it.

He set it down. He went through all nine slowly, the way a man chooses a peach at a market. He chose the fifth one. He set the box aside.

He said, "This one. " Octave said, "What's the difference? " Augustine said, "The one you are wearing now is for keeping a thing from finding you. This one is for keeping a thing from using your voice if it has already found you.

" Octave said, "Can it? " Augustine said, "Can it what? " Octave said, "Can it use my voice? " The old man looked at him a long time.

He said, "Son, if she told you what is in that well, then yes, it can use your voice. It has heard you say words near it, and it has heard you say words to her, and she and it are very close. The bag will not change that. The bag will only make it harder.

"

"Harder is the most you can hope for in this country," Octave said. "What does that mean? " Augustine said, "It means for the rest of your life, when you speak, you will sometimes hear yourself say a word you did not mean to say. A small word.

A child's word. You will think, 'Where did that come from? ' You will go on with your day. Eventually, you will stop noticing.

That is the best you can hope for. The worst is that someone you love will hear that word, and the word will be the word that thing wanted said, and the saying of it will open a door somewhere that does not look like a door. " He said, "The bag makes the door heavier. It does not make the door gone.

" He gave Octave the second bag. He said, "Wear them both. Always. Replace the herbs in this one when they go stale, and the herbs are these and these and this.

" He wrote them down on a slip of paper. Octave folded the slip and put it in his wallet. Augustine said, "Now eat. " Octave ate.

He could not taste the food. He ate anyway because the old man had set it in front of him. After he ate, he sat on the dock with Augustine in the dark. The frogs were loud.

Mister the dog watched the path. The lamp in the house behind them threw a small yellow light onto the boards. After maybe an hour, the old man said, "You going to write the report? " Octave said, "No.

" Augustine said, "What are you going to write? " Octave thought about it for a long time. He said, "I am going to write that the levee at Bend 17 is sound and the pasture is empty, and there is no need to send men down there until after the high water. " The old man drew on his pipe.

He said, "Good. " He said, "The high water is coming in May. " Octave said, "I know. " The old man said, "The high water this year is going to be the worst high water in fifty years.

" Octave said, "I know that, too. " Augustine smoked for a while. He said, "Then your report will be true by the time anybody goes to check it. " Octave said, "Will it solve it?

" The old man took a long breath. He let it out slowly. He said, "No, son. It will not solve it.

It will only put it underwater for a while. Water is not the answer. Water is only the curtain. But the curtain will hold for as long as you are alive, and probably longer.

And that is more than your uncle Remy got, and more than my mother got, and more than Cleovas Hebert got. And you should take it, and you should be grateful for it. " Octave said, "I will. "

That was the spring of 1928.

In the April of that year, the rains came hard up the valley, and in May the river crested seven feet over the level that anyone alive had ever seen, and the levees south of the city held in some places and broke in others, and Bend 17 was one of the others. The pasture went under, the cypress went under, the road went under. Old Augustine Pellerine went up to his sister's place in Plaquemines for the season and came back in July. And when he came back, his house was still standing because it was on stilts, but the country around it had been rearranged.

The house on the pasture was gone. There was no trace of it. No timbers, no bricks, nothing. The pasture itself was gone, too.

Where the long, slow dish had been, there was now a stretch of open water, deep and brown, that joined the river by a narrow channel. The fishermen avoided it. They said the catfish ran heavy there, but the meat tasted of something they did not like. They called it the Sink.

After a few years, they stopped calling it anything because they stopped going. Octave Theot never went back to that bend. He filed his report. He wrote what he had told Augustine he would write.

No one questioned it because by the time anyone went looking, the country was underwater and the question was moot. He stayed with the parish board for two more years, and then he took a job with the customs house in the city, and he did that until he retired, and he lived a long quiet life in a small white house off Esplanade with the wife he had ridden home to and the son who had been the hope inside her that spring. His son grew up. His son became a man.

His son had a son of his own. Octave was a grandfather by the time he was fifty-five. And he was the kind of grandfather who could sit on the front step of an evening with his grandson on his knee and listen to the streetcars. And the grandson would point at things, and Octave would name them slow and patient.

And the grandson would say the names after him. And Octave would correct his pronunciation in French and English and let it go in Spanish, because the Spanish was rare in that house and his wife had no ear for it. He was a good grandfather. He was a good husband.

He was a quiet man, and a quiet man is sometimes a hard man to live with, but his wife had grown up with quiet men, and she did not ask him for the noise he could not make. He kept the cloth bags in his shirt pocket every day of his life. There were two of them, side by side against his ribs. When the herbs went stale, he replaced them.

He carried Augustine's slip of paper in his wallet for forty years, and when the paper finally wore through, he copied the words over onto a new slip in his own careful hand. He never told his wife what was in the bags. He never told his son. He never told his grandson.

There was a thing he did, though, that I noticed when I knew him. There was a thing he did all his life that nobody else paid attention to, but I paid attention because I am the kind of man who pays attention. When he spoke, every so often he would pause in the middle of a sentence. Not the pause a man takes to find his next word.

A different pause. A pause as if he had heard himself about to say something, and he was deciding in the half second before it came out of his mouth whether to let it out. Sometimes he would let it out, and it would be the word he meant. Sometimes he would change the word mid-breath, and the new word would be the word he meant, but the rhythm of the sentence would be off, the way a song is off when a singer has changed the note at the last instant.

I only asked him about it once. I was about twenty. We were on the back porch of his house off Esplanade in the spring of 1964, and the canal was running high after a rain, and the smell of the river was thick in the air. I said, "Mr.

Theot, why do you do that? " He said, "Do what? " I said, "That pause. " He looked at me.

He looked at me for a long time. His eyes were a faded blue. His hands were folded in his lap. He had a small spot of pipe ash on his vest.

He said, "Son, you are very observant. Don't ever ask me about it again. " I never did. He told me the story two years later, on a warm evening in the spring of 1966, when the windows were open and the smell of river water came in off the canal.

And he stopped in the middle of a sentence about something else entirely, and he said, "You know, I never told anybody this. " And then he told me all of it the way I have told it to you, only slower, with longer pauses, with the bag pressed against his chest under his shirt the whole time. He told it to me from beginning to end, and when he was finished, it was almost morning, and the canal was quiet, and the smell of riverwater had gone. He died two years after that, quiet in his sleep.

His wife found him in the morning with his hand at his chest, holding the cloth bags through his shirt, and she did not understand it, and she did not ask anyone what it meant, because she was a woman who had been married to a quiet man for forty years, and she had learned the shape of his silences, and she knew which ones were not to be opened. She buried him with the bags. I think about that sometimes. I think about a man holding two small bags of herbs against his chest for forty years, the way a sailor holds a coin from the country he came from, the way a soldier holds a letter, the way you hold something that you do not believe in exactly, but that you cannot put down because the day you put it down might be the day you needed it.

I think about a woman in a gray dress on a sinking porch telling a young man to leave, please, because she had decided a long time ago to stay. I think about the Sink out there past the city, still there, full of slow brown water, joined to the river by a narrow channel, and the river running past the city, and the city drinking from the river, and the lid that is sometimes on and sometimes off. And how no one alive remembers anymore that the lid was ever a lid. I do not know what was in that well.

Octave did not know either. He only knew what the woman told him, and the woman told him only as much as he needed to leave. The rest she kept. She kept it the way she had kept it for sixty years before he ever rode down that road, and the way I think she is keeping it still, somewhere under the slow brown water, in a house that is not there anymore, with the porch creaking in its slow rhythm and her hand on the doorframe and her bare feet on the boards, waiting for the next man the parish sends, because the parish always sends another man eventually.

I went down there once in the summer of 1971, three years after he died. I borrowed a small boat from a man in Belshassier, and I pulled it out into the channel that joined the Sink to the river. The water was still. There were no birds.

There were no insects. The air smelled of wet stone. I sat in the boat for an hour. I did not say anything.

I had remembered the old man's rule. After an hour, I felt something move under the boat. Not a fish. Not a current.

Something larger. Something with intent. I pulled back to the channel, and I rode back to Belshassier, and I gave the man back his boat, and I drove home, and I have not been back. I have not said the name of that place out loud since.

I am not saying it now. You will notice I have not said it in this whole story. I have called it Bend 17, which is what the parish board called it. But the parish board is gone, and the bend is gone.

And the name the old folks used, I have not said. I will not say it. Not to you, not to anyone.
content_html:
Some men carry a thing inside them for the rest of their lives and never name it out loud. They walk past it every morning. They sit beside it at supper. They lie down with it at night.

And when somebody asks how they are, they say fine, and they mean it the way you mean a closed door. The man I’m about to tell you about was one of those. He carried his quiet for almost forty years before he said the first word of it to me. And when he finally did, it was not because I asked.

It was because of a smell that came in through an open window one warm evening, and the smell was riverwater, and the look that crossed his face was the look of a man hearing his own name called from a room he thought was empty. His name was Octave Theot. He was thirty-one years old in the spring of 1928 and he worked as a levee inspector for the parish board, which meant he spent most of his weeks walking earthen banks south of New Orleans with a notebook in his coat pocket and a long iron rod in his hand. He used the rod to test the ground.

He used the notebook to write down what the rod told him. He stood a little over six feet, lean, not slim, the lean of a man who walked twenty miles a day. He had black hair that he kept short under a wide gray hat and a thin scar above his left eyebrow from a horse that kicked him when he was twenty-two. His hands were the hands of a man who worked with rope and clay every day of his life.

They had no softness in them anywhere. He was born in a town called Belshassier, which does not appear on most maps because most maps are not drawn carefully enough to find it. It sat at the end of a dirt road that ran south through canefields and then through cypress and then through nothing at all. The people there were Creole and Cajun mostly, with a few Anglo families who had drifted in after the war and never drifted back out.

Octave’s mother was a Theot. His father was something he did not talk about. He spoke English at work and French at home and a little Spanish when he was angry, and he could pray in Latin if you put a priest in front of him, but he did not pray often. He used to say that the bayou had its own kind of church and you did not need to kneel in it.

You only needed to listen. In March of 1928, he was sent down to a stretch of levee about eleven miles below the city, near a bend in the river the old folks called the Ostiaba. Most maps just called it Bend 17. The parish had been getting reports that the ground there was sinking faster than it should, and the board wanted someone to walk it and write down what he saw before the high water came in May.

Octave did not want the job. He did not say so to his foreman. You did not say no to a paying job in 1928. Not in that parish, not with a wife at home and a baby on the way.

That was not yet a baby, only a hope. But when his foreman handed him the work order and said, “And to Diablo, son, you know the country down there,” Octave felt the small cold thing in his stomach that a man feels when his life is about to bend. He said only, “I know it. ”

The foreman, whose name was Hollis Vanderlice, and who had been a Navy man before the parish board, looked at him for a moment longer than he needed to.

Hollis had hired Octave nine years before. Hollis knew his men the way a captain knows a ship, which is to say he knew when the wood was tired and when it was not. He said, “Son, if you don’t want to take it, I can put Bedro on it. ” Octave said, “Bedro’s got his back.

” Hollis said, “Bedro’s back will mend. Yours might not. ” Octave said, “I’ll take it. ” Hollis nodded.

He did not say anything else. He folded the work order and handed it across the desk. And when Octave took it, their hands touched for a second, and Hollis held on a beat too long, the way a father holds on when he’s sending a son somewhere he is not sure he should be sending him. Then Hollis let go and went back to his ledger and did not look up again.

“Be back by Sunday,” he said to the ledger. Octave left on a Wednesday morning by mule. The road south of the city in those days was not really a road. It was a high ridge of packed shell and dirt with cane fields on one side and cypress swamp on the other.

And once you got past the parish line, there was no telegraph and no electric light and no doctor closer than a half day’s ride. The mule’s name was Felix. Felix did not like the trip either. Octave had ridden Felix down that road a dozen times.

He knew the bend where the wild plums grew. He knew the stand of cypress where the herons nested in April. He knew the broken wooden sign that said Pellerine’s Landing in faded blue paint and pointed at a path that was no longer there. He knew the road.

The road that morning did not seem to know him. Octave rode for most of the first day under a sky the color of dirty linen. The wind came off the gulf. There was a smell in it that was not quite salt and not quite anything else, and he could not place it, and the not placing of it began to bother him after the first hour, the way a word you cannot remember begins to bother you.

He kept stopping to test the air. He kept telling himself it was nothing. The mule’s ears kept moving. The mule’s ears, in his experience, were a more honest instrument than his own nose.

Around four in the afternoon, the cypress closed in on both sides of the road. The light went green. The cicadas, which had been so loud all morning that he had stopped hearing them, stopped. Just stopped.

He pulled Felix up and listened. There was the small wet sound of water moving somewhere out of sight. There was the creak of the saddle. There was his own breathing.

There was nothing else. He had been in that country his whole life. He knew the difference between a quiet wood and a wood that had gone quiet. This was the second.

He sat very still on Felix’s back, and he counted slowly to thirty in his head, the way his mother had taught him to count when he was small and scared of thunder. At twenty-two, the cicadas started up again all at once, the way they had stopped. He let out a breath he had not known he was holding. He clicked his tongue and Felix walked on, and Octave told himself it had been a bird passing overhead.

A hawk maybe, and the small things had hushed for the hawk and then forgotten. He told himself that for the rest of the afternoon. He almost believed it. He spent that night at the house of a man named Augustine Pellerine.

Augustine was old. Octave did not know how old. He had been old when Octave was a boy fishing with his uncles, and he had been old when Octave’s uncles were boys themselves. And the math of that did not quite work out unless you assumed Augustine had simply been born old and stayed that way.

He lived alone in a one-room house on stilts at the edge of the swamp with a cypress dock and three traps and a yellow dog that did not bark, only watched. The dog was called Mister. Octave had not stopped at Augustine’s place in three years. He had meant to.

He had meant to a dozen times. But the old man’s house was a half mile off the main road down a path that flooded in winter and grew over in summer. And every time Octave had ridden past the turning, he had said to himself, “Next trip, next trip. ” That afternoon when he came to the turning he did not say next trip.

He turned in. Augustine was on the dock when Octave rode up. He was mending a trap. He did not stop mending the trap.

He said only, without looking up, “You took the long way, son. ” Octave said, “I did. ” Augustine said, “You knew I was here. ” Octave said, “I knew.

” The old man finished the knot he was tying, set the trap aside, and stood. His knees made a sound like a small dry branch. He looked Octave up and down. He looked at Felix.

He looked at the iron rod across Octave’s saddle and the notebook in Octave’s coat and the work order folded in the band of his hat. He said, “Where are they sending you? ” Octave said, “Bend 17. ” Augustine said nothing for a long moment.

Then he turned and walked toward his house, and the dog Mister stood up from where he had been lying and followed. And the old man said over his shoulder, “You’ll stay the night. ” It was not a question. Octave dismounted.

Augustine took Octave in the way old men in that country took anyone in. He fed him red beans and rice and a piece of catfish, and he poured him a small glass of something clear from an unlabeled jar. And he asked after Octave’s mother, who had been dead for nine years, and he listened to the answer as if he had not known. That was his way.

He held the dead in the present tense until you were ready to let them go. After supper, with the lamp turned low and the cypress dark outside the open door, Augustine filled his pipe. He said, “You remember what your uncle Remy used to say about that bend? ” Octave said, “My uncle Remy said a lot of things.

” Augustine said, “He said, ‘The ground down there don’t keep what you put in it. ‘” Octave looked at the old man for a long time. The dog Mister was watching them from the doorway and the dog did not blink. Octave said, “That’s a saying.

” Augustine said, “It is. ” Octave said, “Sayings are how old men tell young men to be careful without admitting they’re scared. ” The old man smiled at that. It was a small smile, and there was something tired in it that was not quite kindness.

He said, “You’re right, son. That’s exactly what they are. ” He drew on his pipe. He looked out the open door into the dark where the cypress stood, where the water moved, where the cicadas had started up loud again, as if they had something to drown out.

He said, “You’re right, and you should be scared anyway. ”

Octave said, “Tell me what you know about that place. ” Augustine shook his head slowly. He said, “What I know is not worth telling.

What I know is what an old man hears from older men who heard it from older men still, and by the time a thing has come that far down the line, it is mostly water and very little fish. But there is one thing I will tell you. ” Octave waited. The old man said, “My mother went down to that bend once.

She was a young woman then. She had business with a midwife who lived on that pasture in a house that was already old in the year before the war. She walked the eleven miles down and she walked the eleven miles back the next day. She would not say what she saw.

She would not say what she heard. She would only say all her life, every time the river smell came in through the window the way it is coming in now, ‘The lid is loose tonight. ‘” Octave said, “The lid. ” Augustine said, “The lid.

” He drew on his pipe. The smoke went up into the rafters where the light did not reach. He said, “And the night before she died, she said it twice. I went to the window and I looked out and I could not smell anything but the swamp.

But my mother had a nose for water that I did not inherit. She knew. ” He said, “The next morning she was gone. And three days later the parish sent a man down to Bend 17, and the man came back and he did not file his report and he quit the parish that same week and he moved to Mobile, Alabama.

And I have not heard his name spoken in forty years. ” Octave said, “Who was he? ” Augustine said, “His name was Cleovas Hebert. ” Octave said, “I never heard of him.

” Augustine said, “That is on purpose. ”

They sat for a long time after that. Octave watched the lamp. The lamp’s flame moved very slightly, even though the door was open only a crack and there was no draft to speak of.

He watched it move, and he thought, “The lid is loose tonight,” and he could not say why he was thinking it. Octave slept poorly. He did not dream so much as drift in and out of a half sleep, and in the drifting he heard the water lapping against the stilts of the house. And once near three in the morning by his watch, he thought he heard a voice out there in the dark.

Not words. A voice. The sound a voice makes when it is talking quietly to itself a long way off, and you cannot make out the language. He sat up.

He listened. He heard only water. He lay back down. He told himself it had been the dog.

But when he looked toward the door, the dog was awake, sitting upright, looking out into the night with his ears flat against his skull, and the dog had not moved in what might have been a long time. He left at first light. Augustine walked him to the edge of the dock. The morning was cool and gray with that thick gulf mist that turns the world into a held breath.

The old man handed Octave a small cloth bag that smelled of dry herbs and something like sweet tobacco. He said, “Put it in your shirt pocket. ” Octave said, “What’s in it? ” Augustine said, “Things my mother put in her shirt pocket.

” Octave said, “Did it work for her? ” Augustine said, “She lived to be ninety-two. ” He did not smile when he said it. Octave put the bag in his shirt pocket.

Augustine said, “One more thing. ” Octave waited. Augustine said, “If anyone speaks to you down there, you answer them once, civil. You do not answer them twice.

” Octave said, “Why? ” Augustine said, “Because the second time you answer is the time they learn the sound of your voice, and after that they can use it. ” Octave thought about that for a moment. He thought about asking who “they” were.

He decided he did not want to know. He said, “All right. ” The old man nodded. He patted Felix’s neck.

He stepped back from the dock and he raised one hand, and that was the goodbye. Octave rode out under the cypress with the cloth bag in his shirt pocket and the iron rod across his saddle, and behind him the dog Mister sat on the dock and watched him go without making a sound. He rode the last seven miles to Bend 17 alone. The cypress thinned out around midmorning, and the river opened up in front of him, brown and wide and slow, and the levee ran along its eastern bank like a long low wall of grass.

He tied Felix to a willow at the foot of the bank and climbed up with his iron rod in his hand and his notebook in his coat. From the top of the levee he could see the bend, the long lazy curve of the river, the dark line of cypress on the far side, and on his own side a stretch of low pasture that ran back maybe a quarter mile to the wall of the swamp. In the middle of that pasture stood a house. He had not expected a house.

It was a planter’s house, two stories, white once but mostly gray now, with a wraparound porch and a sagging center and a row of empty windows on the upper floor that did not catch the light the way windows should. The roof was half gone. The chimneys leaned. A fig tree had grown up through one corner of the porch and shouldered the boards apart.

There was a smell coming off it, faint at that distance, that was something like wet stone and something like old leather and something like nothing he could put a name to. The parish board had not told him about a house. He stood on the levee for a while and looked at it. He looked at the ground around it.

The ground was wrong. It was hard to say at first what was wrong about it. The pasture should have been flat. It had been pasture once.

But around the house, for maybe two hundred yards in every direction, the ground bowed inward, not all at once, in a long slow dish, as if the earth were exhaling under the house, and had been exhaling for a long time, and would keep exhaling until the house went under. He took out his notebook. He wrote, “Residence present at coordinates not previously recorded. ” He wrote, “Structure approximately seven decades old, advanced decay.

” He wrote, “Ground subsidence in radial pattern, depth indeterminate, estimated dish 30 feet across by 2 feet deep at center. ” He stopped writing. He looked at the house again. He had the strong sense that the house was looking back, not with the windows, with something behind the windows.

He had felt the same thing once at a wake in his cousin’s house in Huma, where the coffin had been at the far end of a long parlor, and he had been at the other end with his back to a wall. And every time he had turned away from the coffin, he had felt the eyes of his dead cousin on the back of his neck. And every time he had turned back, the coffin had been a coffin, and nothing more. The house felt like the coffin.

He climbed down off the levee and walked across the pasture toward it. The closer he got, the more the smell took on a shape. It was the smell of river water that had been standing in a closed room. It was the smell of a thing that had been wet a long time and had never been allowed to dry.

He pulled the cloth bag out of his shirt pocket and held it against his nose without thinking about it, and the dry sweet smell of the herbs cut through the wet smell of the house, and he was grateful for old Augustine’s mother for a moment without knowing why. He noticed, walking across the pasture, that there were no insects. There should have been insects. It was March in Louisiana.

The grass should have been alive with grasshoppers and small things skipping out of his boots with every step. There was nothing. The grass parted around his boots and closed behind him, and that was all. He noticed halfway across that there were no birds.

He stopped. He looked up. The sky was a clean spring blue with thin clouds moving slowly to the southeast. There were no birds in it.

Not high, not low, not on the cypress at the edge of the swamp, not on the levee behind him. He had not seen a bird since he came over the rise. He started walking again. He kept the herb bag against his face.

He stood in front of the porch. He pushed the iron rod into the ground at the foot of the steps. The rod went in. It went in the way a rod goes into soft mud, which is the way it should have gone in if the ground was saturated, but it kept going in.

He had brought a six-foot rod. He had used it for nine years. He had never lost a six-foot rod into soft ground in his life. He lost it.

The rod slid out of his hand and was gone, and the ground closed quietly over it, and he stood there with his empty hand still curled around the memory of the grip, and he heard himself say out loud in his own voice, “That’s not possible. ” The house creaked. It was not the wind. There was no wind.

He took two steps back from the porch. He took out his notebook. His hand was steady. That surprised him later.

His hand was perfectly steady. He wrote down, “Ground at base of structure, saturated to depth exceeding 6 feet. Possible sinkhole. Recommend evacuation of pasture.

” He looked at what he had written. He thought about what to write next. He could not think of what to write next. He looked up.

There was a woman on the porch. She had not been there a moment before. He was sure of that. He had been looking at the porch when he pushed the rod in.

The porch had been empty. Now she was standing in the doorway of the house with her hand resting on the frame, and she was looking at him the way you look at something you have been waiting on for a long time. She was not a young woman. She was not an old woman.

She was somewhere in between, in that long gentle country where a woman can stay for thirty years if her life is kind to her. She wore a gray dress that might have been white once. Her hair was dark. Her feet were bare.

Her hand on the doorframe was a hand that had worked. Her face was the face of a woman who had decided something a long time ago and never gone back on it. She said, “Are you the one they sent? ” Her voice was low and clear.

It carried across the pasture as if there were no air between them. Octave remembered very faintly, like a hand laid on his shoulder, what Augustine had told him. “You answer them once, civil. You do not answer them twice.

” He said, “I’m with the parish board. ” She said, “I know. ” She did not move. She stood in the doorway with her hand on the frame, and the house creaked again behind her, and Octave realized that the creak had a rhythm, that it had been creaking the whole time he had been standing there in a slow, regular rhythm, the way a porch swing creaks, or a rocking chair, or a chest rising and falling.

He said nothing. He let her speak again. She said, “The parish records don’t show a residence at this location. You will have noticed that.

” She said it the way a teacher prompts a student. He thought, “That’s one. I have answered her once. I will not answer her again until I must.

” She tilted her head a little, as if she had heard the thought. She said, “You are a careful man. ” She said it almost approvingly, the way a woman compliments a horse for not bolting. She said, “The careful ones live longer.

” The smell of wet stone moved around them like a slow current. Somewhere out in the swamp, a frog called once and then was quiet. She said, “You should leave. ” She said it more softly now, the way you say the important thing in a long conversation.

“You should leave now. ”

Octave did not leave. He told me later that he wished he had. He told me that for the rest of his life, when he was alone in a quiet room, he could hear that woman saying “You should leave now” in that low patient voice, and he could feel the cloth bag pressed against his chest, and he could feel the way the air had thickened on the porch, the way it slowed in his lungs, the way it tasted of stone, and he would think, “Why did I stay?

Why did I stay? ” The answer was that he was thirty-one years old, and he had a baby coming that was not yet a baby, and he had a work order in his coat pocket signed by a man who paid him every Friday, and you do not walk away from such things in the spring of 1928. He tipped his hat to her because he had been raised to tip his hat to women. And he walked the perimeter of the house with his notebook in his hand and a hollow place where his iron rod should have been.

He walked the south side first. He kept his eyes on the ground and on the foundation, and he wrote down what he saw, which was that the foundation had no foundation. The house was resting on the dish of the earth. Where there should have been brick piers, there were only the rotted stumps of brick piers, and the house was sitting on those stumps the way a man sits on a chair he is too tired to fall out of.

He wrote, “Structure unsupported. ” He wrote, “Will not survive next high water. ” He wrote, “Occupant present, single woman, refuses identification. ”

He walked the east side.

The fig tree had pushed up through the porch boards and into the eaves, and there were small, dark things growing in the bark that he did not look at closely. He smelled them anyway. They smelled of wet stone, like everything else, only stronger. He moved past quickly.

He walked the north side. On the north side there was a well. It was a brick well, old, with a low stone lip and a wooden cover laid loose across the top. The cover was crooked.

He could see down into the well between the boards and the lip. The well was full of water. The water was very still and very dark, and even at noon, with the sun directly overhead, the surface of it did not catch the light. He had been a levee man for nine years.

He had looked into a lot of water. This water was wrong. He could not have told you in what way. He told me when he finally told me that the water looked the way a closed eye looks.

He told me that it looked patient. He told me that he stood there for what might have been a full minute with his notebook open in his hand and the pencil resting against the page, and he did not write anything, and he did not move, and somewhere behind him the house creaked in its slow rhythm and the porch creaked under no weight at all. He noticed after a while that the well cover had carvings on it. They were not the sort of carvings you would notice from across the pasture.

They had been cut shallow into the wood and then weathered down by rain and sun and the dragging of the cover back and forth across the lip. But up close, with his eyes adjusted to the green half-shade of the fig tree, he could see them. They were not letters. They were not anything he recognized.

They were small, careful marks made in a steady hand, in a pattern that went around the rim of the cover in a circle. He counted them without meaning to. There were sixty-three of them. He thought, “My God, somebody has been counting.

” Then he heard the small sound from the well. It was the sound a hand makes when it touches water from underneath. Soft. Once.

He stepped back. He stepped back two paces and three. And he turned around, and the woman was standing behind him on the grass. He had not heard her cross the pasture.

He had not heard her come down the steps. She was standing about four feet from him, and her bare feet were on the grass, and her hand was at her side now, and her face had not changed. She said, “I told you to leave. ” He said, “Ma’am, what is in this well?

” He had answered her twice now. He knew he had. He had felt the moment the second answer left his mouth, the way a man feels the moment a coin leaves his hand into a fountain, gone and not coming back. He had broken Augustine’s one rule.

He had broken it because he could not stand not knowing what the sound under the cover had been. The woman closed her eyes for a long moment, the way a person closes their eyes when they hear a piece of bad news they have been expecting. She opened them. She said, “You have a wife.

” He said, “I do. ” She said, “She is carrying. ” He said, “Yes. ” She said, “You should not have answered me twice.

” She said it with great gentleness, the way a doctor tells a man that the leg cannot be saved. She said, “But it is done now. So I will tell you what is in the well, because you have made yourself a man who needs to know. And a man who needs to know cannot leave until he does.

”

She said, “My husband put them there a long time ago, before the war, before his war, before any war you would remember. ” She said it the way you say something you have said in your own head every day for so many years that the words have worn smooth and they come out of your mouth without effort, the way a coin comes out of a pocket. She said his name was Etienne Rocheblave. He came to this country from Santo Domingo when he was a young man after the troubles there, with a great deal of money and a smaller amount of God.

He built this house. He planted indigo in the pasture and then sugar in the pasture and then nothing at all in the pasture, because by the time he stopped planting things he had stopped wanting things to grow. She said he became interested in his middle age in a question. She said the question was: what is the most a man can take from another man without taking his life?

She said it without any change in her voice. Octave felt the cloth bag against his chest. He pressed his hand to it. The herbs had gone warm.

She said he tried to answer his question over a period of about eleven years. He kept careful records. He was a careful man. “I was his wife.

I knew what he was doing. I did not stop him because I was a woman of my time, and there were no doors in my life that I could open by myself, and the door to that particular room was the most closed of all. I have lived with that for sixty years. I will live with it for as long as he requires me to.

” She said, “When he died in the year 1868, he asked me one last thing. He asked me to keep the lid on the well. He had put them in the well one at a time over the eleven years after he was done with his question. He had put them in alive because his question required it.

He had put the cover on after the last one. He had made the marks. And he had told me on his deathbed that they would not stay still, that they would push, that the cover would have to be sat upon and prayed over and kept. ” She said, “He made me promise, and I promised.

I have kept the lid on for sixty years. ”

Octave looked at her. He looked at her bare feet on the grass. He looked at her gray dress.

He looked at her hand, which had returned to her side and which now hung very still. He said, “Ma’am, are you alive? ” She said, “That is the third question you have asked me, and that is the one I will not answer. ” She said, “I will tell you only this.

The ground has been giving way under us for sixty years. The house is sinking. The well is sinking with it. When the well goes under, what is in it will come out into the river, and the river will carry it past your city, and your city will drink it.

Do you understand me? ” He did not. He understood the shape of it. He did not understand the thing inside the shape.

He said, “Ma’am, I have to make a report. ” She said, “You will make no report. ” He said, “The parish board. ” She said, “The parish board has sent men out here before.

Three of them in the year my husband died, and again twelve years later, and again seven years after that. None of them made a report. You will not make a report either. ” He felt the cloth bag against his chest.

It was warm now, almost hot, the way a stone is warm after a long day in the sun. He said, “What happened to those men? ” She said, “They listened to me. I told them to leave.

They left. But you have asked me twice, and now I have told you what is in the well, and the well has heard you ask. The well remembers voices. My husband taught it to.

You spoke into it when you spoke to me, because I am near it, and what is near it is part of it. The well knows your voice now. There is only one way I can keep it from knowing more. ” He said, “What way?

” She said, “You have to leave now. Right now. You have to walk away from this porch and you have to not look back. You have to ride to old Augustine’s house and you have to ask him to give you the second bag.

And you have to wear the second bag for the rest of your life. And you have to never come back to this bend. And you have to never speak my name aloud. And you have to never speak my husband’s name aloud.

And you have to never, ever speak the name of this place aloud. If you can do all of those things, the well will forget. Eventually. ” She said, “Please.

”

That word almost undid him. There was no please in her voice the way there is please in most voices. There was a please in her voice the way there is please in the voice of a person who has been carrying a heavy door for sixty years and is not asking you to help her, only asking you not to push. He said, “I will leave.

” She said, “Thank you. ” He said, “But I have to come back with the board. ” She said, “They will send other men. I know.

And I will tell them what I told you. And some of them will listen, and some of them will not. And the ones who do not listen will go into the well, and I will put the lid back on, and the ground will keep sinking, and one day the lid will not hold. But that is not your day.

Your day is this: you can walk back across that pasture to your mule, and you can ride back up the road to your wife, and you can let the baby that is coming be born, and you can grow old somewhere away from this bend in the river. That is your day. If you take it. ”

He took it.

He did not run. A man who runs in a place like that calls attention to himself the way a child calls attention to himself by holding still in a game. He walked. He walked back across the pasture the way he had come, with the notebook closed under his arm and the cloth bag pressed against his shirt by his hand.

He walked over the long, slow dish of the sinking ground. He could feel the dish beneath him now in a way he had not felt it before. He could feel the slight inward tilt of every step. He could feel the ground listening.

He climbed the levee. He untied Felix. He mounted. He rode.

He did not look back until he was a mile up the road. And when he did look back, he could see the levee, and he could see the cypress on the far side of the river. And where the house had stood, he could see only pasture, and a faint silver dish in the green, and a single dark spot in the middle of the dish that might have been a stone, or a well, or nothing at all. He rode hard for an hour.

Then Felix stopped. Not lame exactly. Felix stopped. He stopped in the middle of the road in a stretch of cypress where the light was green and the cicadas were doing their work, and he would not move.

Octave clucked at him. He pulled the reins. He dismounted and checked the hooves. There was nothing in the hooves.

There was no thorn. There was no stone. He led Felix by the bridle, and Felix walked. But the moment Octave tried to mount Felix again, Felix went still as a wall.

Octave looked at the mule for a long time. He said, “All right. ” He led Felix the rest of the way to Augustine Pellerine’s on foot, in the slow heat of the early afternoon. It took him four hours.

He did not run. He walked the way the woman had told him to walk, with his hand on the bag against his chest and his eyes on the road and his mouth closed. He thought the whole way about the mule. He thought about it because it was something to think about that was not the well.

He thought, “The mule knows. The mule knows something about my voice that I do not know yet. The mule knows I am carrying something. The mule does not want it on his back.

”

He arrived at Augustine’s at sundown. The old man was on the dock smoking. The dog Mister was at his feet. The dog had not moved.

The old man did not turn around when Octave came up the path on foot leading the mule. He said only, “You come back early. ” Octave said, “Yes. ” Augustine said, “You got your rod.

” Octave said, “No. ” The old man nodded. He said, “You talked. ” Octave said, “Twice.

” The old man closed his eyes for a moment. He opened them. He said, “All right. Come inside.

”

He took Octave inside. He sat him at the small wooden table. He went to a shelf and he took down a tin box. He opened the box.

Inside the box was a row of small cloth bags, neatly tied, each about the size of the one Octave was already carrying. He counted them. There were nine. He picked one up.

He weighed it in his palm. He set it down. He picked up another. He weighed it.

He set it down. He went through all nine slowly, the way a man chooses a peach at a market. He chose the fifth one. He set the box aside.

He said, “This one. ” Octave said, “What’s the difference? ” Augustine said, “The one you are wearing now is for keeping a thing from finding you. This one is for keeping a thing from using your voice if it has already found you.

” Octave said, “Can it? ” Augustine said, “Can it what? ” Octave said, “Can it use my voice? ” The old man looked at him a long time.

He said, “Son, if she told you what is in that well, then yes, it can use your voice. It has heard you say words near it, and it has heard you say words to her, and she and it are very close. The bag will not change that. The bag will only make it harder.

”

“Harder is the most you can hope for in this country,” Octave said. “What does that mean? ” Augustine said, “It means for the rest of your life, when you speak, you will sometimes hear yourself say a word you did not mean to say. A small word.

A child’s word. You will think, ‘Where did that come from? ‘ You will go on with your day. Eventually, you will stop noticing.

That is the best you can hope for. The worst is that someone you love will hear that word, and the word will be the word that thing wanted said, and the saying of it will open a door somewhere that does not look like a door. ” He said, “The bag makes the door heavier. It does not make the door gone.

” He gave Octave the second bag. He said, “Wear them both. Always. Replace the herbs in this one when they go stale, and the herbs are these and these and this.

” He wrote them down on a slip of paper. Octave folded the slip and put it in his wallet. Augustine said, “Now eat. ” Octave ate.

He could not taste the food. He ate anyway because the old man had set it in front of him. After he ate, he sat on the dock with Augustine in the dark. The frogs were loud.

Mister the dog watched the path. The lamp in the house behind them threw a small yellow light onto the boards. After maybe an hour, the old man said, “You going to write the report? ” Octave said, “No.

” Augustine said, “What are you going to write? ” Octave thought about it for a long time. He said, “I am going to write that the levee at Bend 17 is sound and the pasture is empty, and there is no need to send men down there until after the high water. ” The old man drew on his pipe.

He said, “Good. ” He said, “The high water is coming in May. ” Octave said, “I know. ” The old man said, “The high water this year is going to be the worst high water in fifty years.

” Octave said, “I know that, too. ” Augustine smoked for a while. He said, “Then your report will be true by the time anybody goes to check it. ” Octave said, “Will it solve it?

” The old man took a long breath. He let it out slowly. He said, “No, son. It will not solve it.

It will only put it underwater for a while. Water is not the answer. Water is only the curtain. But the curtain will hold for as long as you are alive, and probably longer.

And that is more than your uncle Remy got, and more than my mother got, and more than Cleovas Hebert got. And you should take it, and you should be grateful for it. ” Octave said, “I will. ”

That was the spring of 1928.

In the April of that year, the rains came hard up the valley, and in May the river crested seven feet over the level that anyone alive had ever seen, and the levees south of the city held in some places and broke in others, and Bend 17 was one of the others. The pasture went under, the cypress went under, the road went under. Old Augustine Pellerine went up to his sister’s place in Plaquemines for the season and came back in July. And when he came back, his house was still standing because it was on stilts, but the country around it had been rearranged.

The house on the pasture was gone. There was no trace of it. No timbers, no bricks, nothing. The pasture itself was gone, too.

Where the long, slow dish had been, there was now a stretch of open water, deep and brown, that joined the river by a narrow channel. The fishermen avoided it. They said the catfish ran heavy there, but the meat tasted of something they did not like. They called it the Sink.

After a few years, they stopped calling it anything because they stopped going. Octave Theot never went back to that bend. He filed his report. He wrote what he had told Augustine he would write.

No one questioned it because by the time anyone went looking, the country was underwater and the question was moot. He stayed with the parish board for two more years, and then he took a job with the customs house in the city, and he did that until he retired, and he lived a long quiet life in a small white house off Esplanade with the wife he had ridden home to and the son who had been the hope inside her that spring. His son grew up. His son became a man.

His son had a son of his own. Octave was a grandfather by the time he was fifty-five. And he was the kind of grandfather who could sit on the front step of an evening with his grandson on his knee and listen to the streetcars. And the grandson would point at things, and Octave would name them slow and patient.

And the grandson would say the names after him. And Octave would correct his pronunciation in French and English and let it go in Spanish, because the Spanish was rare in that house and his wife had no ear for it. He was a good grandfather. He was a good husband.

He was a quiet man, and a quiet man is sometimes a hard man to live with, but his wife had grown up with quiet men, and she did not ask him for the noise he could not make. He kept the cloth bags in his shirt pocket every day of his life. There were two of them, side by side against his ribs. When the herbs went stale, he replaced them.

He carried Augustine’s slip of paper in his wallet for forty years, and when the paper finally wore through, he copied the words over onto a new slip in his own careful hand. He never told his wife what was in the bags. He never told his son. He never told his grandson.

There was a thing he did, though, that I noticed when I knew him. There was a thing he did all his life that nobody else paid attention to, but I paid attention because I am the kind of man who pays attention. When he spoke, every so often he would pause in the middle of a sentence. Not the pause a man takes to find his next word.

A different pause. A pause as if he had heard himself about to say something, and he was deciding in the half second before it came out of his mouth whether to let it out. Sometimes he would let it out, and it would be the word he meant. Sometimes he would change the word mid-breath, and the new word would be the word he meant, but the rhythm of the sentence would be off, the way a song is off when a singer has changed the note at the last instant.

I only asked him about it once. I was about twenty. We were on the back porch of his house off Esplanade in the spring of 1964, and the canal was running high after a rain, and the smell of the river was thick in the air. I said, “Mr.

Theot, why do you do that? ” He said, “Do what? ” I said, “That pause. ” He looked at me.

He looked at me for a long time. His eyes were a faded blue. His hands were folded in his lap. He had a small spot of pipe ash on his vest.

He said, “Son, you are very observant. Don’t ever ask me about it again. ” I never did. He told me the story two years later, on a warm evening in the spring of 1966, when the windows were open and the smell of river water came in off the canal.

And he stopped in the middle of a sentence about something else entirely, and he said, “You know, I never told anybody this. ” And then he told me all of it the way I have told it to you, only slower, with longer pauses, with the bag pressed against his chest under his shirt the whole time. He told it to me from beginning to end, and when he was finished, it was almost morning, and the canal was quiet, and the smell of riverwater had gone. He died two years after that, quiet in his sleep.

His wife found him in the morning with his hand at his chest, holding the cloth bags through his shirt, and she did not understand it, and she did not ask anyone what it meant, because she was a woman who had been married to a quiet man for forty years, and she had learned the shape of his silences, and she knew which ones were not to be opened. She buried him with the bags. I think about that sometimes. I think about a man holding two small bags of herbs against his chest for forty years, the way a sailor holds a coin from the country he came from, the way a soldier holds a letter, the way you hold something that you do not believe in exactly, but that you cannot put down because the day you put it down might be the day you needed it.

I think about a woman in a gray dress on a sinking porch telling a young man to leave, please, because she had decided a long time ago to stay. I think about the Sink out there past the city, still there, full of slow brown water, joined to the river by a narrow channel, and the river running past the city, and the city drinking from the river, and the lid that is sometimes on and sometimes off. And how no one alive remembers anymore that the lid was ever a lid. I do not know what was in that well.

Octave did not know either. He only knew what the woman told him, and the woman told him only as much as he needed to leave. The rest she kept. She kept it the way she had kept it for sixty years before he ever rode down that road, and the way I think she is keeping it still, somewhere under the slow brown water, in a house that is not there anymore, with the porch creaking in its slow rhythm and her hand on the doorframe and her bare feet on the boards, waiting for the next man the parish sends, because the parish always sends another man eventually.

I went down there once in the summer of 1971, three years after he died. I borrowed a small boat from a man in Belshassier, and I pulled it out into the channel that joined the Sink to the river. The water was still. There were no birds.

There were no insects. The air smelled of wet stone. I sat in the boat for an hour. I did not say anything.

I had remembered the old man’s rule. After an hour, I felt something move under the boat. Not a fish. Not a current.

Something larger. Something with intent. I pulled back to the channel, and I rode back to Belshassier, and I gave the man back his boat, and I drove home, and I have not been back. I have not said the name of that place out loud since.

I am not saying it now. You will notice I have not said it in this whole story. I have called it Bend 17, which is what the parish board called it. But the parish board is gone, and the bend is gone.

And the name the old folks used, I have not said. I will not say it. Not to you, not to anyone.
