content_text:
In a Connecticut field in 1999, a woman in a nightdress watched her Georgian country house burn to the ground. She was forty-seven years old, and she had nothing left to grab. Only six years earlier, she had been the most photographed hostess in New York, the wife of the most feared man on Wall Street, the queen of nouveau society, mistress of a sixteen-room duplex on Park Avenue, three Manet paintings, her own fashion house, and the presidency of the Council of Fashion Designers of America. Then came a quiet divorce, a new wife on his arm, and a slow, deliberate erasure of her name from every guest list she had once written.

This is the story of Caroline Roehm, the woman who built the most beautiful room in 1980s America, and who learned the moment her husband closed the checkbook that none of it had ever belonged to her. Jane Smith was born in a Missouri town so small that the social rules she would later master in New York might as well have come from another planet. The town was Kirksville, set in the rolling farm country of the northeastern corner of the state, two hundred miles north of St. Louis.

In 1951, the year of her birth, it held perhaps fifteen thousand people. Her father was the principal of the local high school. Her mother was a school teacher. The house was small, the income steady, and the view from the front porch ran to soybeans.

She was an only child, and from a very early age she behaved as if she had been born into the wrong picture. She drew dresses on the backs of envelopes. She cut clothes for her dolls from leftover dressmaking scraps. She watched television and noticed in the way only a certain kind of child notices that the women on the screen moved their hands differently from the women in her mother’s bridge group.

By twelve, she had taught herself to sew on her mother’s old Singer. By sixteen, she was making her own prom dresses. Her mother would later remember her as a girl who never wanted to be told what to wear. She also studied.

The school teacher’s daughter earned the grades, wrote the essays, and read the magazines that came in the mail. The magazine she read most carefully was Vogue. Her mother bought it occasionally and saved the copies. Jane read each issue several times, and what she was reading was not the fashion.

She was reading the captions. She was reading the names. She was studying who was photographed at which gala in which dress, and who was standing next to whom in the small black-and-white pictures at the back of the magazine. Before she could afford a single ticket of admission, she was learning the map of a world she intended to enter.

She left Kirksville for Washington University in St. Louis, where she enrolled in the fashion design program, graduating in 1973 with a bachelor of fine arts. The diploma, by the standards of the world she planned to walk into, was almost meaningless. The girls she would compete with had degrees from Vassar and Sweet Briar and Smith, or no degrees at all because their fathers had Whitney money and they did not need them.

She had a diploma from a Midwestern university and $300 in savings. She bought a one-way ticket to New York. She arrived in Manhattan in the autumn of 1973, found a sublet on the East Side whose rent she could barely make, and talked her way into an interview at the Koos van den Akker studio. She worked there for a few months.

Then, through the kind of doggedness the Vogue captions had not warned her about, she found her way to Oscar de la Renta’s studio. She was hired in 1974 as an assistant designer. She was twenty-three years old. Around the same time, she married a young man named Axel Roehm, a member of the Roehm family of Darmstadt, the German chemical dynasty behind the company that bore the same name.

The marriage was short, never publicly explained in detail, and ended in divorce inside a few years. Jane Smith of Kirksville, Missouri, walked out of it with a hyphenless German surname that sounded like an old name in any language. She kept it. By the time the divorce papers were dry, she was no longer Jane Smith.

She was Caroline Roehm. The choice of name was the first signal of who she had decided to become. She was a designer with a European last name and an apprenticeship in the studio of the most important American fashion designer of the 1970s. She rented a small apartment.

She wore Oscar de la Renta samples to events she could not otherwise afford to attend. She learned day by day the codes of the rooms she had only read about in the captions. Oscar de la Renta would later say, in interviews given decades afterward, that she was the most observant assistant he ever had. He meant it not as a comment on her tailoring but as a comment on her social intelligence.

She watched, she copied, she did not embarrass herself. By the end of her ten years in his studio she had made herself fluent in the language of a world she had not been born into, so fluent that almost nobody she met after 1980 would have guessed where she had started. She had taught herself society the way a graduate student teaches herself German: she had memorized the irregular verbs, read the literature, and practiced the accent until she could pass at any embassy dinner. What she had not yet understood, in the autumn of 1980, when she was twenty-nine and at the top of her assistant career, was that fluency in a foreign language is not the same as citizenship.

The natives can still send you home. She met Henry Kravis at a party for very rich men, and within months he had paid for a fashion house bearing her name. The party was, by the most consistent retelling, a charity event in 1984 at which Oscar de la Renta was a sponsor and Caroline Roehm was attending as part of his entourage. Henry Kravis was there escorted by another woman entirely.

Kravis was forty years old. He was already wealthy by any normal measure, and more importantly he was already on the cover of trade magazines as the man who was changing American corporate finance. He stood about five foot six, and he wore his suits with the slightly compressed energy of a man who knew he was the most important person in any room he entered. He did not look like a movie star.

He looked like the person who paid the movie star. He noticed her. The version of the story she has told in interviews over the years is gracious. The version Henry Kravis’s biographers have told is more direct.

He saw a tall, thin, perfectly groomed young woman across the room, asked who she was, was told, and decided that he wanted her. He was at that moment in a complicated position. His first marriage, to a New York woman named Helen Schulman, had ended in 1976, leaving him with two sons. By the standards of his class he had been quietly single for several years.

He was looking, although he would not have said so, for the next wife. The next wife had to be presentable in any social setting his business now required. She had to be photogenic. She had to be ambitious enough to manage the role and submissive enough to accept it.

Caroline Roehm was all of those things, and one more: she was a working designer with her own apprenticeship under one of the most respected men in fashion. On paper, she was a near-perfect candidate. They began seeing each other in 1984. They were photographed together at a few events.

The fashion press noticed; the financial press noticed slightly later. By the end of that year the wedding date had been set. They married in 1985. The wedding was small by the standards of nouveau society, held in his Upper East Side apartment and officiated by a judge, with perhaps forty guests.

The bride wore a dress of her own design. The groom wore a dark suit. Photographs were tightly controlled. The press release came out the following morning.

Three years later, GQ magazine, in a retrospective on the great weddings of the twentieth century, would list the Kravis-Roehm marriage alongside the wedding of Prince Charles and Diana Spencer, on the grounds that it had inaugurated a particular kind of American social fame. The comparison was probably overstated at the time and absurdly overstated in retrospect, but it captured something true: the two of them, walking into a room together in 1986 or 1987, were the publicly recognizable face of a new kind of American money. The same year as the wedding, Kravis funded the launch of Caroline Roehm Incorporated. The seed money was, by the most consistent reporting, approximately $20 million.

It was not described in public as seed money. It was described as her business. The press releases said she had founded a fashion house. The trade press said that the famous financier’s new wife had opened a couture line.

The truth, which both of them knew, was that she had been given a sandbox the size of a Midwestern factory and told to play. She did not play. She worked. She designed two full collections a year, personally selected fabrics, sat through fittings, and gave the customers her time.

She built in a few short seasons a customer list of women whose husbands paid for everything they wore. The dresses ranged in price from roughly $2,000 for a simple cocktail piece to $20,000 or more for the embroidered ball gowns the most lavish hostesses required. Bergdorf Goodman carried her. Neiman Marcus carried her.

Saks Fifth Avenue carried her. What no public account at the time mentioned, and what only became visible later in the trade press post-mortems, was that Caroline Roehm Incorporated never operated at a profit. The overheads were enormous. The customer base was tiny.

The press was respectful but cool, and the reviews, when they came, often described her work using a word she came to dislike. The word was “correct. ” Her dresses were correct. They were also, by the rougher reading, what a society wife with $20 million and a mentor named Oscar de la Renta would make.

In 1987 and 1988 they were not the dresses that any other working designer of her generation would have made. They served a single small market, and they served it well. The business burned through her husband’s seed money at a steady rate. He did not seem to mind.

The fashion house was for him a strategic asset of a different kind. It put her name on dresses photographed in Vogue. It put her face in the trade press. It gave him a wife who could be described in the social columns as a designer rather than as a banker’s wife.

In the language his world used in private, it produced optical returns rather than financial ones. The marriage, in the same way, was a strategic asset. He had not bought her with the engagement ring. He had bought her with the $20 million he had put into the company that carried her name.

The price of the marriage in 1985 was approximately what she would have earned in three hundred years as a working assistant at Oscar de la Renta. Neither of them said this aloud. Neither of them needed to. By 1987 she stood under three Manet paintings in a sixteen-room duplex on Park Avenue, and Vogue called it her drawing room.

The address was 740 Park Avenue, an art deco limestone tower at the corner of 71st Street, completed in 1929 and considered by the 1980s the most exclusive cooperative address in Manhattan. The Kravis residence occupied a sixteen-room duplex, almost entirely acquired and redecorated in the two years since the wedding. The decorator was Albert Hadley of Parish-Hadley. The art consultant was a discreet figure from the Wildenstein orbit.

The budget for the project was, by the most reliable contemporary press estimates, somewhere between $15 and $25 million on the apartment alone, not counting the major paintings. Three Manet canvases hung in the principal room. Several Monets and a Renoir were placed throughout the apartment. The dining room held a major John Singer Sargent portrait of a woman in white.

The library held two early Cézannes. The bedroom held a Vuillard. The total value of the paintings in 1987 ran above $100 million. The vast majority were in Kravis’s legal title alone.

The most prominent had been bought through dealers Kravis had retained since the late 1970s. The art consultants did not work for Caroline Roehm. They worked for her husband. She presented the room as if it were hers.

She received guests at the entrance hall and walked them through the long enfilade of public rooms. She paused at each picture and named the artist, the period, the small biographical fact about the painter that made her hosting feel personal rather than recited. She did this several nights a week for years. The room she walked them through was, in retrospect, the single most photographed private interior in New York between 1986 and 1992.

It was published in House & Garden, in Vogue, in Architectural Digest. It appeared on the cover of Town & Country. It appeared in the famous 1988 Vanity Fair photograph by Helmut Newton, behind the Kravises as they posed by the fireplace. In that photograph he wears a dark double-breasted suit; she wears an emerald silk taffeta gown of her own design.

The three Manets are visible above the mantel. He is looking at the camera. She is looking at him. The image was reproduced in glossy magazines on three continents for the following eighteen months.

It fixed the Kravises in the public imagination of the period more than any other image. The room that surrounded them in the photograph was the center of what the writer Tom Wolfe was in real time naming. His novel The Bonfire of the Vanities had come out in 1987, and one of its key inventions had been the figure of the social x-ray: the very rich Manhattan wife of the late 1980s, conspicuously thin, conspicuously dressed, conspicuously hostessing. Wolfe never used Caroline Roehm’s name.

He did not need to. The journalists Liz Smith and Bill Cunningham named her almost weekly. Vanity Fair named her in a long profile in 1988 by Maureen Orth that included the words “steel magnolia” in the title. The phrase entered her press identity and never left.

The pattern of her week was as photographed as the room. On Monday she lunched at La Grenouille or CIRCA. On Tuesday she met fabric suppliers at her studio on West 37th Street. On Wednesday she hosted a charity board meeting at the apartment.

On Thursday she dressed for the night’s event. On Friday she or her husband flew to Connecticut. The country house was Weatherstone, a 1765 Georgian mansion on roughly sixty acres in Sharon, in the far northwest corner of the state, bought by Kravis and converted into a country house for the marriage. The gardens, at her insistence, ran to several walled rooms with seasonal beds modeled on English garden plans she had been studying for years.

The pace of her hostessing during this peak was relentless. Conservative reconstructions from the social columns of the period suggest that she planned somewhere between eighty and 120 private dinners a year, plus another twenty to forty charity events at which she was the hostess of record. Each dinner required a seating chart. Each seating chart was discussed in advance with her husband, who specified which deal partners and which museum trustees were to be placed where.

Each dinner required a menu approved several days in advance, and flowers. The flowers, more than any other element, were Caroline Roehm’s particular signature. They were never small. They were never neutral.

They were enormous masses of seasonal blooms arranged at scale across the center of the table. For the 1988 Metropolitan Museum Gala she chaired, which the New York Times described as one of the most lavish private dinners ever held inside the museum, the flowers totaled, by her own later count, more than three thousand cut stems. Each guest had an individual hand-painted menu. Each place card was scented.

Each napkin was monogrammed. The dress she wore that night, the strapless emerald taffeta of her own design, was photographed for the cover of Town & Country the following month. She was at the absolute peak of what she had set out to do. She was the most photographed hostess in New York.

She was the president of the CFDA. She was the wife of the most famous private equity figure in America. She was thirty-seven years old. Her face appeared on the social pages every week.

Her dresses were carried in the most expensive stores in the country. Her dinners were the dinners the social columns described as the dinners. And not a single object in the room where she received her guests was registered in her name. The dresses she designed were carried by Bergdorf Goodman, photographed in Vogue, and quietly costing her husband $16 million over six years.

The mechanics of Caroline Roehm Incorporated were only honestly described in the trade press post-mortems that came after the company closed. While it was operating, the press treated it the way it treated every other socially adjacent fashion house: respectfully, and at a slight polite remove from the question of profit and loss. The numbers, when reconstructed from later reporting, told a consistent story. The company was launched in 1985 with approximately $20 million in startup capital from Henry Kravis.

The studio was a Midtown loft on West 37th Street. The staff peaked at approximately thirty-five employees. Two collections were produced each year, plus a smaller resort collection and a custom bridal capability. The dresses were priced from roughly $2,000 at the entry end to $20,000 and above for the top embroidered evening pieces.

Wholesale revenue was carried by Bergdorf Goodman, Neiman Marcus, Saks Fifth Avenue, and a small number of specialty boutiques in Palm Beach, Beverly Hills, and Dallas. The revenue model never balanced. The dresses required couture-grade construction. The fabrics ran to silk taffeta, silk satin, silk velvet, lace from Calais, and embroideries from Lesage in Paris.

The cost of goods on a single embroidered evening gown ran, by reasonable reconstruction, to between $4,000 and $7,000 before any overhead. The wholesale price recovered the cost of goods and a small margin. The overhead, including the studio, the staff, the showroom, the runway shows twice a year, the lookbook photography, and the press relations, ran to several million dollars annually. The customer base, the women who paid the full retail price, numbered probably no more than three hundred globally.

They were the hostesses Caroline Roehm herself socialized with: Susan Gutfreund, Mercedes Bass, Anne Bass, Pat Buckley, Blaine Trump, a handful of Texan and Californian wives, and two or three royal customers from the Middle East. Three hundred customers each buying perhaps four or five pieces a year at an average retail price of seven or eight thousand dollars generated, at full sell-through, approximately $10 million in retail revenue annually. The wholesale share of that, after the stores took their margin, was perhaps four to five million. The overhead and cost of goods together ran ahead of it.

The company lost money every year of its life, and the losses were absorbed by Henry Kravis. By the spring of 1991, when she would later announce the closure, the cumulative losses since founding ran, by the most consistent reporting, to between $15 and $20 million. Kravis’s $20 million seed had been almost entirely consumed. He did not appear to care.

The fashion house was for him a long advertisement for the wife rather than a business expected to clear its overhead. He had paid more than that for other forms of social positioning in the late 1980s. The art collection had cost more than five times the fashion house losses. The duplex had cost three times.

The buyout retainers, the political donations, and the philanthropic commitments together were a multiple of the fashion house losses in any given year. For Caroline Roehm, the experience inside the building she worked in five days a week was significantly less serene than the photographs in Vogue suggested. She was the founder of a money-losing business that her husband was funding, and simultaneously the president of the trade association that judged her work. Several designers of her generation, including Donna Karan, Calvin Klein, and Ralph Lauren, were running profitable houses of vastly larger scale.

The trade press never said in print that Caroline Roehm was a kept designer. It did note, in occasional asides, that her staff were paid above industry standard, that the shows were more expensive than they needed to be, and that the press packets were the most elaborate in New York. The implication was clear enough to anyone who could read between the lines. She felt the implication.

The interviews she gave in 1988, 1989, and 1990 contain a consistent low note of defensiveness. She insisted that she designed the dresses herself. She insisted that the company would in time become independently profitable. She insisted that she had not married Henry Kravis to start a fashion house, and that she had been working in fashion before she met him.

All of these things were true. None of them mattered. The world she was speaking to had already decided what she was, and the world she was speaking to was paid for by her husband. She worked harder.

She was at the studio by nine in the morning and did not leave before seven in the evening on the days when she was not flying somewhere. She personally cut some of the patterns. She personally approved every fitting. She brought her assistants and seamstresses small Christmas gifts she had wrapped herself.

She gave interviews to small magazines as readily as to Vogue. She showed up at the trade events. She paid her bills on time. The harder she worked, the more visible the loss became.

The Vogue spreads were beautiful. The reviews from the New York Times were polite. The press packets were the most elaborate in the industry. The customer base did not grow.

The press did not become enthusiastic. The reviewers continued to use the word “correct. ” She had built by the end of 1990 the most carefully made wardrobe in the social x-ray world and the most expensive fashion experiment in the country, both running on her husband’s account. She had also, in the same period, built something else that the photographers did not photograph: the only piece of her life that she was actually doing herself.

She designed the dresses. She made the calls. She ran the meetings. She read the receivables.

She knew the seamstresses by name, the embroidery houses in Paris by name, the silk mills in Como by name. When the company closed, that too would go. In 1989, she became president of the CFDA, and the same season Henry Kravis closed the largest buyout in American history. The Council of Fashion Designers of America was the trade body that organized the official American fashion calendar, ran the most important industry awards, and represented American designers in policy and trade discussions.

It had been founded in 1962 by the publicist Eleanor Lambert. Its presidents since founding had included Bill Blass, Oscar de la Renta, and Mary McFadden. The presidency was not paid. It was a marker of status, decided by a unanimous board vote conducted in private and announced as an accomplished fact.

In January of 1989, the board unanimously elected Caroline Roehm to succeed Oscar de la Renta. She was thirty-seven years old, the youngest president the organization had had, and almost certainly the least commercially successful designer the organization had elected to its top role. The election was understood within the industry accurately as a transfer of patronage from de la Renta to his most prominent former assistant, and as a recognition that the CFDA needed access to her husband’s circle of donors more than it needed her résumé. She did not waste the role.

She brought the CFDA’s fundraising relationship with AIDS research, which had begun in a small way in the mid-1980s, to a vastly larger scale. She personally raised in her first year as president more than $4 million for the research foundations the CFDA was supporting. She organized black-tie events at which her own husband and her own circle of friends were the seat holders. She brought designers and donors into conversations that had not previously included one another.

In interviews of the period she gave the AIDS fundraising work the most personal language she ever used in public. She did not consistently moralize it. She named names of designers who had died. The same season she was running the CFDA, her husband was running the largest corporate deal in American history.

The RJR Nabisco buyout had begun in October of 1988 when the company’s chief executive, Ross Johnson, proposed taking the company private for around $17 billion. KKR entered the bidding within days. The contest ran through November with multiple bidders and a constant churn of investment banks, attorneys, and journalists. It closed on the 30th of November 1988 with a winning bid from KKR of approximately $25 billion.

It was the largest leveraged buyout in history, and would not be matched in real dollar terms for another seventeen years. By the start of 1989, Henry Kravis was on the cover of Time, on the cover of Forbes, and in the lead of the business sections of every newspaper in the country. The deal had made him, on paper, a billionaire, and in cultural memory the personification of a particular kind of 1980s American capitalism. The journalists Bryan Burrough and John Helyar were already at work on the book that would the following year name the era.

Barbarians at the Gate would be published in 1990, would sell more than half a million copies in hardcover, and would fix Henry Kravis in the public mind for the rest of the century. Caroline Roehm in the same season was hosting the Metropolitan Museum Gala. The gala fell in the spring of 1989. She chaired the dinner, chose the menu, designed the place settings, wrote the seating chart, and approved the floral arrangements.

She wore that night a black silk velvet evening gown of her own design, set off by a single emerald necklace borrowed from a Bond Street jeweler for the night. The photographers placed her on every list of the most photographed women of the season. The marriage was that season operating on two of the largest cultural stages in the country at the same time. He had built the largest deal.

She had built the largest dinner. The press treated them as a single phenomenon. The phrase “nouveau society” had not yet acquired its later, slightly contemptuous edge. The phrase “the new establishment,” used in a TIME piece of the period, captured the thing the Kravises were taken to embody.

They were the new establishment. They were what the new American money looked like when it dressed for dinner. What neither of them said in public, and what both of them knew in private, was that they were not the same kind of operator. He had built the largest deal because he had a partner who would walk away from the table if the numbers did not work, a team of fifteen who could pressure target boards by reflex, and a willingness ultimately to spend other people’s money to acquire other people’s companies.

She had built the largest dinner because she had hired the right florist and the right calligrapher. The dinner produced no return except photographs. The deal produced billions of dollars of carried interest over the following decade. In financial terms, his work was the work.

In social terms, her work was the work. The asymmetry between those two definitions of work would not begin to cost her until the social term stopped being valued. She did not that season see it coming. In the months after the gala and the buyout closure, she gave several long interviews to magazines about the future of American fashion.

She spoke about supporting young designers, about AIDS fundraising, about whether American fashion could become a global force at the scale of Parisian or Italian fashion. She did not speak about her own marriage. She did not speak about her husband’s deal. She was disciplined.

She also did not yet know that the social x-ray world was about to begin a slow contraction. The crash of October 1987 had bruised certain fortunes, but not the Kravis fortune. The recession of 1990 would bruise more of them. The press, which had treated the social x-ray world as glamorous, would begin to treat it as something else.

Tom Wolfe’s novel had crystallized one kind of judgment. The Burrough and Helyar book about her husband’s signature deal would crystallize another. By the time both books had finished their cultural work, the world she had spent fifteen years learning to enter would be on its way out of fashion. She had less than two years left at the peak.

On the Fourth of July weekend in 1991, Henry Kravis’s nineteen-year-old son was killed in a car wreck in Boulder, and inside two months her fashion house was closed. The son was Harrison Kravis, the elder of the two children Henry Kravis had had with his first wife, Helen Schulman. He had been born in 1971, a quiet boy by every account, gentle, more interested in books and music than in his father’s deals. He had enrolled at the University of Colorado at Boulder, and was a student there in the summer of 1991.

On the night of the 3rd of July, he was a passenger in a car driven by a friend on a road in Boulder County. The car left the road. The friend survived. Harrison did not.

He was nineteen years old, pronounced dead at the scene. Henry Kravis received the call in New York, flew to Colorado the same day, and returned with the body. The funeral was small and private, the press kept at a distance, and the Kravis household at every address fell silent for weeks. Caroline Roehm has spoken, in the very small number of interviews in which she has discussed this period, with a real grief that is not stylized.

She did not have a biological relationship with Harrison. She had, in her own description, tried to build a stepmother’s relationship over the six years of her marriage to his father. The relationship had been complicated, as such relationships often are, between a young second wife and a teenage son. She had, by her own account, been fond of him, though not close to him in the way his mother was.

She also had not been a stranger to him. The death broke something in her household that did not repair itself. It also broke something in Henry Kravis. Friends of the period reported that he became for a season a different man.

He canceled travel. He did not appear at the office for several weeks. He spent unbroken time at home for the first time in the marriage. He grieved publicly, speaking about Harrison in language he had previously reserved for closing dinners.

In that household, in the middle of that grief, Caroline Roehm made the decision to close her fashion house. The closure was announced on the 10th of September 1991, two months after Harrison’s death, in a press release that was tightly written and composed entirely of a single argument: in light of the recent family loss, she could not in good conscience continue with the planned expansion of her business, which had included a contemplated production agreement with a Paris manufacturer. She would therefore wind down the operations of Caroline Roehm Incorporated effective immediately, and devote herself to her family. She thanked her staff, her customers, Bergdorf Goodman, Neiman Marcus, and Saks Fifth Avenue.

The press release was gracious and short. It was reported in the New York Times the following day as the end of a fashion fairy tale. The trade press, more honestly, noted that the company had been operating at a loss for several years, and that the death of Harrison Kravis had provided a face-saving public reason for what had become a commercially necessary closure. Both readings were true.

The financial truth and the human truth were not in competition. They sat side by side. The death of the stepson was real. The losses were real.

The decision was real. The press release was a frame placed over all three. What the press release did not say, but what is now visible from the outside, was that the decision to close ended Caroline Roehm’s only piece of independent professional identity. The fashion house had been the only thing in her life that was not owned in legal title by her husband.

Even at a loss, it had been the only piece of the architecture that listed her as the responsible party. The staff worked for her. The customers met with her. The reviews named her.

The shows were hers. The closure took all of that away. What was left on the morning of the 11th of September 1991 was a thirty-nine-year-old woman with a famous husband, a Park Avenue apartment in her husband’s name, a country house in her husband’s name, a wardrobe paid for by her husband, and no studio to go to in the morning. In the language of corporate restructuring her husband used in his own office, she had become a non-operating asset.

The household was still extensive, still photographed, still hosting. But the woman at its center no longer made anything that did not exist to serve the household. For a marriage where the wife had been valued in part for her independent productivity, this was a structural change. For a husband who treated his life as a portfolio, the change registered.

It did not register on the day of the announcement, or that autumn, or in any way Caroline Roehm could see for another full year. But in the years afterward, when the Manhattan press reconstructed the chronology of the breakdown of the marriage, the closure of the fashion house in September 1991 was the moment always identified as the structural turn. Up to that moment, she had been the working wife of the dealmaker. After that moment, she was the social wife of the dealmaker.

And the social wife of the dealmaker was a position with a known shelf life. While Roehm was in mourning beside her husband, a quiet woman with a Hudson Institute fellowship was already in the next room. Marie-Josée Drouin had been on Henry Kravis’s professional periphery for several years before she became central to his personal life. She was born in Ottawa, Canada, and earned a master’s degree in economics from the University of Ottawa in 1970.

She joined the Hudson Institute in 1973 at the age of twenty-three, the youngest senior fellow in the organization’s history at that time. The Hudson Institute was a center-right policy think tank founded by Herman Kahn, studying long-range strategic and economic questions, publishing the kind of papers that members of corporate boards read on airplanes. Drouin specialized in economic policy and competitiveness. She wrote a regular column for Les Affaires in Montreal, a column for the Montreal Gazette, and occasionally for the Wall Street Journal.

She hosted a weekly television show in Ontario. By the late 1970s she was a public intellectual of a kind that Canada produced more of than the United States, widely read in the boardrooms of Toronto and Montreal, and by the early 1980s a board member or frequent speaker at a number of American institutions. Henry Kravis joined the board of the Hudson Institute in the early 1980s, serving as a donor, an outside director, and a presence at the institute’s annual donor dinners. Marie-Josée Drouin was at those dinners as a senior fellow.

They knew each other professionally for a decade before there was any private connection between them. The professional relationship was, by every contemporary account, entirely correct. What was happening slowly and almost invisibly, to Caroline Roehm and to the New York social press, was a cultural shift in what the very rich of the country considered the marker of seriousness. Through the 1980s, the gala society world had been the public face of upper-class life: the Costume Institute ball, the Library Lions dinner, the Winter Antiques Show, the Save Venice gala.

These were the dinners that defined a person as inside the world. The press covered them. The wives ran them. By the early 1990s, that began to change.

Museum boards became more important than gala chairs. Policy institute fellowships became more important than charity board memberships. University trustee seats became more important than the seating charts at La Grenouille. The men in the leveraged-buyout class who had spent the late 1980s cultivating the social x-ray world began to spend the early 1990s cultivating the museum and university board world instead.

They were almost without exception looking to acquire reputational durability that the gala world had not been able to give them. Caroline Roehm could not give her husband that next layer of credibility. She had built her identity entirely inside the gala world. She had a CFDA presidency, a fashion house now closed, a Vogue cover history.

She did not have an economics degree. She did not have a Hudson Institute fellowship. She did not have a board seat at the Museum of Modern Art. She did not have a New York Times opinion piece.

She had a beautifully decorated apartment. Marie-Josée Drouin had the other set of credentials: the fellowship, the columns, the television show, the academic profile, and, more importantly, the capacity to walk into a museum board meeting or a foreign policy dinner and contribute substance to the conversation. She was, in the precise language of his world, the next wife. The timeline of the personal relationship has never been publicly itemized.

Caroline Roehm has never spoken about it on the record. Henry Kravis has never spoken about it on the record. Marie-Josée Kravis has never spoken about it on the record. The press reconstruction is partial.

What is known is this: Kravis and Drouin had served on the Hudson Institute board together throughout the 1980s, with a professional friendship over many years. By 1992, that friendship had become, by the accounts of mutual friends to magazine writers, something more than professional. By the early months of 1993, the separation from Caroline Roehm was being negotiated in private. By the autumn of 1993, the divorce was final.

By the early months of 1994, Kravis and Drouin were married. The compression of the timeline tells its own story. The marriage to Caroline Roehm ended, and the marriage to Marie-Josée Drouin began inside a single span of months. There was no public waiting period, no extended single life in between.

The portfolio rebalance, to use the language his world used, was clean. It was also, for the woman being rebalanced out, a quiet and very fast end. The press called the divorce friendly, but a friendly divorce in 1993 meant exactly what it had always meant in this set: that the wife had agreed not to publicly fight. The Kravis-Roehm separation was announced quietly through the social columns in the first months of 1993.

The divorce was finalized later the same year. The settlement terms have never been publicly itemized. Both parties signed mutual non-disclosure agreements. The press releases from both sides used a near-identical and very brief language: they had decided, after eight years of marriage, to part on friendly terms.

They wished each other well. They asked the press to respect their privacy. The press largely complied. Liz Smith mentioned the separation in a single sentence in her column.

Vanity Fair did not publish a long take. Vogue did not. Town & Country did not. The trade press of fashion noted the separation as a footnote to coverage of the closed Caroline Roehm fashion house.

The financial press noted it as a footnote to coverage of Henry Kravis’s continuing buyouts. The privacy of the divorce was an engineered product. The settlement included, as such settlements often did in that set, an agreement to not discuss the terms or the circumstances. Caroline Roehm signed it.

She did so for a reason that was on its face sensible. She did not have the capital to fight a public divorce against her husband. She had a fashion house that had closed at a loss. She had no separate fortune.

She had a husband whose net worth had been estimated in the financial press in 1992 at over $500 million in personal holdings, and considerably more in carried interest in partnership stakes at KKR. The asymmetry of resources was total. A public divorce trial would have been a financial and reputational disaster for her and a survivable embarrassment for him. The settlement she signed traded the right to fight in public for a guarantee of a particular kind of future.

She would keep Weatherstone. She would receive a financial settlement that, while never publicly disclosed, was widely understood in the small world that knew to be in the low to mid-eight figures. She would receive a continuation of her health insurance. She would not be barred from continuing to use her name professionally, or from using her social contacts.

In exchange, she would not speak. She did not speak. What she lost in the settlement was, by inference from later visible facts, very large. She did not keep 740 Park Avenue; the apartment remained in Kravis’s name and was eventually sold or transferred.

She did not keep the three Manet paintings, the Sargent, the major French furniture, or the principal jewelry collection. She did not keep the corporate jet access. She did not keep, by the autumn of 1993, the membership at the Knickerbocker Club, the Maidstone Club, or the box at the Metropolitan Opera, all maintained by her husband’s accounts. She kept the country house, the financial settlement, her dogs, her name, and her clothes.

She was thirty-nine years old. The settlement allowed her, by the most reasonable later calculation, to live for the rest of her life as a wealthy upper-class American woman with a beautiful country house. It did not allow her to live as the wife of a billionaire. The order of magnitude difference between those two lives is not always intuitive to people outside the very top of American wealth.

A wealthy upper-class American woman in 1993 with eight or twelve million could maintain a sixty-acre country house, three or four staff, a car, several flights to Europe a year, and a comfortable retirement. The wife of a billionaire could maintain all of that and an additional sixteen or twenty million of variable spending a year, plus access to private aircraft, plus access to philanthropic capital with which to chair charity galas, plus a household staff that ran at twenty or thirty people. She had gone from the second tier of those two lives to the first. This was, in the published voice of the period, the kindest possible divorce a New York wife of her position could have hoped for.

It was a generous and humane exit on civil terms. It was, in the unpublished voice, an exit. She was, by the standards of the world she had walked into in 1984, no longer of the place. The duplex on Park Avenue had been the center of her life; it was no longer the center of her life.

The dinners at the Metropolitan Museum had been her stage; it was no longer her stage. The walls hung with Manets and Monets were no longer hers to walk her guests past. She moved her things out quietly. She did not give a long interview.

She did not write a memoir about the marriage in 1993, or 1994, or in any of the decades that followed. She has to this day not publicly discussed the divorce in any detail. In her silence, Henry Kravis married Marie-Josée Drouin in 1994. The wedding was small, reported as a footnote in the business press.

The Manhattan social columns very politely transferred their language about the senior Mrs. Kravis from Caroline Roehm to Marie-Josée Drouin within the same twelve months. The hostesses she had counted as friends quietly transferred their dinner invitations. Within a year in the social diary of New York, she did not exist.

The mechanics of being dropped in the New York social world have been documented many times in the post-mortem literature of the period. A divorce in the very small set Caroline Roehm had been at the center of triggers an immediate informal receding across all of the social calendars she had been on. The dinner invitations she had been receiving for the autumn season do not get renewed for the following spring. The reasons given, when reasons are given at all, are gentle and apparently logistical.

The hostess has decided to keep the dinner smaller this year. The seating chart has been reduced from twelve to ten. The chair on the gala dinner is taken by someone whose husband has just made a larger pledge. The board seat is up for rotation.

None of the reasons are stated as what they actually are. What they actually are is that the wife is no longer in residence on the senior wife’s side of the marriage that the table was built around. The new wife, by contrast, enters the same calendar at the same level. Marie-Josée Drouin Kravis was placed within a few months of the wedding at the senior tables at the same charity events Caroline Roehm had previously chaired.

She was placed at the central dinners at the Museum of Modern Art, where she was already a board member and where she would in time become chair. She was placed at the Library Lions dinner. She was placed at the Costume Institute ball. The seating charts that had held Caroline Roehm now held Marie-Josée Drouin Kravis.

The reassignment was, in the same gentle, apparently logistical language, complete inside twelve months. The women who had been Caroline Roehm’s social peers were not, by any reading available to her, cruel to her in this period. They were, in the language of the world, polite. They did not invite her to the dinners.

They did not cut her in public. They did not write about her unkindly. They simply, with the same coordinated muscle memory the set used in every previous divorce, moved their attention. The few invitations that did come during the first months of 1994 were to events of lower social ranking.

Smaller hostesses called. A few designer friends called. Oscar de la Renta, by every account, was constant in his loyalty. He continued to invite her, to seat her, to call her in private.

He was an exception, a man and an industry mentor not interested in the wartime logic of the senior wife transition. He was also one of perhaps four or five people in the original Roehm-Kravis circle who behaved that way after the divorce. The press in the same months made the same transition. The New York Times social column began to refer to Marie-Josée Drouin Kravis as the wife of Henry Kravis without further qualification.

Town & Country profiled her. Vanity Fair profiled her. The cover image of the Kravises by the fireplace, the famous 1988 Helmut Newton photograph, slipped out of regular rotation in the magazine retrospectives. The new image, taken at a Museum of Modern Art event, became the iconic Kravis photograph for the new chapter.

In it, Henry Kravis stands beside Marie-Josée Drouin, who wears a dark suit and small pearl earrings. The image is sober, professional, museum-board appropriate. It is the image of a different kind of marriage. Caroline Roehm in the same period made no public counter-move.

She did not give an interview about the divorce. She did not appear at the social events to which she was not invited. She did not publish a memoir. She did not pursue a lawsuit.

She did not engage a publicist to defend her position. She did, in the quiet phrasing she has used since, move on with her life. What moving on with her life looked like in the practical sense was retreat to Weatherstone. She spent the autumn of 1993 and the winter of 1994 primarily in Connecticut.

She gardened. She entertained quietly at smaller dinners with old friends from outside the inner New York set. She began work on what would become her first published book, A Passion for Flowers, eventually published by HarperCollins in 1997. She accepted in herself the structural fact that the world she had spent fifteen years entering would not have her back.

What she had not yet seen, but what was already true by the spring of 1994, was that the position she had constructed had not survived her. The architecture had collapsed when its sole structural support, the marriage, had been removed. The dinners she had hosted were now being hosted by Marie-Josée Drouin Kravis. The flowers she had arranged were now being arranged for Marie-Josée Drouin Kravis.

The dresses she had designed were no longer being designed at all. The CFDA presidency was now in the hands of her successor. The face of nouveau society was no longer her face. The accuracy of the displacement was almost mathematical.

There was no remaining variable for which she was the answer. She had been the public face of one kind of capital. The capital had been redirected. The face had been changed accordingly.

She turned, with the discipline she had taught herself by reading Vogue captions at twelve, toward the only resource she had left in her own name. She turned toward the country house. She turned toward the garden. She turned toward the books.

She turned toward Weatherstone. She had always loved Weatherstone more than the city. She kept it in the divorce and went there to learn what she still owned. The house sat at the end of a long private drive off a quiet road in Sharon, Connecticut, in the foothills of the Berkshires, two hours north of New York City.

Built in 1765, it was a Georgian frame structure with a center-hall plan, low ceilings, and a wide front porch. Around it sat roughly sixty acres of meadow, orchard, walled garden, and pond. The original property had been bought by Henry Kravis in the late 1970s and converted into a country house for the marriage in the mid-1980s. Caroline Roehm had spent every season since then refining the gardens.

In the settlement, Weatherstone was hers. Her decision to make Weatherstone the center of her life was not gradual. It was nearly immediate. She had stopped giving Manhattan dinners by the end of 1993.

She had given up the city apartment where she had once received guests, taking a smaller pied-à-terre on Park Avenue for the nights she still wanted to be in town. She moved her books, her flowers, her dogs, and her clothing to the country. She built her days around the garden. She replanted the walled garden several times in the first three years, settling on a design that combined an English mixed border with a more disciplined parterre.

She built a kitchen garden and a cutting garden, so that the flower arrangements once bought from the most expensive florist in Midtown could now be cut by her own hand. She began photographing the garden. She began writing about it. A Passion for Flowers was published in 1997.

It was a hardcover from HarperCollins, containing 250 photographs. It described the gardens at Weatherstone and taught the reader to make a bouquet by season and by feel. It was reviewed politely. It sold well, particularly to a readership of upper-middle-class American women who had watched Caroline Roehm in Vogue in the late 1980s and now wished to know how to fold their napkins the way she had folded hers.

She had begun, very quietly, to build the next thing. The next thing was small. The next thing was real. The next thing was hers.

She also, in the same period, began to articulate a private theory of taste that the galas had not let her speak. The theory was that beauty did not have to be expensive to be useful. The flowers in her cutting garden came from heirloom seeds. The fabrics in her Weatherstone rooms were chintzes she had been collecting for years.

The furniture was a mix of inherited family pieces and pieces she had bought herself at country auctions in Litchfield and the Hudson Valley. The theory was a quiet rejection of the social x-ray world she had been the public face of: that one could live beautifully without being the wife of a billionaire. She did not say this aloud as a polemic. She said it in the form of arrangements of zinnias and dahlias in a milk pitcher on a kitchen table, photographed for her books.

The polemic was visible to anyone who could read pictures. The dogs throughout this period were a continuous presence. She kept dachshunds and small terriers. She named them, photographed them, placed them on the kitchen sofa beside the cutting tables.

They served in the slow construction of her new authorial identity the same role the spaniels of Edwardian English country writers had served: the visible companions of a woman who was no longer married. They were also, by themselves, a small and self-contained social world. The dogs did not require a seating chart. She did not remarry.

She did not pursue another rich husband. She did not, in any of the interviews she has given over the following decades, speak about the possibility of a second marriage as a particular goal. She built, very quietly, a single life. The single life was at Weatherstone, involving books, gardens, dogs, and the slow construction of a publishing brand around her own first name.

By the end of the 1990s she had published two more books. She had begun a small business in branded scented candles and floral-arranging supplies. She had started a website. She had developed a regular readership through a quietly maintained mailing list.

The Manhattan social columns by then had stopped writing about her almost entirely. Vogue had moved on to a new generation of hostesses. Architectural Digest, when it covered her at all, covered her as a garden writer rather than as a society wife. She had become, by approximately 1998, a different person from the person who had stood under three Manets in 1987.

The new person owned her own house. The new person earned her own income from her own books. The new person was, in a strict accounting sense, not displaced by anyone, because the new person was not in a position from which displacement was possible. It was, by every reasonable reading, the first time in her adult life she had been her own employer.

In 1999, an electrical fire ate the Weatherstone house she had loved more than her marriage, and she watched it from the lawn in her nightdress. The fire started, by the report of the fire marshal, in the wiring of the upper east wing of the original 1765 house, in the early hours of the morning. By the time the smoke detectors in the bedroom wing woke her, the fire had already taken most of the upper floor. She got out of the house.

She got the dogs out of the house. She did not get out the books, the photographs, the dresses, or the small collection of objects she had brought with her from the Kravis years and kept on shelves in a sitting room. She stood in the field in her nightdress and watched the original house disappear. The fire department from Sharon arrived, then the fire from Cornwall, then the fire from Lakeville.

By dawn, the house was a stone foundation with a chimney standing in the middle of it. The garden, on the other side of the lawn, was untouched. The greenhouse fifty yards away was untouched. The barn was untouched.

The house itself, the only original building on the property, was gone. She did not weep on camera. The press did not photograph her on the lawn. In those hours of the morning of the fire, she was far enough from any reporter that the moment was hers alone.

The press got the story later. She gave a short statement. She thanked the fire crews. She said she would rebuild.

She did. The decision to rebuild was made within weeks. She hired the architect Christian Sander to design the new house, and gave him a brief that was, by every report from people who worked on the project, unusually decisive. She wanted a pure Georgian house in the style of the original, but with the proportions she had always wished the original had had.

She wanted higher ceilings. She wanted a two-story great room as the central feature, where the visitor walked in and looked straight up into the volume of the building. She wanted a kitchen large enough for her cooking and a study large enough for her writing. She wanted, in essence, a house designed for her by her.

The new Weatherstone was completed in 2001. The construction was photographed and processed for House & Garden and Architectural Digest. The finished house was photographed for both magazines and for her own books. The press described it as a magisterial reinvention of an American Georgian.

It was also, more importantly to her, the first house she had ever lived in that was hers from the start. She has spoken in interviews about the fire and the rebuild as if it had been, on balance, a freedom. The original house, even in her ownership, had still been a Kravis acquisition. The architectural choices of the original Kravis renovation had not been hers.

The framing of the rooms, the chimney heights, the kitchen layout, the placement of bathrooms had all been the work of decorators commissioned in the early years of the marriage. The fire, by destroying all of that, had freed her to build a house that did not carry the fingerprints of the marriage that had paid for the original purchase. She did not say this in those words. She said something close to it: that the rebuilt house was the first house that felt, on every wall, entirely her own.

The rebuilt house has been the center of her life since. She has lived there for approximately twenty-five years, gardening, writing, photographing, hosting small dinners for friends, keeping her dogs. She has, in interviews, occasionally been asked whether she misses the city. The honest answer she has given in different forms is that she misses certain people.

She does not miss the dinners. She does not miss the seating charts. She does not miss the calendar. She has not missed the apartment on Park Avenue where she once received her guests.

The apartment in the years since the divorce has had at least one other owner. The three Manets have been moved, sold, or rotated through other private collections. The Sargent has been sold. The world she once walked her guests through in that long enfilade of public rooms no longer exists as a single room.

It exists as a memory. Weatherstone exists as a house she can walk through on any morning. She walks through it. She cuts the flowers.

She feeds the dogs. She works on the next book. The field in the nightdress, in retrospect, was the last involuntary moment of her life. From that morning forward, everything in the Weatherstone construction was her decision.

She had been displaced from one architecture. She had built, in middle age, with her own hands, her own settlement money, and her own discipline, a different one. She never remarried, and over the next twenty-five years she wrote eleven books that built, paragraph by paragraph, a life that no husband could repossess. The books came in a steady cadence: A Passion for Flowers in 1997, A Passion for Interiors in 1999, A Passion for Blue and White, A Passion for Parties at Home with Caroline Roehm, Presentations and Flowers, and a small set of more recent volumes on entertaining, gardening, and small luxuries.

The total by the most recent count runs to eleven. They are sold in the better bookstores, on her website, and to a readership that has stayed loyal to her for almost three decades. The voice of the books is consistent. It is not the voice of the Manhattan hostess of 1987.

It is the voice of a Connecticut country writer who knows that readers want to be told what arrangements to make for a Saturday lunch in autumn. It is the voice of a woman who is finished worrying whether the world she is speaking to is the most important world in the country. The voice is calm. The voice is direct.

The voice is hers. The lifestyle brand around the books is small. There are scented candles, sachets, floral-arranging tools, an annual gift guide, a small mailing list. The whole enterprise generates, by all available external indication, a comfortable middle-six-figure income on top of the original divorce settlement.

It does not generate, and has never been intended to generate, the kind of capital that Henry Kravis generates. It generates instead a steady income that belongs to her. In the world she walked out of, the world continued. KKR became one of the largest private equity firms in the world.

Henry Kravis stepped back as co-chief executive in 2021 and remained co-executive chairman. His net worth by the published estimates of the early 2020s ran past $9 billion. Marie-Josée Kravis became in 2005 president of the Museum of Modern Art board and in 2021 the chair of that board. The Marie-Josée and Henry R.

Kravis Foundation became a major American philanthropic vehicle. The couple bought a Hamptons estate on Meadow Lane that had been previously owned by the Kennedys and others. None of this would have looked plausible from the 740 Park Avenue dining room of 1987. All of it traces forward from the moment in 1993 when Roehm was removed and Drouin took her place.

The architecture that had been built around Caroline Roehm in the late 1980s was, viewed from the present, the rehearsal version of the architecture that has been built around Marie-Josée Drouin since. The Kravis house has continued to be one of the great houses of American social life. It has simply been a different woman’s house. In the same period, Caroline Roehm has kept Weatherstone.

She has kept her name. She has kept her dogs. She has published her books. She has, in the latest available reporting, listed her Park Avenue pied-à-terre for $5.

5 million in 2024. The listing is a small public reminder that she remains a wealthy woman by ordinary American standards, and a small reminder that she has continued to live primarily in Connecticut. The deeper truth the story illuminates is uncomfortable for anyone who has ever tried to build social position by aesthetic excellence rather than by capital. Roehm did the entire feminine project of 1980s American society correctly.

She was beautiful, thin, polite, talented, ambitious, generous, charitable, and disciplined. She was loyal. She had taught herself a foreign language to native fluency. The system she had volunteered to be the visible center of did not, in the end, value any of those things at the moment of decision.

The system valued a different wife. The system retained the husband. The system replaced her with someone who fit the next chapter of his strategic life. Old money does not corrupt only those who inherit it.

It corrupts those who marry into it as well. It corrupts them by teaching them to believe that the beauty they assemble belongs to them. The duplex is theirs. The art is theirs.

The seat at the dinner is theirs. The presidency of the CFDA is theirs. The cover of Town & Country is theirs. The applause is theirs.

The work very often actually has been theirs. The work and the ownership of the work are not the same thing. The work belonged to them. The ownership of the work belonged to him.

The lesson Caroline Roehm has spent the last thirty years quietly demonstrating is that survival after the marriage ends requires building something the husband cannot take. She built a writer’s career, a gardener’s life, and a country house she rebuilt herself after the fire. It is, by the measure of the world she once belonged to, a smaller life than the one she lost. It is also, in the strict sense, the first life that has actually been hers.

She is, at the time of this telling, seventy-four years old. She lives at Weatherstone. She gardens. She writes.

She has not remarried. She does not appear in the social columns. She did not come back to fight. The world she lost has continued without her, in a slightly chillier light, under a different wife.

The world she built in her own name in the country has continued under her hand. The two worlds do not communicate. The wider history will record her, when it remembers her at all, as a footnote to the leveraged-buyout era. The narrower history, the history that lives in the people who have read her books and who arrange flowers on their own kitchen tables on Saturday mornings, will remember her as something else.

She is the woman who learned at thirty-nine that the beautiful room she had built around her husband had never belonged to her. She is also the woman who built, in middle age, a smaller and entirely owned room of her own. That is the only kind of survival in the system she once served that the system cannot eventually take back.
