Frank Williams' first mill shut down in 1929, the same year the old Cypress King died, and the company he built saw its very last cypress log in 1934. By that year, Louisiana had more than a million and a half acres of cutover swamp, stripped bare, and only about 22,000 acres of standing cypress forest left in the whole state. They had cut almost all of it in roughly forty years. And the cruelest part was that, unlike the Michigan pine or the Maine forests, the cypress could not simply grow back.

The pullboat canals and the skidder runs had drained and torn up the swamp, and in many places saltwater from the Gulf crept in through the cuts. A bald cypress seedling needs particular conditions to take hold. Its seeds need wet ground that is not under deep permanent water and not poisoned by salt: a narrow window the natural swamp used to provide on its own. But the pullboat canals had drained some areas and flooded others, and through those same cut channels, saltwater from the Gulf began to creep inland year after year into swamps that had always been fresh.

In place after place, the conditions a young cypress needed simply no longer existed. So in many of the places where thousand-year-old giants had stood in 1900, nothing of the kind ever returned. The forest that had taken since the days of the Roman Empire to grow was taken down in the span of a single human career, and a great deal of it was simply gone for good. Stand in the Atchafalaya Basin today, and you can still read the whole story in the land.

It is still the largest river swamp in the country, and it still holds the biggest remaining stretch of coastal cypress in America, around a quarter of a million acres. But almost all of that is second growth: younger trees that came up after the cut. The true ancient giants survive only in a few small remnant stands that the loggers somehow missed. And everywhere from the air you can still see the straight scars of the old pullboat canals and the faint wheel-spoke patterns pressed into the wetland: the ghost of where the cables once dragged the giants out.

Those pockets of true ancient cypress are still out there in the Atchafalaya, a scattering of giants that were already a thousand years old when the pullboats came and somehow lived through the whole boom. People go looking for them now the way you would go looking for a cathedral.

Across that quarter of a million acres, a younger cypress forest has slowly come back: not the same forest, never the same, but green and alive and full of herons and egrets. The swamp is not what it was, but it is not dead either. And the giants the cut missed still stand in the black water, older than anything else for a thousand miles. We remember Frank Williams because he made a fortune and his name is on the records of the largest mill in the world.

We can just barely name William Baptist because he built the pullboat. But the man who stood balanced on two planks over black water, swinging an axe into a tree older than his entire country, in the heat, with snakes below him and six whistle blasts always a possibility: we do not know him at all. The ledger gave him a number and a daily wage. The swamp gave him nothing but the work.

And the giant cypress he pulled out of that water is still out there, in ten thousand old houses and water tanks and barns across the South: the wood eternal, long outliving the man who cut it.

And it was not even unusual. For about forty years, from the 1890s into the 1920s, America reached down into the flooded swamps of Louisiana and pulled out the oldest, largest trees on the eastern half of the continent.

A million and a half acres of giant cypress were cut, and almost all of it was done with axes, saws, and human muscle, with men standing on narrow boards over blackwater full of snakes. And there is one detail that makes the whole enterprise seem almost unbelievable: a fresh-cut cypress does not float. It sinks. So, before the loggers could move these giants, they had to kill them while they still stood and then wait.

Two real men stood at the two ends of this strange industry, and only one of them is remembered. The first was called the Cypress King. His name was Frank Williams. Born in 1851 in Mobile, Alabama, he lost his father when he was still a boy.

He came up through the railroads and then through engineering and surveying across the South, and in the 1870s he settled in the little town of Patterson, Louisiana, and started milling cypress. In 1892, he bought out his partner for $350,000 and built the F. B. Williams Cypress Company into what the people of the day called the largest lumber mill in the world.

He came to control more than 100,000 acres of cypress swamp, some of it bought for as little as 75 cents an acre, and at his peak, his one operation cut something like 85 percent of all the cypress in Louisiana. The second man is barely a name in the record at all, and yet without him none of it could have happened. His name was William Baptist, a man out of New Orleans, and somewhere around 1891 he developed a machine that cracked the swamp open. It was called a pullboat: a steam winch mounted on a barge, able to reach a cable far out into the flooded forest and drag a giant cypress log through the muck to open water.

Before the pullboat, the deep swamp was simply unreachable. After it, the whole drowned forest was for sale. Between those two men stood thousands of others. Cajun locals and northern loggers who came south for the winter cut, whose names the company kept as a number on a payroll and nothing more.

The place itself is part of the story. Most of this happened in and around the Atchafalaya Basin in southern Louisiana, which even today is the largest river swamp in the United States: a wilderness of bayous and flooded forest covering more than 3,000 square miles. Picture a forest that is also a lake. The water moves slowly through it.

The cypress and tupelo rise straight out of it, and for much of the year there is no dry ground to stand on at all. To a farmer, it was useless. To a traveler, it was a maze. But to a lumberman who looked up at the timber instead of down at the mud, it was the richest stand of building wood in the eastern half of the country.

It grows slowly, which makes its wood dense, and it is naturally resistant to rot and insects in a way almost no other American timber is. People called it the wood eternal. It made the perfect material for anything that had to live in weather or water: shingles, water tanks, cisterns, greenhouse benches, docks, railroad ties, coffins, the trim and siding of houses all across the country. And the finest stands of it on Earth grew in the swamps of Louisiana.

A mature bald cypress in those swamps could rise 120 feet into the air, with a trunk 25 to 40 feet around at the flared base, far too thick for a man to reach even halfway around. Standing among those trees must have felt like standing inside a cathedral, with gray trunks rising like stone columns out of black water into a roof of green far overhead.

Nothing in the eastern forest of America was older or larger, and almost all of it stood in water that no ordinary crew could cross. So for a long time, the giant cypress just stood there. They knew exactly what was standing in the water, and they knew that whoever solved the problem of getting it out would own one of the great timber fortunes in America. Through the 1870s and 1880s they quietly accumulated enormous holdings of cypress swamp for almost nothing.

But the man who stood balanced on two planks over black water, swinging an axe into a tree older than his entire country, in the heat, with snakes below him and six whistle blasts always a possibility: we do not know him at all. The ledger gave him a number and a daily wage. The swamp gave him nothing but the work.

And the giant cypress he pulled out of that water is still out there, in ten thousand old houses and water tanks and barns across the South: the wood eternal, long outliving the man who cut it.
