content_text:
Ellery Vance was standing at the window of the east room in the dark with his hand on the frame when somebody in the yard said his name. A woman’s voice, not loud. Conversational. The volume you would use for somebody about fifteen feet away.

She said, “Ellery. ” She hummed off key, and never the same amount off. She tapped her thumbnail twice against a cup before she drank. And she called him Ellery.

Never Tom. Not once in five years. In the whole of Tallow County, Kentucky, in 1883, there was not one living human being who knew that name. He had introduced himself at that table as Thomas Vance.

He had signed the register as T. E. Vance, Bourbon Co. He had said “Ellery” out loud in that hollow exactly one time, on the first night at supper, telling Absalom Seismore about a dead wife who used to call him that, in a warm kitchen with the youngest brother sitting on a stool by the woodbox.

And now it was in the yard. He did not answer. But he did not step back from the window either. He stood there with his hand on the frame, and he looked down into a black yard, and he said nothing, and his heart was going so hard he could feel it in his teeth.

After about thirty seconds, the voice said it again. “Ellery. ” Then, in the same conversational tone from the same place: “Come see, I am cold out here. ” And underneath it, before and after the words, she was humming, low, the way she used to hum without knowing she was doing it while she worked at something with her hands.

The tune was one he knew. And it was off key. And it was off key by the exact same amount every single time, on every single repetition, like a thing that had been learned. Dileia was never wrong the same way twice.

Thomas Ellery Vance stood at that window and listened to something in a black yard hum his dead wife’s tune with mechanical precision. The thing that saved his life was not courage. It was an error of craftsmanship. Somebody had copied her, and copied her well, and copied her a little too well.

A man who had spent five years listening to that woman get a tune wrong in a hundred different ways heard a machine get it wrong in one way, over and over. He backed away from the window. He got the pistol. He sat on the floor with his back against the wall on the far side of the bed, where he could see the door and the window both.

The voice said his name eleven times. He counted. It was the first counting he ever did in that hollow. And in between it hummed.

And once, at around the eighth or ninth, it laughed. It laughed the way Dileia used to laugh at her own story before she got to the end of it, all in one breath with her whole chest. And there was nothing to laugh at. Nobody had said anything.

It was a laugh with no joke in front of it, played out into an empty yard in the dark at midnight in October. Then it stopped. The creek came back. The guineas made a small sleepy complaint.

And nothing else happened that night. At first light, Ellery Vance went down the stairs with his boots in his hand and out the kitchen door and around to the east side of the house under the window of his room in the wet frost. He was looking for footprints. There was heavy frost on the grass, and the ground was soft.

There were prints. A single line of them. A woman’s size, or near it. Barefoot.

Coming out of the grass from the direction of the barn, crossing the yard, stopping directly below the window of the east room. There was a place where they had stood a long while, both feet side by side, the frost melted out in two clean patches. And then going back, the prints going back to the barn were the same feet in the same direction of travel. And the stride was eleven inches longer.

He measured it with a piece of harness leather and his handspan. The same feet had walked out to his window at a woman’s ordinary walk, had stood under it for some while, and had gone back to the barn at a stride no woman of that foot size could take. Not running. A running stride does not just lengthen; it changes the whole print.

The toe digs, the heel lifts. These were the same flat, even, unhurried prints, just longer. Whatever had come to the window, walking as a woman, had gone back to the barn as something taller. He followed the line of them across the yard with his eyes.

They went to the south end of the barn. The far end. The end with no door. The end that was warm.

And at the base of the wall, eighteen inches from the boards, they stopped. Not turned. Not scuffed. Stopped.

The frost between those last prints and the barn wall was undisturbed. Behind him from the porch, Absalom Seismore said, “You are up early. ” Ellery Vance turned around. Absalom was in the doorway in his shirtsleeves with a cup of coffee.

Wade was behind him in the dark of the kitchen. Ria was not visible. And Ephraim Seismore was standing at the corner of the springhouse, forty feet to Vance’s left. Absalom looked at the line of prints in the frost, and looked at Ellery Vance, and said in the friendliest voice you ever heard, “Did you sleep?

” And that is the moment Thomas Ellery Vance understood that everyone in that house knew. Not suspected. Knew. Knew what it was.

Knew it had been in the yard. Knew it had been at his window. And had lain in their beds and listened to it call a dead woman’s pet name at a paying guest, and had come down in the morning and started the coffee. He said, “I slept fine.

” Absalom said, “Good. Frost is heavy. Cobb will be wanting to sell you that other mare before it gets any colder. ” And he went back inside.

Now, Ellery Vance had four hundred and ten dollars, a good mare, a mule, daylight, and eleven and a half miles of road between him and Beaver Ford. Why in God’s name did he not leave? He was asked that directly by the minister Coyle in 1928, when he was seventy-nine years old, and his answer is the truest and most terrible thing in this entire case. He said, “Because she called me Ellery.

You are asking a sensible question, and I will give you the answer, and the answer is not sensible. I knew it was not her. I knew it that first night when it hummed. I knew it in my bones.

I never once, not for one hour, believed my wife was in that yard. And I could not leave because it had her voice. And in four years, I had gone from being a man who could not stop hearing her voice to being a man who could not quite remember it. That is what happens.

Nobody tells you that. You think grief is the pain of remembering. It is not. It turns into the pain of the remembering going out a little at a time, like a lamp somebody is turning down in another room while you are trying to read.

And on the 18th of October, 1883, something in a barn in Tallow County gave it back to me. Wrong. But gave it back. I stayed three more nights, Reverend.

And I have had fifty-one years to be ashamed of it. And I do not know that I am. ”

That is the hook this place used. Not fear.

It did not hunt men with hunger, and it did not hunt them with fright. Because fear puts a man on a horse. It hunted them with the one thing a grieving man will walk toward with his eyes open and his hands empty. And that is why Absalom Seismore asked every guest at that supper table, in the middle of a funny story about a mule, whether he was married.

Because the whole business—the good food, the fair price, the thirty-one years, the eleven and a half miles of cut brush, the row of brushed hats in the crib—ran on one question asked warmly on the first night by a likable man with his hands open and up. Are you married? There were nineteen answers to it that we know of. And on the 19th of October 1883, there was one man left in the east room who had answered it, who was still breathing, and who had three days to go.

On the morning of the 20th of October, with the family out of the house, Thomas Ellery Vance did the single most dangerous thing he did in ten days. He took the register off the shelf in the front room and read it. It ran from 1852. Thirty-one years of names in five or six different hands.

He turned pages, and after about two minutes he began to see it. There was a mark in the left margin beside a name. A short vertical pencil stroke, about a quarter of an inch, with a single dot beneath it. Roughly one name in nine carried the mark.

Never two in the same week. Never two in the same month. They were spaced. They were rationed.

And after every marked name, without exception, there was a gap in time. Five weeks. Six weeks. Once, in the winter of 1866, eleven weeks.

A lodging house on a road with forty travelers a year does not take five weeks off. The gaps were the stand not needing any. And every one of those marks, and every one of those words written in the margin beside them, across thirty-one years and six months, was made in the same handwriting. Identical.

Not similar. The same pressure, the same slant, the same little hook coming off the tail of the “t. ” He held pages from 1854 and 1882 side by side against the window light, and they were the same word written twice by the same hand on the same afternoon. He said later that this was the exact moment—not the voice in the yard, not the prints in the frost—that he stopped being a frightened man and became a man in a trap.

Because a voice in the yard is a thing that happens to you. A pencil mark made in the same hand for thirty-one years is a thing that has been running for thirty-one years on a schedule, with a bookkeeper. He turned to the current page. There were four entries for that autumn.

A tinsmith peddler in September. A man and his son in the first week of October. A woman traveling with a hired driver on the 9th. And the fourth entry: T.

E. Vance, Bourbon Co. , in his own handwriting, dated the 11th. There was a mark beside it.

Beside the mark, in that same margin, in that same unchanging hand, was the word “kept. ” And underneath the word, there was a place where the paper had been scuffed and thinned, the way paper is when something has been rubbed out of it with a crumb of bread. Something else had been written there first, and then erased, and then “kept” had been put down over the top of it. He held the page up to the window and tried to read the ghost of it.

He got two things. It had been longer than “kept. ” Five or six letters, maybe seven. And the last letter of it had a tail that went below the line.

Like a G or a Y. He never found out what it said. Neither has anybody else. He put the register back on the shelf, square to the edge.

Then he went out and put a saddle on his mare in broad daylight with his hands shaking. Wade Seismore came around the corner of the barn and saw him doing it. Neither of them said anything for a long moment. Then Wade said, “Not today.

” Vance said he thought today suited him fine. And Wade Seismore, twenty-two years old, the youngest of three brothers, standing in a barn lot in Tallow County, said, “Absalom has took the team down to the second ford. He will be on the road till dark. If you go down the fork today, you will meet him on it.

Here I can put a light in a window. There I cannot do nothing. ” Then he said the sentence that matters more than almost anything else in this case. He said it looking at the ground.

He said, “I have not carried one yet. ” Ellery Vance did not know what that meant at the time. He would know by the day after tomorrow. Vance took the saddle back off.

That night, he sat on the bed in the east room with nine hours to get through, and he looked at the room properly for the first time. It was a plain room. Whitewashed plank walls, a wainscot of wide boards running about waist high, then plaster and lath above. Rope bed, straw tick, washstand, one chair, one small square window facing east.

And he saw that one board of the wainscot on the north wall, behind where the head of the bed stood, was out of plumb. It leaned in at the top by something less than a quarter of an inch. He got up and moved the bed out from the wall. The board came away in his hand with almost no resistance.

It had been cut clean at top and bottom and set back in place, and it had been going in and out of that wall so many times that the nail holes had gone soft. Behind it, in the dead space above the sill plate, there was an oilcloth packet tied with a bootlace. Inside there was a book. It was a peddler’s daybook, about seven inches by four, bound in scuffed brown leather with a flap.

On the first page, in a careful copperplate, was written: “Silas Meek, notions, tin, and the word. Bought and sold in Clay, Tallow, Osley, and Perry counties, Kentucky. Begun June 1871. ”

Ellery Vance read that book from twenty minutes to nine until the candle went out, and he lit the second one, and then until that one was a stub.

He took it with him when he left. That is why we have it. Silas Meek was a traveling preacher and tinsmith who had lodged at the stand eleven times between 1872 and 1874. On the 9th of June, 1871, he wrote: “Come up the cold water from Beaver Ford, 11 mile and a half, and lodged at the stand of one A.

Seismore, 75 cents, which is a fair price, and no more, and the supper was better than fair. Sold to the woman of the house two papers of pins, a card of hooks, and a tin funnel, 40 cents the lot. Sold to a Seismore nothing, he wanting nothing. But he bought a testament off me at cost for the youngest boy who is 10 years old and cannot read and is to be taught.

” That youngest boy was Wade. Then, on the 16th of April 1872: “Woke at some hour with the room cold as a spring house, and lay listening, and a woman was in the yard below, and spoke to me by name. Not Silas, not Mr. Meek.

She said ‘Sis. ’ Which is what my sister Anne called me, being unable at three years old to say Silas. And which no living soul has called me since she went in 1859. I did not answer.

I got down beside the bed and prayed till day. ” And in August of 1872, he wrote the confession that Ellery Vance understood completely: “I have come back. I could not stay away, and I want to be honest in this book if I am honest nowhere else. I did not come back for the trade.

The trade on this fork is three dollars in a good week. I came back because of Anne. I want to hear it again. God forgive me.

I want to hear it again. ”

Meek worked it all out. He worked out the register: “There is a mark against some names and the word kept by the mark. A Seismore did not write those marks.

I have seen a Seismore write. He writes a big slow round hand like a boy at a slate. The marks are made by a small tight hand that has not altered since 1852. ” He worked out the barn.

A man named Cob, in liquor, told him that the barn was built in 1852 by the father, Jeppa Seismore, and that it was set over a sink hole in the limestone, a hole a wagon would go into, with warm air coming up out of it in winter. “Jepp the Seismore built the barn over the hole. The third stall on the left is over it. ” And Meek gave it a name for his own use.

He called it the tenant. “I will not call it a devil. I have preached devils for twenty years off the back of a wagon, and I find I do not want to use the word here, because a devil is a thing with a will against God, and this has no more will against God than a fox has against a hen. It is a thing that lives in a hole and takes what is brought.

” And he wrote the key to the whole thing: “It cannot make anything new. It can copy. It copies better than anything I ever heard of, but it cannot make. Every particular of it that has struck me as wrong is the same wrongness.

It is a thing that has copied and cannot vary. Anne’s voice in the yard says my name. The same. Not near the same.

The same, the way a bell struck twice is the same. A living woman never said one word twice alike in her life. The trees in that orchard are of one size because they are not eleven trees. They are one tree that has been set down eleven times.

The hand in the book has not altered in twenty year because it is not a hand. It is the memory of a hand. Whatever a man brings it, it can wear. It cannot invent so much as a hair.

And so if you would keep it off, you must give it a thing that has no copy in it. ”

He tried scripture. It did not work. On the night of the 17th of May, he stood at the window and said the 23rd Psalm out loud.

It said it with him. It came in one word behind him at first, and by the second verse it was level with him, and by the valley of the shadow it was ahead of him, saying his words before he said them. In Anne’s voice. Out of the dark under his window.

He stopped at “they comfort me” and never finished it again. He could not say it in a church without hearing her get to the end of it first. Then, on the 22nd of May, he got it: “Numbers. I have got it.

A number is not learned. It is made one after the next. And there is no end of them and no two alike. And a thing that copies cannot go along with a man who is making.

” He stood at the window and counted out loud, and it could not take it off him. It said his name in the gaps. It never once said a number. He counted to four hundred and some, and it went away.

And he wrote the warning that would save Thomas Ellery Vance’s life: “Count out loud. Out loud is the whole of it. It must hear that you are making. And a man counting in his head is a man saying nothing.

And do not lose your place. ”

But the counting had a cost. It knew exactly where you were while you did it. It came and stood under the window and stayed there the whole time.

And by January of 1874, Meek was coming apart. He was staying at the stand nearly every week. He had stopped selling. He was hearing his sister’s voice in the yard on most nights whether or not there was anything in the yard.

And there was a woman upstairs in the front room that he had never seen. “A plate goes up. The plate comes down empty. The floor takes weight, and it takes it slow.

Two steps and a wait. Two steps and a wait. ” He asked at Beaver Ford, and Mrs. Blount at the store told him that Jeppa Seismore’s wife Melindy was buried in the church ground there in 1868.

Six years. Somebody was in that front room, and the family carried her supper up, and the family did not go up with it. A woman named Ria carried it. Ria was nineteen years old, and had come there with her people two years before, and Meek did not know what had happened to her people.

The last entry in Silas Meek’s daybook is dated the 11th of February, 1874. “I have thought and prayed and I am settled. I do not think it will let me leave. And if it does let me leave, I know now that I will come back.

So I will go and open the third stall. I have got a bar and a lantern, and I have got the counting. I mean to go tonight when the house is down, and I mean to see it, not to fight it. I am 44 years old and I never fought nothing in my life.

I want to see the thing that has been talking to me for 2 years, and I want to know if any part of what it gives back is her. Whoever finds this book, the counting works. Do it out loud. Do not lose your place.

Do not say the name of your dead out loud on this ground. Not once, not ever, for it takes the name out of your mouth and wears it. And do not go in the barn. I am going in the barn, and I am aware of what I am, and I have no answer for it except that she called me Sis, and there is nobody else left alive who ever did.

If I do not come back out, tell my brother—” And that is where it stops. Mid-sentence. At the bottom of a page, with the next page blank. There is no mark on that page.

No blot. No struggle. He simply stopped writing in the middle of a word to his brother, and closed the book, and put it in his coat, and went out. The name Silas Meek appears in the register of the Seismore stand for the last time on the 11th of February, 1874.

There is a mark beside it. Beside the mark, in that small, tight, unchanging hand, is the word kept. And his daybook was in the wall of the east room, behind a board that had been taken in and out so many times the nail holes had gone soft. He knew he was putting it where the next man who could not sleep would find it.

On the morning of the 21st of October, 1883, Thomas Ellery Vance came down the stairs at first light with the daybook of Silas Meek in his coat and his memorandum book in his pocket and his money belt under his shirt. Wade Seismore had done what he said he would do. The mule was fed. The crib door stood open.

There was a plate on the table with cold biscuit and side meat on it, and a cloth over it. He rode out of the yard of the Seismore stand at about twenty minutes past six on the morning of the 21st of October 1883, and he turned down the fork toward Beaver Ford. He got two miles. At the second ford, the brush was uncut.

The whole eleven and a half miles of that road had been cleared back, uniform on both sides, and at the second ford the cut brush stopped. Not tapered off. Stopped. Across the road in a line, the way the tree line stops at the edge of a mowed pasture.

On his side of the line, over there, it had been kept. Beyond it, greenbrier and cane and second growth over the roadbed, thick as a hedge, with no gap in it that a horse could take. Grown. Not laid there.

Grown, with three-year canes in it and dead cane under the live cane. He sat his mare and looked at three years of growth on a road he had ridden down four days earlier. He got off. He walked up to it.

He put his hand in it. He got a thorn in the heel of his hand, deep enough that it left a white scar he still had at seventy-nine. He walked the mare into the creek and went forty yards downstream to see if he could get around it. The cane came right down to the water on both banks and out into it.

And while he was standing in that creek, up to his boottops, something up on the right-hand ridge said, “Ellery. ” He did not answer. He led his mare back up out of the water, and he turned her, and he rode back up the fork the way he had come. At the stand he turned up, not down.

The head of the Cold Water Fork was three and a half miles above the stand. The road got worse, and then stopped being a road and became a track. Audi Redwine’s cabin sat at the very top of the hollow, where the two ridges came together, on a bench of ground above a spring. She was ninety-one years old.

She was sitting on the porch in the cold with a blanket over her knees, and she said before he had his hand on the latch, “You are the cattleman. ” He said he was. She said, “You have been down there ten nights. ” He said he had.

And she said, “Then you can come in, and you can shut my door behind you, and you can put that mare in the lot with the gate shut, because it is a good mare and it has done nothing to nobody. ” She fed him, and then she said, “Say it out. ” And he said it all out. The barn, the warmth at the south end, the three sounds falling into one rhythm, the apple trees, the hats in the crib, the register and the mark and the word, the prints in the frost with the stride eleven inches longer, the voice in the yard, the cane at the second ford, and the daybook.

She put her hand flat on it and closed her eyes. Then she said, “Silas Meek sat in that chair you are in in the winter of ’74. Sat there and told me he was going to go and look at it. ” Vance asked what she had said to him.

She said, “I told him it would be his own doing. And he said yes, it would. And I give him his supper. And he went off down the hollow.

And I have thought about him every winter since. ”

Then she told him the closest thing to a cosmology this case has. “Some ground is thick, and some ground is thin. That is all it is.

There is no more to it than that. Most ground is thick. You can dig in it and build on it and bury in it, and it holds. Thick ground does not care about you, and that is a mercy, and you ought to be grateful for it every day of your life.

Some ground is thin. Not bad. Thin. It is worn through, the way a knee goes in a britches leg.

That bottom is thin. And there is something behind it, and it has always been there. It was there when the Shawnee come through, and they knew it and did not camp on that bottom. It did not come because Jepp the Seismore called it.

Jepp the Seismore found a hole and looked in it, which is what a certain kind of man will always do, and it looked back, and they come to an arrangement. ” He asked her what the arrangement was. She said, “The same arrangement as ever. It keeps that bottom, and they feed it.

” And she laid out the other side of it. “Did you see a sick beast on that place? Did you see the crop fail? Did you see a hail?

The black diphtheria come up this fork in ’61 and took eleven children between the mouth and my house, and took none at that stand. And there was four Seismore children in that house at the time, and not one of them so much as coughed. It keeps that bottom. The weather goes around it.

The sickness goes around it. That family has not had a bad year since 1852. And there is not another family on eleven and a half miles of this creek that can say the same. And every one of them knows it.

That is why nobody up this hollow will say a word to a stranger. They are not in league. They are downstream. ”

He asked her why nobody had ever burned the barn.

She said, “The barn is not the thing. The barn is a lid. Jepp the Seismore did not build a barn to keep something in. He built it to keep the weather off it, the same as you would build over a well.

Burn the lid, and you have got a hole in a bottom with no lid on it, and three men who have got nothing left to lose, and a whole hollow of families who will hate you for the rest of your life. ” And she told him the rules. Three of them, refined off Silas Meek. “One: you count backward out loud from a hundred, not up.

Meek counted up, and it worked, and it near killed him. When you get to naught, you start again at a hundred. And if you ever lose your place, you do not guess. You go back to a hundred and start clean.

A guessed number is a copied number, and it will take it off you. Two: you keep your hand on iron the whole while, and it has got to be iron you brought in yourself. Not a nail out of that house, not the latch, not their fire irons. A horseshoe in your coat, a knife, your own gun barrel will do.

Three: do not say the name of your dead out loud on that ground. Not once. Not in prayer. Not in temper.

Not in your sleep, if you can help it. It has got her voice off you already. Ten nights, it has been standing under your window learning. It has not got her name off you yet because you have not said it.

And I know you have not said it, because if you had said it, you would not be sitting in my kitchen this morning. You would be one of the nineteen. ”

He asked her what it did with them. She said, “You have been in that crib.

You have seen the hats. Was there bones? ” He said there had not been. She said, “There is never bones.

Not in thirty-one years, not in Feba’s time neither. Sheriff Bledsoe come up here in ’81 with two men and a dog and went over that bottom and that barn and that sink mouth down at the lower end, and did not find so much as a button. And that is why there was never no charge brought, and never could be. I do not think it eats them.

There is a difference between eat and keep. And that book on my table has the right word in it, in that little hand, and the word is kept. A man goes down that hole, and the man is gone. And something down there knows how he laughed, and how he said his wife’s name, and how he was wrong about a tune.

That is what it takes. That is the rent. It does not want your meat, son. There is deer on that ridge.

It wants the part of you that could be worn. ” And she said the thing about the laugh. “That is why it never gets it exactly right. Because every one of them it ever took, it took at the worst hour of their life.

In the dark. Frightened. Calling out for somebody. That is all it has ever had to learn off of.

It has had ninety men’s last ten minutes, and not one man’s ordinary Tuesday. It can do a voice, and it cannot do a person. It has never in its existence seen anybody happy. It does not know that a woman hums a tune wrong different every time, because it never heard nobody hum in a kitchen.

It only ever heard them scream. And screaming is all one note. ” Ellery Vance sat with his hands flat on the table and thought about a laugh coming out of the dark with no joke in front of it. And he asked about Ria.

Audi Redwine said, “Ria Vessels come up this fork in the spring of ’77 in a wagon with her husband and her husband’s brother, going to Manchester. And the husband and the brother is in that book with a mark by them, and she is not. She has been in that house six years, and she has never come up this hollow to my door. And there is only two reasons a body does not walk three miles to an open door.

Either she cannot, or there is somebody in that house she will not leave. ” Vance said, “The woman upstairs. ” And Audi Redwine said, “Ah. So you have heard the floor.

” He said he had. Two steps and a weight. And Audi Redwine said, “Melindy Seismore was buried at Beaver Ford in the church ground in 1868. And I helped wash her, and I helped dress her, and I stood at the hole.

That is fifteen years ago. There has been a plate carried up them stairs every day since. ”

Ellery Vance slept that night at the head of the Cold Water Fork on a cornshuck tick on the floor by the fire, and he slept nine hours without moving. Over breakfast, she laid out his choices.

There were two. The first was the ridge. A footpath out of the head of the hollow, over the gap, and down the far side into Osley County. Nine miles on foot.

He would have to leave the mare and the mule and the kit and his saddle and walk out with what was in his pockets. She recommended it. She said, plainly and more than once, that nine miles of walking and a hundred dollars of gear left behind was the cheapest anybody had ever got out of that bottom. The second choice was to wait for the road, because the road would open again.

“It is holding the road because it is not done. It will not hold it forever. It cannot. There is a mail rider comes up that fork once a month, and there is a preacher comes up in the spring, and there is families up this hollow that has got to get down to Beaver Ford to sell and to bury and to marry.

It will open when it is done with you. One way or the other. ” And Ellery Vance asked her the question that decided the rest of his life. He said, “Ria.

” And Audi Redwine put down what she was holding. She said, “You cannot carry a woman out over that gap that does not want to go. ” He said, “Have you ever asked her? ” And the old woman was quiet a while.

Then she said, “No. Because in sixty-one years, I have learned what I can do and what I cannot. And I sit at the top of this hollow, and I keep a door that opens, and I do not go down it. If I go down it, I am one more, and then there is nobody at the top.

That is not courage, son. I want you to hear me. That is not courage. It is arithmetic.

And I have done it every morning for six decades, and I have got the same answer every morning, and I do not like it any better now than I did the first time. ”

Thomas Ellery Vance walked out of that dooryard at about half past eight on the morning of the 22nd of October 1883, and got on his mare, and rode back down the Cold Water Fork toward the Seismore stand. He was not a brave man in any way that he ever recognized. He had no plan.

What he had, and what Silas Meek did not have, is the difference between the man who came out and the man who did not. Silas Meek went back down that hollow eleven times for the dead. Ellery Vance went back down once for somebody living. Whatever was in that barn had spent thirty-one years perfecting a hook baited with grief.

And grief pulls a man inward, down, toward the hole, toward the voice. It had never in its existence had to deal with a man who was walking toward the bottom for a reason that had nothing to do with what it was holding. It did not know what to do with that. He rode into the yard at a quarter past nine.

Absalom Seismore was on the porch. Vance said the road was blocked at the second ford. Absalom said, “It does that. ” Two words.

Said the way a man says the chimney smokes when the wind is out of the north. Then Absalom said, “You went up the hollow. ” Vance said he went to Audi’s. And Absalom Seismore nodded, looked off at the ridge for a second, and said the most chilling thing anybody said to Ellery Vance in that entire fortnight.

He said it kindly. “She is a good old woman, and she has told you the truth. I want you to know I have got no quarrel with her, and never have. She has said her peace to a good many, and it has never yet changed nothing, and it will not change nothing now.

Somebody has got to sit at the top of it. ” The exact phrase her aunt Feba gave her in 1822. They knew both ends of that hollow. Both.

And had known for sixty years, and had arrived at an understanding. Vance said he would stay until the road opened. Absalom said, “It will open. It generally does.

” And then he said, “Forty cents, same as before. ”

That afternoon, he got Ria alone at the springhouse. He had worked out he would have ninety seconds, and no more. He said, straight out, “There is a footpath over the gap at the head of the hollow.

Nine miles. Audi Redwine will put you on it. I will walk it with you. We can be in Booneville by dark, and I will pay your way anywhere from there, and never see you again.

” Ria Vessels stood in the door of that springhouse with a crock in her hands. She said, “No. ” He said, “Ma’am. ” And she said, “You do not know what you are asking.

And you are going to feel very fine about yourself for asking it, and then you are going to leave. So I am going to tell you the whole of it in one go, and then I am going to carry this in, and you are not going to speak to me again. ” He wrote it down that night in the back of his memorandum book, in pencil, running sideways across two pages of cattle purchases. She said, “I come up this fork in April of ’77 with my husband Lel Vessels and his brother Amos.

We was going to Manchester. We stopped here one night. I have been here six years and four months. They went out to the barn on the second morning, and did not come back.

And Absalom Seismore sat me down in that kitchen and told me my husband had took the wagon and gone on and left me. And I knew it was a lie while he was saying it. And he knew I knew, and he said it anyway. And that is the only lie any of them has ever told me in six years.

They have told me the truth ever since. And it has been worse. ” Then she told him why she would not walk over the gap. “There is a room at the top of them stairs.

There is something in it. They call it mother. I carry a plate up three times a day. Near enough four thousand times.

And it talks to me through the door. And it talks to me in Lel’s voice. It is not him. I have known it was not him since the second month.

It says the same things. It says a thing he said to me at the ford the day we come up, and it has said it now maybe four hundred times. The same words. At the same speed.

And a man does not say a thing four hundred times the same. I know what it is. I have had six years to know what it is. And I am not stupid, and I am not mad.

And every day I go up them stairs. ” She said, “I want you to understand what you are offering me. You are offering me a nine-mile walk to a place where nothing has his voice in it. He has been dead six years.

He was thirty-one. He was not a good man in any large way. He drank, and he was hard with a horse, and he could not keep money. And he is the only person that ever in my life come and got me when I was sick.

And I have got in the whole world one thing left of him. And it is behind a door at the top of them stairs. And it is a lie. And it says his words in his voice.

And if I walk over your gap into Osley County, I will never hear it again as long as I live. So no. Not today. Ask me again in ten years, and I might have got tired enough.

But you will not be here in ten years. And I will. ” She picked up the crock and went past him. At the corner of the springhouse, she stopped and said one more thing without turning around.

She said, “They have marked you. Absalom put the mark by your name on the 11th, the first night, before you had your boots off. And it has been changed since. And I have looked at it, and I do not know what it means, and I do not want to.

And Wade has not carried one yet. He is twenty-two. Ephraim carried his first at nineteen, and Absalom at seventeen. They are going to make him carry you.

It has been coming since the summer. That is what they was arguing about at the crib on Tuesday. ”

Carrying. That is the word.

And Audi Redwine confirmed it to Vance the following year in a letter that a neighbor wrote out for her. The tenant did not come out and take men. It could come up out of the barn into the yard. The prints in the frost said so.

The voice at the window said so. But in thirty-one years, there is not one account of anybody being taken out of the house or off the road or out of a bed. It called. That is all it did.

It called in a voice you would open a door for, and it waited to see if you would come. Most did not come. But some came. Some got up out of that bed at two in the morning and went down the stairs and out the kitchen door and across eighty yards of mowed yard toward a voice.

And a man walking across a dark yard toward a barred barn door cannot get in. So somebody had to open it. Carrying was not carrying a body. Carrying was walking out ahead of a man with a lantern and lifting the bar and standing aside.

That is the family trade. That is what Jeppa Seismore taught three sons. And Vera Blount had told Ellery Vance in a store in Beaver Ford eleven days earlier, “Do not let any man of that family carry your lamp into that barn ahead of you. ” She knew the word.

She had known it for years. She used it to a stranger’s face, and he heard it as ordinary English, and rode on down the fork. On the 22nd of October, in the middle of the afternoon, in full sunlight, alone, Vance went down to the lower end of the bottom and looked at the sink. The creek went into a wooded pocket of maybe three acres and did not come out.

It went under into the limestone. About a hundred and fifty yards in, he came into an opening in the timber, maybe forty feet across, that was not natural. It was too round. And around the edge of it, driven into the ground, was iron.

Horseshoes, hundreds of them, point down, at intervals of a foot or so, in a ring all the way around. And not only horseshoes. Wagon tire cut into lengths. Plow points.

Broken hoe blades. Bar iron. Old iron and new iron together. The oldest of it was rust-colored stain in the sod.

The newest of it was bright at the edges and had been driven that year. Somebody had been maintaining a ring of iron around that opening for a very long time. And somebody was still maintaining it. And on the north side of the ring, the side toward the barn, a section about eleven feet long had been pulled up.

Not rusted out. Not grown over. Pulled. The horseshoes were lying in a heap in the leaves beside their own holes.

And the earth in the holes was fresh enough to be dark. Two years, maybe three. Somebody had spent a hundred years fencing that thing in with iron. And in the last two or three years, somebody had gone down there and taken a gap out of the fence on the side facing the barn.

In the center of the ring, the ground went down into a bowl, and at the bottom of the bowl was the sink. An opening in the limestone, eight feet by five, going down at a steep angle into the dark, with the creek running into it. He lay down on his belly at the lip and looked in. He could see perhaps twenty feet.

And there was a smell coming up out of it. The smell of the inside of a well. And cold coins. Exactly the same as the runway of the barn on his first night.

Coming back out, he walked into a foundation on a bench of ground above the sink. Four courses of dry-laid stone, roughly sixteen by twenty feet. A hearth at the east end, still standing four feet high. Trees growing inside the walls.

One poplar he put at better than a hundred years old. And a puncheon floor, or what was left of one, black rotted slabs of split log lying in the leaf mold with the flat sides up. Audi Redwine had told him that morning what her aunt Feba had told her: there was a woman on that bottom who had a cabin over that hole, with a puncheon floor, and she is in the church ground at Beaver Ford under a stone with no date on it. On the underside of the mantle stone, on the face that a person would only see if they were sitting on the hearth looking up, somebody had cut letters and numbers with a chisel.

He cleaned them with his thumb for about ten minutes. A name that was gone except for the last four letters. Those were E-S-T-E-R. And under it, a date.

Complete. 1791. Jeppa Seismore built his barn in 1852. He was, at the outside, the third tenant of that bottom.

There had been somebody living directly over that hole with a floor of split logs, sixty-one years before he ever laid a sill. And that somebody had cut her own name and a date into the underside of her own mantle, where nobody would see it. Which is not a thing you do to be remembered. It is a thing you do to leave a marker.

And there is a stone with no date on it in the church ground at Beaver Ford, eleven and a half miles away, which means somebody carried her out of that hollow. The night of the 22nd of October, 1883, he went up to the east room at eight. He did not undress. He put the chair under the latch.

He put the pistol on the bed beside his right hand. A Colt . 44, a heavy iron thing that had come with him from Bourbon County, and had never been in that bottom before the 11th. Iron he brought in himself.

At about eleven, the creek stopped. At about a quarter past, the guineas went up and were cut off. And at about a quarter to twelve, he heard the kitchen door open downstairs and close. And then he heard the stairs.

Something came up those stairs one tread at a time, at an ordinary domestic pace, the pace of a person going up to bed. It got to the landing, and then it stood there. He said it stood on that landing for what he believed was close to an hour. And in the whole of it, there was no sound whatever from the west room, where two men were sleeping twelve feet away.

They were not sleeping. He knew that then and said so. Then it knocked two knocks on the door of the east room. Not loud.

The two polite knocks of somebody who does not want to wake the house. And Ellery Vance felt every hair on his body stand up, because the knock was not a knock. It was a thumbnail. Two taps of a thumbnail on a wooden panel, at exactly the spacing that Cordelia Vance had tapped her thumbnail twice against the rim of a cup before she drank, every time, for five years, without knowing she did it.

And here is the part he did not tell anybody for forty years. When he finally told it to the minister Coyle in 1928, Coyle wrote in his own account that Vance stopped three times getting it out. He said, “It did not learn that off her. She was dead four years before that thing ever heard of me.

It never heard her. It has never in its life heard my wife do anything. It learned it off me. Because I do it.

I have done it since about a year after she died, and I did not know I did it until a woman at a boarding house in Winchester asked me why I always knocked on my cup, and I could not answer her. I had been eleven days in that house, drinking coffee at that table three times a day, and tapping my thumbnail on the cup like she did. And something had been watching. And it had took it off me.

And give it back through a door at midnight. There was nothing left of her on this earth except a few little habits that had got into me without me knowing. And it went in and got one of them. And that thing knew where every one of them was.

And it was going to ask for them, one at a time. ”

Then the voice on the landing said, “Ellery. ” He started counting out loud backward from a hundred, the way Audi Redwine had told him, with his right hand flat on the iron barrel of the Colt. 100.

99. 98. And the thing on the other side of that door went to work on him. It worked on him for somewhere between three and four hours.

It said his name in the gaps. It hummed. It said, “I am cold out here. ” At about seventy, it started saying things that were harder.

It said the name of the street in Paris, Kentucky. It said the word typhoid. It said, “You left the window open. ” Which was true, and which was a thing he had privately, stupidly, sinfully blamed himself for since October of 1879, and had never said out loud to one living soul.

He never found out how it had that. At some point between sixty and fifty-five, it laughed. That laugh again. All in one breath, with the whole chest, with no joke in front of it.

And Ellery Vance lost his place. He had been counting for well over an hour. His mouth was dry. His tongue had gone thick.

And he came up out of it and did not know what he had last said. And he guessed. He said, “Fifty-eight. ” And from the other side of the door, immediately, in Dileia’s voice, the thing said, “Fifty-eight.

” A guessed number is a copied number, and it will take it off you. He had handed it one. And the instant it had one, it was in through the gap with it. It said, “Fifty-seven.

” And it said “Fifty-six. ” And it began to count down on the other side of that door in his dead wife’s voice, at his own speed, taking the count off him the way it had taken the 23rd Psalm off Silas Meek in 1873. And Thomas Ellery Vance said that this was the only moment in eleven days, and the only moment in fifty-one subsequent years, when he came genuinely close to opening a door. Not because he wanted to.

Not because he was fooled. It was that it was counting for him. He was so tired. He had been counting for an hour and a half, and there was a thing on the other side of the door doing the work now.

“It felt like somebody taking a weight out of your hands. ” He got his hand tighter on the gun barrel. The cold of it got through. And he did what she had told him to do.

He went back to a hundred, clean, from the top, out loud. 100. 99. 98.

At a fresh pace, in a voice that had gone to pieces. And the thing on the other side of the door was at fifty-four. And it could not follow him. It had one thread.

He had dropped it and started another one. And it went on counting down alone, on the wrong count, in a dead woman’s voice, all the way to naught. And when it got to naught, it stopped. And it said his name once more.

And then there was nothing on that landing at all. He counted until the window went gray. At full daylight, he came out of the east room. At the head of the stairs, outside the front room door, there was a plate with the food gone off it.

And Ria Vessels was on her knees on the landing boards, scrubbing at something on the floor with a rag and a bucket. She did not look up at him. She did not stop. He never learned what she was scrubbing.

He asked her nothing. Downstairs, Absalom was at the table with his coffee. He looked at Vance’s face and said, “You did not sleep. ” Vance said, “No.

” Absalom said, “You counted. ” Not a question. Then he said, “Audi give you that. She has given it to four or five over the years.

It works. I will not tell you it does not. But it works tonight. You will do it again tonight, and it will work again.

And a man can go a good while. Meek went a year and a half. And every night, it is a little harder to get to naught. And every night, it has got a little more of you to say through the door.

You cannot count for the rest of your life, Mr. Vance. That is all I am telling you. There is not a man born that can count for the rest of his life.

” And Ellery Vance, standing in that kitchen in the daylight with his hands shaking so badly he had to put them behind him, asked Absalom Seismore the only question he ever asked him straight. He said, “Why do you do it? ” And the eldest Seismore brother, who was kind, who told good stories about mules, who had done this ninety times, looked up at him and gave an answer that Vance said he could see the man had prepared a long time ago and had never had occasion to use. He said, “My daddy give it to me, and I will give it to my brother’s boy if Wade ever gets one.

And if he does not, it will stop with us, and this hollow will go back to being what every other hollow in this county is, which is poor. I have got four families up this fork that has buried no children since 1852. I am not asking you to think well of me. I have not thought well of me since I was seventeen years old and my daddy handed me a lantern and we walked out to that barn.

I am telling you that there is a price on this ground, and it has been paid by somebody every one of thirty-one years. And the ones paying it is strangers, and the ones getting it is my people. And I know precisely what that makes me, and I have made my peace with it. And I sleep, sir.

I do sleep. That is the part you will want to know. I sleep like a stone. ” And then he said, “Wade will not.

Though Wade has got it in him to not sleep. That is why it has to be soon. ” He said it into his coffee. He may not even have meant Vance to hear it.

That was the morning of the 23rd of October 1883. And that night was the night it almost happened. There were four things different about the Seismore stand that evening, and Thomas Ellery Vance noticed all four of them between four in the afternoon and dark. The first was his mare.

She was not in the first stall on the left. She was in the fourth stall at the south end of the runway, in the warm. Somebody had moved her while he was at the house. He moved her back himself and said nothing.

The second was the crib. The corn crib had stood open every day he had been there. That afternoon it was shut, and the hasp was through, and there was a peg in the hasp. He knew what was on the back wall of it.

The third was Ephraim. At about a quarter to six, Ephraim walked from the springhouse to the barn carrying two lanterns. Two. One in each hand.

He had carried one lantern to that barn every evening for twelve evenings. The fourth was supper. Supper on the 23rd of October was the best meal served at the Seismore stand in the whole of the time Ellery Vance was under that roof. By a distance.

There was a chicken killed that afternoon. There was a pie. There were the dried apples stewed with sugar that he had said on the first night out loud at that table were the best he had ever eaten, and had not been served since, and were served that night in a bowl set down in front of his place, and nobody else’s. Absalom was warm and easy and funny for two solid hours.

He told the story about the mule that could open a gate latch with its lip, which he had told on the first night, and he told it better the second time. Vance sat at that table and ate a chicken and laughed in the right places and understood exactly what was being done to him. He was being sent off. Wade came in at dark and sat down and ate nothing.

He sat at his brother’s table with his hands in his lap and did not lift a fork one time. Vance said good night at eight. Absalom stood up when he did. That was new.

And he said, “Sleep well, Mr. Vance. ” Vance said he expected he would. And Absalom said, and this is the last sentence Absalom Seismore ever said to him, “It is a kindness of you to say so.

”

He went up to the east room and put the chair under the latch and sat down on the bed with his back to the headboard and his right hand on the barrel of the Colt. He started counting at about a quarter to nine, before there was anything to count against, because he had worked out that a man who begins the count early begins it with a full voice. 100. 99.

98. At some point past ten, he heard the kitchen door open and close, and he heard out in the yard two men’s voices, and one of them was raised. He could not make out words. It went on for a good while, and then it stopped.

The creek stopped at about eleven. The guineas went up and were cut off. Then he heard the stairs, and something came up them at an ordinary domestic pace, and stopped on the landing. And it was worse than the night before, because it had another day’s worth of him.

It said the street in Paris. It said typhoid. It said, “You left the window open. ” It hummed.

It said his name in the gaps. And then, at somewhere around forty, it said a thing it had not said before. It said, in Dileia’s voice, perfectly conversational, through a plank door at midnight, “Ellery, put down the gun and come out. You are being so silly.

” He counted 39. 38. He got to naught. He went back to a hundred, clean, out loud.

He was somewhere in his second pass down, around the sixties, when the thing on the landing stopped talking and went away down the stairs. He counted for a while into the silence, and then he stopped, and the house was quiet, and the creek was running. And he thought, and this is his own account, “Well. That was easier than last night.

” And then somebody knocked on the door. Two knocks. Knuckles. A fist.

A voice said, “Mr. Vance. ” He did not answer. The voice said, “It is Wade, Mr.

Vance. The road is open. ” And now you have to appreciate the problem, because it is the exact problem this entire case is built on. He had eleven days of evidence that whatever was in that hollow could copy any voice it had heard.

It had heard Wade Seismore’s voice every day of Wade Seismore’s life. He had a wooden door, a gun, and no way on this earth to tell. And then he remembered Silas Meek, in a peddler’s daybook in a wall six inches from his shoulder, in 1873. It cannot make anything new.

And Ellery Vance said through the door, in a voice he described as sounding like somebody else’s, “Tell me a thing I have never heard in this house. ” There was a pause. And then Wade Seismore said, “In 1871, a peddler sold my daddy a testament at cost, because I was ten and could not read. My daddy give it to me and never asked after it again.

I taught myself out of it over four years, with nobody helping, and I done it in the loft of that barn, because there was no other place a body is let alone here. I can read now. I have never told nobody in my life that I can read. And Absalom does not know it.

And it is the only thing I have got that is mine. ” Nothing in that hollow had ever heard that. Nobody had. It had never been said out loud by anybody, anywhere, in twelve years.

A thing that can only copy cannot say a sentence that has never been said. Ellery Vance took the chair out from under the latch and opened the door. Wade Seismore was on the landing with a lantern in his hand and his coat on and his hat on. He said, “The road opened at dusk.

I walked down and looked at it myself. The cane is gone at the second ford. Not cut. Gone.

Your mare is saddled and tied at the lot gate, and your mule is loaded. I done it an hour ago while they was on the porch. I am going to walk out ahead of you with this lantern all the way to Beaver Ford, and you are going to come behind me, and you are going to count out loud the whole eleven mile and a half, and you are not going to stop counting if I speak to you, and you are not going to stop counting if it speaks to you. And if you lose it, I will pick it up and carry it till you get a hold of it again.

” Vance looked at that boy standing on that landing with a lantern in his hand, walking out ahead of a man, and understood what he was being offered. He said, “Wade. If you take me down that road, they will know what you are. ” And Wade Seismore said, “They know what I am.

I have knew what I am since I was ten years old and could not read. It is them that has been waiting to find out. ”

They went down the stairs. Ria Vessels was standing at the bottom of them in the dark kitchen, with no lamp lit.

She had a leaf of paper folded twice in her hand, and she put it into Ellery Vance’s hand as he came past her, and she closed his fingers on it. It was a leaf torn out of the register of the Seismore stand. October of 1883. Four entries.

And T. E. Vance, Bourbon Co. , dated the 11th, with a mark beside it, and the word in the margin, and under the word, the place where the paper had been rubbed thin.

She had gone into that front room and torn it out of the book. Wade said, “Ria. Come on. ” And Ria Vessels said, “No.

” Wade said, “Ria. ” And she said, “Not tonight, Wade. ” Then she said, “Go on. He is on the porch, and Ephraim is at the barn, and you have got about four minutes.

” The last he saw of her was a woman standing in a dark kitchen holding a shawl closed at her throat. She said one more thing to him, in an ordinary voice, the way you say a thing to somebody who is going out. She said, “Tell Audi Redwine I know her door opens. ”

They went out the kitchen door into the yard.

Absalom Seismore was on the porch. Wade walked out into the middle of that yard with the lantern held up at the height of his shoulder, and stood there so that his brother could see him plain, and he did not say one word. And Absalom Seismore sat on that porch and looked at his youngest brother standing in a yard at midnight with a lit lantern held up, walking ahead of a marked man in the wrong direction. Vance said the old man made a sound.

He would not ever describe it further than that. And then Absalom Seismore said, quite clearly, across thirty feet of moonlit yard, “Then it will want somebody tonight. ” And Wade Seismore said, “I know it. ” And his brother said, “Go on then.

” That is the whole of it. That is everything that was said. Two sentences and three words. And a man let his brother go.

They went out the lot gate at about twenty past eleven on the night of the 23rd of October 1883. Ellery Vance began to count. Eleven and a half miles is a long way at night, on foot and horseback, in October. It took them a little under five hours.

Wade walked the whole of it ahead with the lantern up. Vance rode behind him at a walk, with the mule on a lead and his right hand on the iron of the gun barrel and his voice going out loud, 100, 99, 98, down to naught, and back, over and over, for four hours and forty minutes. He estimated afterward that he counted from a hundred down to naught somewhere between fifty and sixty times on that road. At the first ford, nothing.

Between the first and second fords, something came into the timber on the right-hand side and paced them. It stayed off the road, level with the lantern. It went through cane and blowdown at the speed of a walking horse on a hillside at night, without a light, and it did not once make the sound that a body makes going through cane. It made a different sound.

Vance said it sounded like a hand going along a wall in the dark. At the second ford, the cane was gone. There was bare, packed road. Vance got down and led the mare across and got back on.

62. 61. 60. Between the second and third fords, it said his name eleven times from the right-hand timber, and Wade never once turned his head.

At the third ford, it got in front of them. Something was standing in the road on the far side, at the edge of the lantern light, sixty or seventy feet off. It was upright. He could not see it in any detail, and he was careful all his life not to claim that he could.

He said it was the height of a tall man, and that the proportion of it was wrong in a way he could not put a word to for fifty years, and eventually put this word to: unfinished. It was like a shape somebody had made out of a description. Wade did not stop and did not slow down and did not raise the lantern. He walked straight at it.

Vance rode after him, counting 44. 43. 42. 41.

And at about thirty feet, the thing in the road stepped aside into the water and stood in the creek and let them go by. And as they came level with it, it hummed once. Four or five notes. Off key.

By the exact same amount. Between the third and fourth fords, Vance’s voice gave out. He had been counting for something over three hours. He got down into the twenties, and the words stopped coming, and he lost his place entirely.

And Wade, walking ahead of him in the dark with a lantern, said, “Nineteen. ” And Vance got a breath and said, “Eighteen. ” And Wade said, “Seventeen. ” And the two of them counted that stretch together, turn and turn about.

And Vance said that at some point in those minutes he began to cry, and went on counting while he did it, and that he was not ashamed of it, and never had been. They came into Beaver Ford at about ten minutes past four in the morning on the 24th of October 1883. Vera Blount’s house was behind her store. There was no light in it.

Wade stopped at her gate and set the lantern down on the ground. Vance got down and was going to say something. He did not know what. Wade said, “Go on and knock.

She will open it. She has done it before. ” Vance said, “Come in with me. ” And Wade Seismore said, “Ria is up there.

” And that was all. He picked the lantern back up, and he turned around, and he walked back up the Cold Water Fork at ten minutes past four in the morning, on foot, alone, with a light. Ellery Vance stood at a gate in Beaver Ford and watched that lantern go up the road and out of sight. He never saw Wade Seismore again for eight years.

He knocked on Vera Blount’s door. She opened it in about forty seconds, with a shawl over her nightclothes and a lamp in her hand. She looked at him, and she did not say, “What is it? ” She did not say, “Do you know what hour it is?

” She said, “How many nights? ” He said, “Thirteen. ” She put him in a chair by a banked fire and built it up and put a quilt over him and made coffee. She did not ask him one single question for better than an hour.

And when he finally started talking, he talked until the sun was well up. And when he was done, Vera Blount went and got her ledger. Every purchase, every customer, every date, going back to 1869. And the reason it matters is a thing she had started doing years before and had never told anybody why.

When a stranger came into her store and bought goods and said he was going down the Cold Water Fork, she wrote it in the margin. Just “cold water. ” Sometimes with the date they said they would come back through. She had been keeping a list of them for fourteen years.

And she said, “You are the fourth. The fourth that has come back to this door out of that hollow in fourteen years. Two of them would not talk about it. One of them talked about it and went queer and hung himself in Rockcastle County in ’79.

You are the fourth. And you are the first one that has come back with paper. ” And Ellery Vance put on her kitchen table a peddler’s daybook out of a wall, and a leaf torn from a register with his own name on it, and a memorandum book with three rules in pencil between a bay mare and two heifers. That is how this case exists at all.

One man got out with three documents, and a storekeeper had been keeping a fourth one for fourteen years. Everything the county ever proved, everything anybody ever wrote down, comes out of those four pieces of paper on a kitchen table in Beaver Ford, Kentucky, on the morning of the 24th of October 1883. The list of nineteen was assembled in 1891 by a newspaperman out of Louisville named Hollis Duff. He cross-checked Vera Blount’s ledger against the county’s letters of inquiry, the letters families wrote to sheriffs when a man did not come home, and then he wrote to the families himself, for two years.

Of the nineteen, seventeen were traced. Of those seventeen, fifteen had buried somebody they loved within roughly three years of the day they rode down that fork. Widowers. Men who had lost children.

Men who had lost wives in childbed. Men who had buried a son of nine years old and taken to traveling for its own sake because they could not be in the house. Silas Meek, who had lost a sister in 1859, and who went into the barn on the 11th of February 1874, and whose last written words were an instruction to tell his brother. Two of the nineteen were never identified at all, never claimed by anybody, names in a register and nothing else.

One, Bethal Craig, twenty-eight, had according to his mother buried nobody. And one, W. Prather of Virginia, is a name and nothing else. Fifteen out of seventeen, which is not a folktale.

Which is a screening process, with a documented success rate, run by a man asking a warm question over supper for thirty-one years on a road with forty travelers a year. Sheriff Bledsoe took Vance’s sworn statement seriously. He was not a lazy man, and he was not in anybody’s pocket. He went up the Cold Water Fork on the 2nd of November 1883, with four men, and stayed two days.

He found a well-kept stand on a well-kept bottom belonging to two brothers named Seismore. He found a barn in excellent repair, with a swept runway. He found the third stall on the left, unbarred, standing open, empty, with a dirt floor, tamped and level, indistinguishable from the floor of any other stall. He found no hats in the corn crib.

He found no register on the shelf by the door, and was told there had never been one. He found no woman named Ria, and was told by Ephraim Seismore that no woman had lived there in years. He went down to the lower end and found the sink and the iron ring, and was told by Ephraim that his father had put the iron around it to keep stock from going in. He put a man on a rope forty feet down.

The man came back up and said there was water and a passage, and it went beyond his light. He found no bones. No clothing. No buttons.

No boots. No coins. Absalom Seismore was not there. Bledsoe asked after him.

Ephraim said his brother had gone out to Missouri. On the 4th of November, Bledsoe wrote in his daybook: “Went up cold water on the Vance complaint. Nothing found. Do not believe the complainant is lying.

Have no idea what to do about it. ” That is the most honest sentence any official in this entire case ever committed to paper. Absalom Seismore does not appear in any record anywhere in the United States after the 23rd of October 1883. Not a census.

Not a deed. Not a tax list. Not a grave. The 1890 census burned in a fire in 1921.

But the Tallow County tax list for 1884 shows the Cold Water bottom in the name of Ephraim. Only Ephraim. Then it will want somebody tonight. I have my own view about what happened in that yard after a lantern went out the lot gate in the wrong direction, and you can tell me yours.

Ellery Vance went home to Bourbon County in November of 1883 and lived another fifty-one years. He never married again. He kept working as a livestock buyer. He changed his circuit: from 1884 to the end of his working life, he did not buy one head of stock in Tallow County or in any county that touched it.

He took a route that added two hundred and ten miles a year and cost him money every single year for twenty-six years. When a partner in Lexington asked him about it in the nineties, he said only that he did not care for the roads down there. He would not sleep in a room whose door did not have a bar on it. He carried a length of ash he had cut himself, planed and squared, thirty-one inches long, in his kit everywhere for the rest of his life, and he put it across the door of every hotel room and boarding house room he ever slept in.

He carried a horseshoe in the left pocket of his coat. Every coat he owned for fifty-one years. It was the same one, worn down to a bright polish on one face by a man’s hand going into a pocket to find out if it was still there. He counted every night of his life.

A niece who lived with him for two years in the 1910s said that if he woke in the night, which he did most nights, you would hear it from the next room. Backward from a hundred, in a low voice, sometimes once, sometimes for an hour. She asked him about it exactly once, when she was nineteen. He told her the truth, all of it, in about ten minutes, in the kitchen, and then said, “And now I have told you, and I would be obliged if you would not ask me again.

” And here is the last mark. He never tapped a cup again. He had picked it up off a woman who tapped her thumbnail twice against a rim before she drank, carried it out of her life into his own, without knowing. And something in a hollow in Tallow County had watched him do it for eleven days, and had knocked on a door with it at midnight.

So he stopped. Deliberately. He told Coyle that it took him the better part of a year, and that he had to put his hand flat on the table sometimes to do it. He looked at the last little living gesture of a woman dead four years, running in his own hands without his permission, and he put it down and walked away from it, because it was ammunition.

That is what that hollow took off Thomas Ellery Vance. It did not get his life. It got that. In the spring of 1891, Vance was riding a circuit in Estill County, and at a ford on Station Camp Creek, he came up on a man watering a team.

The man straightened up and looked at him. It was Wade Seismore, thirty years old, with a full beard, thin, hauling for a lumber outfit. They stood in that creek for the better part of an hour. Neither of them ever told anybody the whole of what was said.

But Vance told Coyle four things. Wade got Ria Vessels out of that house in the spring of 1884, five months after the night of the lantern. He did not say how. Vance did not ask.

He never carried one. Vance asked him directly. Wade said, “No. ” Vance said, “Not once?

” And Wade said, “Not once. And I have got nothing else. ” Ephraim was still on that bottom in 1891, alone. Wade had not spoken to him since ’84.

And Wade said, “He is not lonesome. There is somebody in that house with him. And I do not know which one of them it is. ” And Vance asked whether he ever thought about going back.

Wade said, “Every day of my life. And I will tell you what stops me. It is not being afraid. It is that I know exactly how it would go.

I would walk down that fork, and I would get to the yard, and Absalom would come off that porch with his hands up, like he does, and he would say, ‘Well, now. ’ And I would be twenty-two years old again. And I would be glad. That is the thing about that place, Mr.

Vance. It never once made me do nothing. It just waited for me to want to. ”

Ria Vessels appears in the record twice more.

In 1892, she is listed in Osley County, Kentucky, as the keeper of a boarding house in Booneville, under her own name. And she is buried in the church ground at Beaver Ford, in Tallow County, under a stone that has her name on it, and the dates 1853 to 1929, cut properly, at the expense of somebody. And there is another stone in that same church ground, forty feet away, with no date on it at all, over a woman who lived in a cabin with a puncheon floor, and cut “Ester, 1791” into the underside of her own mantle with a chisel, so that somebody someday would know she had been there. Ria Vessels got a date.

The Seismore stand stood empty from about 1898. Ephraim’s name comes off the tax list that year, and there is no record of what became of him. The house fell in sometime before the first war. The barn stood a great deal longer, because it was extremely well built, by a man who had a reason to build it well.

It came down in a wet March in 1926, all at once, in on itself. The county put a gravel road up the Cold Water Fork in 1931. It goes past the bottom. There is nothing to see from it but a flat piece of ground with a stone chimney standing in it, and eleven apple trees in two rows.

They were still there in the 1950s. A man from the state agricultural extension, who had no idea what he was looking at, noted them in a survey because they were an old variety he wanted to identify. He wrote in his report that the stand was unusual in that the trees were of a remarkably uniform size and habit, and that he was unable to age them by the usual means. He wrote that in 1952.

Exactly one hundred years after Jeppa Seismore built a barn over a hole. Thomas Ellery Vance died on the 9th of January, 1934, at his farm outside Paris, Kentucky, at eighty-five years old, of pneumonia, in the room he had slept in for thirty-eight years. His grand-niece was in the house, the same woman who at nineteen had asked him once about the counting, forty years old by then, come to nurse him. She said that at some point after midnight on the 8th, she came out of her room because she heard him talking.

She stood in the hall outside his door. And she heard a woman’s voice on the porch say, “Ellery. ” Not loud. The volume you would use for somebody about fifteen feet away.

And she heard her great-uncle, who was eighty-five years old, and who had not been able to sit up by himself in four days, say out loud in the dark, in a perfectly clear voice, “100. 99. 98. ” She went in.

He had his eyes shut. His left hand was in the pocket of the coat that was hanging on the bedpost beside him. She sat down on the edge of the bed and took his other hand, and she counted with him. They went down from a hundred to naught four times, out loud, the two of them, in a cold bedroom in Bourbon County, Kentucky, in January of 1934, while something stood on the porch and said his name.

She said that partway through the fourth pass, it stopped saying his name. And after that, there was nothing on the porch. He lived another day and a half. In the middle of the afternoon of the 9th, he was awake and clear, looking at the window.

And he said one thing to her. It is the last recorded sentence of Thomas Ellery Vance. He said, “It never did get her right, you know. Not once in fifty years.

Not one time. ” She said, “No, uncle. ” And he said, “Well. ” And that is all.

Among his effects, in an oilcloth packet in the drawer of a bedside table, there were four things, kept in order. The daybook of Silas Meek, peddler of Osley County, begun June 1871, ending mid-sentence on the 11th of February 1874. A livestock buyer’s memorandum book for the year 1883, with three rules written in pencil between a bay mare and two heifers. A leaf torn from the register of the Seismore stand, with his own name and a mark beside it, and the word “kept” in the margin, and under the word, a place where the paper had been rubbed thin.

And a horseshoe, worn bright on one face. There was also a page in his own hand, undated, written in old age, folded around the register leaf. It said: “To whoever gets this after me. It is in Tallow County, Kentucky, on the Cold Water Fork, and it is still there, because it does not die, and it does not move, and it does not need to.

It cannot make anything. It can only take a copy. Everything I have told anybody about it comes down to that one thing. So do not give it anything to copy.

Do not say your dead out loud on that ground. Count backward out loud from a hundred, and when you lose it, go back to a hundred, and do not ever guess. And understand what it wants. Because it is not your life.

It does not want your life. It wants the little pieces of the people you have lost that you are carrying around without knowing you have got them. I gave up one of mine to keep it out. I would do it again.

But I want it wrote down somewhere by somebody that I did not want to. ” The leaf from the register still exists. It was photographed in 1954 under a raking light, sideways, which is how you read an erasure. In the photograph, the mark is there.

The word “kept” is there, in that small, tight hand that did not change in thirty-one years. And under the word kept, rubbed out with a thumb or a crumb of bread, there is an earlier word. It is not certain. But it is readable.

It is seven letters. And the last of them has a tail that goes below the line. The word is “waiting. ”

I think Absalom Seismore marked that name on the 11th of October 1883, the way he had marked ninety before it.

And I think he wrote “waiting,” because the decision was not his to make. Because his youngest brother was twenty-two years old, and had not carried one, and it was overdue. And the argument had been going on since the summer. And Absalom, whatever else he was, was a man who kept a ledger honestly.

The man was marked, and the family was not ready. And I think that at some point in the days after, somebody—something—rubbed that word out and wrote “kept” over the top of it. And the hand that wrote “kept” on that leaf is the same hand that wrote it in 1854 and 1866 and 1874, unchanged, identical, in a book kept in a house where three men lived, none of whom wrote like that. Which means the thing in that hole did not wait to be brought a man.

It read the book. And it corrected it. And that is the one and only time in thirty-one years, in something like ninety names, that the book was ever wrong. Because Thomas Ellery Vance rode out of the Cold Water Fork at four in the morning on the 24th of October 1883, behind a boy with a lantern, counting out loud, and he lived another fifty-one years, and died in his own bed with his hand in his coat pocket.

It wrote “kept. ” And it did not get him. A thing that cannot make anything new, that had copied every voice and every habit and every last ten minutes of ninety frightened people for three decades, made exactly one original statement in its entire existence. One word, in a margin, in a book by a door.

And it was a lie. Everybody in this story was warned. Every single one. Vera Blount gave her three and closed her mouth.

Ria Vessels gave her three at a stove, before daylight. Audi Redwine sat at the top of that hollow for sixty-one years with a door that opened, and gave her three to anybody who walked up. Silas Meek wrote his down and put them in a wall for a stranger. Nobody in this case ever died of not being told.

So the question is not whether you would have gone into the barn. Everybody says no to that one. The question is this: somewhere in your own life, there is a voice you would open a door for. You know which one it is.

And if that voice said your name tonight—the one that only they used, the one nobody else on this earth has ever called you, from a place it could not possibly be, at an hour when the house is quiet—and it said, “I am cold out here,” are you certain you would count?
