That word was buried, and the ground around the church was struck from every county map and every railroad map printed after 1867. The congregation, the preacher, the wagons, the eleven-day sermon, and the thing the report said the preacher had been reading from, all of it went into a sealed drawer in the National Archives that was not opened again until 1994. Yet what came out of that drawer in 1994 was not what the archivists expected.

This is not a story about a cult. It is not a story about a hoax. It is a story that suggests something entered the Sacramento River Delta after the war, took the form of a rural preacher, and read before a full hall for eleven days from a book that three witnesses swore was, by the fifth day, reading itself to him. It is a story about what the ground swallowed on the morning of the twelfth day.

And what a 1971 survey team found still resonates under six feet of Mississippi mud. To understand what happened in that wooden church, you must understand the Mississippi Delta of 1866. And to understand the Delta of 1866, you must accept an uncomfortable fact about the year the American Civil War ended. The war did not end in April of 1865.

That is what the textbooks say because that is what the surrender documents say. And the surrender documents are the polished version of history. What actually happened in the Deep South, and in the Mississippi Delta specifically, is that the war stopped and began to fade. Whole counties fell silent, a silence that was not supposed to exist.

Entire towns were emptied. Entire families left homes that were still furnished, still provisioned, still standing, and never returned. The post-war Mississippi Delta became a region the federal government lacked the manpower to patrol, the money to survey, or even the desire to visit. The Freedmen's Bureau kept records, but those records were kept in Vicksburg, Natchez, and Jackson.

The country between those cities was, practically speaking, rumor. Rivers had changed course during the flood years of 1863 and 1864. Roads that existed on the 1860 militia maps were now submerged, or overgrown with kudzu, or gone entirely. The compilers of the 1870 census admitted in a margin almost no one read that entire census districts in the western Delta were, as the margin recorded, "not resolvable by any living inhabitant willing to speak of it.

"

That was the country where a church stood on a low rise between two oxbow lakes that appear on no modern map, because the river changed course again in 1874 and swallowed them. The freedmen who lived in a cluster of cabins about a mile east of the rise called it Ashton Point. The name came not from the elm trees, but from the shape of the land after a thunderstorm that swept across it every spring since time out of mind. The rise attracted lightning the way a metal rod attracts it.

Old survey markers from the 1840s noted the location as "an iron anomaly, to be avoided when using the compass. " The men who set those markers were surveyors for the state land office, cautious men, and it is recorded that they feared this place. By the summer of 1866, Ashton Point held a small church. No one among the freedmen in the cabins a mile east remembered the church being built.

No one in the nearest white settlement, a small village called Rain's Ferry about four miles south, remembered carpenters being hired. The wooden church simply existed one morning, a small rectangular building with one door, one window, and a roof of split cypress. It had a bell, but the bell had no clapper. It had a pulpit, but the pulpit held no Bible.

It had pews for perhaps forty people, and they sat empty through most of that spring, the way a theater set sits empty before the actors arrive. The first man to take notice of the church and record his observation was a Union quartermaster named Elias Rothven, attached to the occupation garrison at Vicksburg. Rothven was, by all accounts, a highly competent man. He kept lists and filed reports.

Before the war he had been an accountant in Cincinnati, and after the war he desperately wanted to return to being an accountant in Cincinnati. In June of 1866 his commander sent him upriver on a supply survey mission, after rumors reached the garrison of a gathering of unregistered people in the western Delta. The army wanted an accurate count before deciding whether to send troops. Rothven wrote a letter to his wife on the evening of June 18, 1866, from the porch of a widow's house in Rain's Ferry.

That letter survives. It is currently in a private collection in Charleston, reproduced in two academic publications, both long out of print. In the letter, Rothven describes the widow's face when he asked her about the little church that seemed to have appeared out of nowhere. He wrote that she went pale, put her hand on the table, and told him in a voice he could barely hear that the church had been there since winter; that no one had built it; that a preacher had arrived in early June; and that the preacher had begun holding services on the first Sunday of that month.

She told Rothven she had not attended. She told him her son had attended, and that he had come home and not eaten for three days, and would not speak of what he had heard, and on the fourth day he left the house before dawn and went to the church and did not come back. Rothven noted, in the same letter, that while the widow spoke, a dog under the porch began to whine in a tone he had never heard before. He asked if the dog was injured.

The widow said, "That is what the dog does when the wind blows. " Rothven checked his pocket watch, which held a small barometer, and noted that the wind that evening was, according to his instrument, perfectly still. He wrote to his wife: "I do not think I will sleep tonight, and I do not think I will write to you again from this county. " He never wrote to her again from that county.

He wrote to her later, from a hospital in Memphis in September, and by then he could not hold a pen, so he dictated the letter to a nurse. The preacher arrived at Ashton Point on the morning of Sunday, June 3, 1866. That date is undisputed. It appears in the widow's testimony, in an interview conducted by the Freedmen's Bureau in October of that year with a laborer named Absalom Reed, and in a letter sent by a traveling Baptist preacher named Josiah Hemp to his bishop in Jackson, complaining that a stranger had begun preaching in his district without a letter of introduction, denominational affiliation, or any visible means of support.

Hemp's letter was filed and forgotten. It was rediscovered in the 1980s when a graduate student at Ole Miss, reviewing parish records for a thesis on post-war religion in the American South, found it wedged between two pages of a hymnal, apparently used as a bookmark. Hemp writes that he first heard of the preacher on June 2 from a farmhand in Rain's Ferry who claimed to have seen the stranger walking up the road from the river that morning. According to the farmhand, the man was tall and thin, wearing a black coat cut in a way no horseman had ever seen, with an unusually high collar and buttons in a single row on the side instead of the front.

The farmhand said the man carried no bag, no book, no cane, no rain coat, though a heavy rain had fallen the night before and the road was, in the farmhand's words, as wet as any road in the state. The man's boots were dry. Hemp wrote that he found the farmhand's account strange but not alarming. What alarmed him was a second account from an elderly freedwoman named Delia Bright, who lived in one of the eastern cabins.

Delia told Hemp, when he went to her cabin on June 5 for his own inquiries, that she had seen the preacher pass her cabin on the morning of the third, and that he stopped at her gate and asked, in a voice "low and gentle as a well," whether her family was well. Delia said she answered yes. The preacher then asked if the children of her family had been baptized. Delia said she answered yes to that too.

The preacher smiled, she said, and asked a third question, which she would not repeat at the time of Hemp's visit. Two weeks later, in an interview with a Bureau agent who had come to inquire about something else, Delia was persuaded to repeat the question. According to the agent's field notes, preserved in the Bureau archives in Vicksburg, the preacher asked Delia: "And were they baptized with the second water? " Delia asked him what the second water was.

She said the preacher smiled again and told her, "You will know when you hear the bell. " He continued walking up the road toward the rise. As established, the church bell had no clapper. It had not rung in living memory.

Delia would later swear, in an affidavit given in 1868 in a lawsuit that never went to trial, that on the evening of June 3, 1866, the bell at Ashton Point rang three times at intervals of approximately one minute, and that its sound was not, as she said, "the sound of a bell to be remembered. " That is what she said, literally, and the affidavit was signed with her mark and witnessed by a lawyer named Cassius Pearl, who died within eighteen months under circumstances the Vicksburg coroner refused to specify. By sunset on June 3, the church at Ashton Point had a preacher, a ringing bell, and a congregation estimated at sixteen people, by Delia's reckoning. By the following Sunday, June 10, the congregation numbered sixty-two, according to a note pinned to the back of the door and copied down by a Bureau agent.

By June 17, the congregation was too large for the church, and the preacher began holding service on the packed earth outside, the door open, and his voice, according to three separate witnesses, carrying downwind a distance no normal human voice should carry. The preacher identified himself, if he identified himself at all, as Brother Ela. He gave no surname. He gave no denomination.

When a visiting Methodist minister from Yazoo City, on the fourth Sunday, asked where he had been ordained, Brother Ela answered, according to two witnesses, "By a hand that has not finished writing me. " The Methodist minister left before the service began. He wrote to his bishop the following week that he had been in the company of a man he did not believe to be a man, and that he would not return to the Mississippi Delta under any circumstances as long as the preacher holding the pulpit was still standing. No two people who saw Brother Ela gave matching physical descriptions.

He was tall in one account, medium height in another. His hair was dark in the widow's memory, gray at the temples in Delia's. His eyes were described, in every account, as light. Otherwise, no two witnesses agreed.

The horseman from Rain's Ferry, when asked years later to describe the man, said only: "I do not remember his face, and I remember every face I have ever tied a horse to. "

The strangest thing, however, is what Brother Ela did in his first evening at Ashton Point, in the last hour before he stood at the pulpit to deliver his first sermon. According to Absalom Reed, who was hired by the preacher himself that day to bring water for the church's baptismal font, Brother Ela went out to the packed-earth yard at about five in the afternoon, knelt, and placed both hands flat on the ground. Reed said he remained that way for about half an hour, without moving, speaking, or appearing to breathe.

At the end of that half hour, the preacher rose, dusted his palms once, returned to the church, and rang the bell that had no clapper three times, in Reed's words, "by pointing at it. " Reed said he did not see the preacher touch the bell. He said the bell simply rang when the preacher pointed at it, and that the sound of the third ring hung in the air of the yard for a length of time Reed, a practical man and former plantation blacksmith, did not attempt to measure in seconds because he did not believe the seconds on his watch kept passing while the bell rang. That is the man who opened the eleven-day sermon on the evening of June 3, 1866.

The first sermon began at sunset and continued without interruption until sunrise on the fourth. The eleven days were not eleven days punctuated by rest periods. They were, according to two records preserved from inside the church itself, a single continuous sermon that paused only when the preacher himself paused, and his pauses over the eleven days totaled no more than four hours. This is physically impossible.

No human throat can produce continuous audible speech for eleven days. No human body can go without sleep for eleven days while maintaining the ability to speak. The Bureau agent who took the testimony of the musician Rubin Alt, hired to accompany the first four services on a small hand organ, wrote in the margin of Alt's testimony: "The witness insists on the duration of eleven days. The witness refuses to amend his statement.

The witness produced a watch and a calendar to confirm the agent's inability to explain. " Alt's testimony is the closest thing to an accurate record of what happened inside the church during the first three days. Alt was a free man of color from New Orleans, who had come across the river looking for work as a musician in one of the Vicksburg hotels, and had been recruited at the docks by a man he did not recognize, who paid him in advance, in silver, for four days of playing. Alt said he arrived at the church on the evening of June 2, a full day before the preacher arrived, and that the church was empty that evening.

The door was open, and the pump organ was already placed beside the pulpit. Alt said he did not know who brought the organ, that it was a make he did not recognize, and that the keys, as he said, were warm when he first touched them. He began playing at sunset on the third as ordered. He was given no hymns to play.

The preacher told him to play whatever the congregation asked for, and that he would know what they asked for. Alt said that in the first hour he played a slow melody in D minor he had never heard before and could not afterwards recall, and that the congregation, seated in the pews and standing in the aisle, listened to the melody without moving, without coughing, without shifting in their seats. At the end of the first hour, the preacher rose, went to the pulpit, opened a book that was lying on the pulpit shelf, and began to read. Alt did not see the book clearly that night.

He said it appeared to be a volume bound in black leather, with a cover free of any lettering, and pages, in his words, "thicker than any Bible page I have seen in my life, and yellower than any book with such a cover. " He said the preacher read from the book through the entire first night, from sunset to sunrise, turning no more than about ten pages, and that the words the preacher spoke were English that night, although an English Alt did not recognize. When asked to give an example of what the preacher said, Alt refused. He said he could remember the sentences, but he had promised himself on the fourth day never to repeat them aloud.

The Bureau agent noted that Alt, when faced with this question, began to cry, in a manner the agent described as "silent and continuous, without any change in the witness's expression. " The agent did not press him further. The second night began at sunset on June 4. The congregation had grown to about forty people.

The preacher had not left the pulpit. He had not eaten, and he had not, as far as Alt knew, drunk any water. He preached through the entire day without pause, in a voice that did not grow hoarse, in a language that shifted, at some point during the daylight hours, from English into a language Alt did not recognize. Alt spoke French and some Spanish, and some Choctaw he had learned at the docks, but this was not a human language he knew.

The congregation did not seem to notice the change. They responded to the preacher's words with faint affirmations—"yes," "amen," "let it be"—though the words they were affirming were in a language none of them had learned, as far as Alt knew. Alt said he asked the woman seated near him at the end of a pew what the preacher had just said. The woman turned to him and told him, in a voice Alt described as "gentle and somewhat puzzled," that the preacher had just spoken the name of her mother, who had died in 1859, and that she had not heard her mother's name spoken aloud in seven years, and that she was very happy to hear it now.

Alt said he did not sleep the second night. He said he was not sure afterwards whether anyone in the church had slept, or whether the congregation had felt the passage of night at all. He said the light of the second sunrise creeping through the church's single window surprised him on the morning of the fifth, and that when he looked at his watch, he found it had stopped, and he could not remember when it had stopped, and the hands pointed to a time that was not any hour of the night he had lived. By the third day, June 6, the crowds had outgrown the walls of the church.

Word had reached Rain's Ferry, and the freedmen's cabins to the east, and also, through two riverboat pilots who had docked for wood at a landing four miles downstream, the town of Rolling Fork, twenty miles south. By the afternoon of June 6, wagons were arriving on the road to Ashton Point at the rate of one every quarter hour. The preacher had begun to step out of the church between passages of his reading, walk to the door, and call out into the yard the names of specific people who were arriving on the road at that very moment, before they appeared in sight. Rubin Alt said that at noon on June 6, the preacher went to the door and called out the name Cornelius Duval, and three minutes later a wagon appeared around a bend in the road, driven by a man named Cornelius Duval, and that Cornelius Duval had not met the preacher, spoken to him, or sent him any word, as far as anyone in the church later knew.

Alt said this happened forty-seven times over the course of June 6 alone. He said that by the evening of June 6, he had stopped playing the organ, because the preacher no longer needed musical accompaniment, and he went to sit in the last pew and began to pray for the first time in his life. That was the end of the first three days. The church was full.

The road was crowded. The preacher was still standing. According to a testimony Alt never gave in court, but disclosed on his deathbed in 1891 to a Catholic priest in New Orleans, the book on the pulpit had begun turning its own pages while the preacher spoke. At this book, the story stops being a strange incident in post-war Mississippi and begins to resemble something else entirely.

All the surviving accounts—from Alt, to Absalom Reed, to the widow at Rain's Ferry, to the Bureau agents who came later and interrogated the survivors—converge on the book. The preacher preached from it. The congregation listened to it. The church itself, in a sense that will become clear as this story continues, had been built specifically to contain it.

On the morning of the fifth day, according to the private testimony Alt gave to the priest at Charity Hospital in 1891, the book was reading itself. This is not a metaphor. Alt told the priest, who recorded it in a private notebook that would later find its way through a chain of church donations to the special collections at Loyola University, that on the morning of June 7, the fifth day of the sermon, he looked up from the pew where he sat and saw the pages of the book turning one by one in a steady rhythm, untouched by any hand. And that the preacher's voice began at that moment to align with the turning of the pages, as if the preacher was no longer reading the book, but being read by it.

Alt said the pages were not turning from wind. There was no wind in the church. The window was closed. The door was closed.

The air in the church, in Alt's words, was "thick and still as the air in a jar. " The pages were turning on their own. The preacher stood at the pulpit, speaking the words that appeared on each page as it settled, in a voice that by the fifth day was not entirely his own. Alt said the voice had begun to contain, alongside the preacher's tone, a second tone, deeper, and a third, higher.

By the sixth day, there was a fourth tone that was not, Alt said, a tone at all, but merely the impression of one. A sound the ear captures without any physical vibration to account for it. Alt said the congregation, by the sixth day, had begun to sway in unison. The swaying followed the rhythm of the page-turning, and the rhythm of the page-turning had begun to accelerate.

What was in the book has remained speculation for over a century and a half. The book itself is in no museum. The book itself, according to the Union officers who reached the church three weeks later, was not on the pulpit when they opened the door. The pulpit was bare.

The pews were empty. The church was empty. But there were marks on the wooden shelf of the pulpit. Faint rectangular marks of a book that had rested there long enough to bleach the wood beneath it.

An officer named Lyman Post measured these marks: eleven inches by seven inches and three inches deep. Post included these measurements in his report—he was accustomed to measuring things, being an accountant. The measurements, with everything in the report, went into the drawer in Washington. Three serious attempts have since been made, over a century and a half, to identify the book that might have stood on that pulpit.

All have failed, because no known book of those dimensions and specifications matches the witnesses' accounts. The first attempt, in 1890, was by a Boston bookseller named Everett Chase, who obtained a torn page that a former Confederate soldier claimed to have recovered from the site in 1867. Chase examined the page under bright light and concluded that the paper was made of fibers he could not identify, the ink was of a composition no chemist could analyze, and the language, whatever it was, was written in a script that read from top to bottom and right to left simultaneously, in a manner he called "folded. " The page was later lost when Chase's shop burned in the Great Boston Fire of 1892.

His notes survived. The second attempt, in 1931, was by a Yale linguist named Harmon Gault, who, through personal friendship with the Librarian of Congress, was permitted to review the sealed file on the Ashton Point incident. Gault was allowed to read the file for six hours in a locked room in the Library of Congress basement. He was not allowed to take notes.

He was allowed to leave with what he remembered. What he remembered, as he later wrote in a private letter to a colleague in Cambridge, was a description of a text that could not exist, and if it existed, could not be read. Gault's letter was published in expurgated form in a volume of his collected correspondence, brought out by his heirs in 1958, and the censored passages were restored in an academic edition in 2009. The third and final attempt to identify the book was in 1994, when the drawer in Washington was reopened.

This attempt was made by a team that included a paleographer, a chemist, a historian of religions, and a Jesuit consultant to the Vatican's Index of Prohibited Books. The team could not identify the book. The team did, however, manage to compare the descriptions in the 1866 witness statements, the 1867 Union report, and the Chase and Gault materials, and concluded, in a final memorandum that was immediately classified, that the book at Ashton Point matched no known religious text of any religion in any recorded language, and that its closest analogue in the historical record was a book mentioned in three late-medieval European manuscripts in the phrase, in the original Latin, "Liber Qui Se Ipse Legit"—roughly translated, the book that reads itself. The medieval manuscripts that mention the Liber Qui Se Ipse Legit are entirely unhelpful.

They mention the book only to warn against it, without describing it, sourcing it, or identifying anyone who has read it. They warn only that the book, wherever it appears, appears in a place that will not exist afterwards, and that those who hear the book read aloud will not afterwards be counted among the living or the dead, but among a third category the manuscripts decline to name. Ashton Point, on the morning of June 15, 1866, was such a place. The rise was still there.

The church was still there. But the road to it, according to a Bureau employee who tried to ride it on the sixteenth, was no longer a road. It had become, at a certain distance from the church, ground the employee's horse refused to cross, and beyond that, when the employee tried to proceed on foot, he found that his footsteps left no impression, though the ground was soft and wet, and though his boots, when he lifted and examined them, were covered, in his words, with a mud that was not the mud of any river bottom his feet had ever touched. The book was still on the pulpit, turning its pages.

The preacher was still reading. By June 15, the congregation no longer went home at night. They slept, if they slept at all, in the yard and in the wagons parked along the road. According to Delia Bright's testimony, they arranged themselves on the packed earth before the church in a formation no one had planned and no one afterwards remembered choosing.

Delia said the formation was a circle within a circle within a circle. The innermost circle was left empty, as if something was expected to arrive and stand in it. On the fourth day of the sermon, June 7, the surviving record begins to fade, because that is the day Rubin Alt left. He did not walk out of the church.

He did not decide to leave, as far as anyone later knew. He said in his testimony that at some point in the afternoon of the seventh, he rose from his seat, walked to the door, went out into the yard, and kept walking, without any definite intention, and did not stop until he reached the landing four miles downriver, where he boarded a steamboat in a condition he did not remember, and paid for his passage back to Vicksburg. He remembered arriving in Vicksburg on the morning of June 9. He did not remember the steamboat journey, or the night that followed.

When he examined his watch in Vicksburg, he found it still stopped at an hour that was not an hour he had lived. He offered no explanation in his testimony for what drove him out of the church. He said only that at a certain moment during the reading on the afternoon of the seventh, he understood something about the book he had not understood before, and that this understanding made it impossible for him to remain in the room. Alt never disclosed in his testimony what he understood.

He repeated that understanding, in whole or in part, only once in the remaining twenty-five years of his life, on his deathbed, to the priest at Charity Hospital in New Orleans, and the priest recorded the conversation in a private journal that the Loyola archives have not made public to this day. The archives have confirmed the journal's existence and date, and that its final entry, in the priest's own hand, is a single sentence in French, which translates: "I will not write what he told me, but I will pray all my life that no one but him ever tells me. "

The record that reaches us from the fourth day is the testimony of Absalom Reed and the testimony of Delia Bright. Reed said that on the afternoon of the seventh, the preacher, for the first time, called members of the congregation forward to be baptized.

Reed said seventeen people came forward, and that the preacher led them one by one to the font at the front of the church, and baptized them not with water but with something else. The Bureau agent pressed him on this point, asking what was in the font if not water. Reed answered that he had filled the font with his own hands from the well that morning, and that the water was ordinary well water when he brought it. He said that as the first baptism began, the water in the font changed to a color he did not name and thickened to a consistency he did not name, and began to radiate, in his words, "a warmth as if it remembered being alive.

" Reed said the preacher immersed each of the seventeen people in the font, holding their heads under for a count Reed could not make because his counting stopped working correctly at that moment, and then raised them. Reed said each of the seventeen rose from the font without gasping, without shaking water from their faces, without any expression on their faces except a faint, gentle smile, which Reed said remained on their faces all that day, and none of them noticed that they were smiling. Delia Bright, in her testimony, confirmed Reed's account of the baptisms and added a detail Reed did not mention. She said the preacher, after each baptism, bent down and whispered a word into the ear of the person he had baptized, and that this word, in none of the seventeen cases, was the person's own name.

Delia was standing near the font and heard some of the words, but she did not repeat any of them in her testimony. She said only that the words were, on her tongue, "names of days," and that when the seventeenth person had been baptized and named, the preacher straightened up, returned to the pulpit, and read again. From that day on, his voice began to sound to Delia like a blend of the voices of the seventeen people he had just baptized, in a single tone. The fifth day, June 8, is the day the book began turning its own pages.

The sixth day, June 9, is the day the road to the church stopped being a road. On the seventh day, June 10, the color of the sky above the rise changed, according to a witness in Rain's Ferry who was watching through a brass telescope from the widow's porch. The witness was a retired riverboat pilot named Amos Slade, who had bought the telescope in New Orleans in 1850 and spent the war watching Union gunboats through it. Slade said the sky above the rise on the afternoon of the tenth took on a color he had seen only once before in his life, on the horizon south of Hispaniola during a storm in 1847 which killed thirty-one men of his crew in forty minutes.

Slade described the color as "not the color of a storm, but the color of a curtain being drawn. " He said it began as a thin line along the highest point of the rise and spread, over the course of the afternoon, downward in a pattern he had never seen in weather. He said it settled by sunset of the tenth into a dome over the church, perhaps two hundred feet high, with a distinct edge, as if the sky had been cut with a knife, and that this edge did not move with the wind. Slade said he set the telescope aside on the evening of the tenth and never touched it again for the rest of his life.

He mentioned that the telescope, sitting in its case in his attic, sometimes made a faint humming sound on quiet nights, which he never bothered to investigate. Inside the church on the evening of the tenth, the seventh day of the sermon, the congregation had grown to a number no one was ever able to determine precisely. Bureau estimates, based on the Union wagon count taken three weeks later, and on descriptions from neighboring residents, ranged from three hundred to four hundred. Delia Bright insisted in her testimony that the number was above four hundred, and that among that number were people she never saw arrive on the road, people she did not recognize from any of the neighboring counties, and people whose clothing, in her words, "did not look like the clothing of anyone living in this year.

" She was asked what year the clothing looked like it was for. She answered that she could not answer that question, because the clothing did not look like it was from any particular year, but from years that had not yet happened. The Bureau agent recorded the answer without comment and moved on to another subject. The testimony is preserved in the file.

The agent's name is struck out in the signature line at the bottom of the page, replaced with an initial, and no personnel record at the Vicksburg garrison has ever been found to match that initial. The eighth day, June 11; the ninth, June 12; and the tenth, June 13 passed in a silence that surviving witnesses in Rain's Ferry and in the freedmen's cabins described in nearly identical terms. The dome over the rise, Slade's cut-out sky, did not move. The church bell did not ring, according to two witnesses who approached as close as they dared, but a faint sound continued to come from the direction of the church, a sound Slade described in a letter to his son as "the sound of a very large room breathing.

" No one from Rain's Ferry approached the rise during those three days. No one from the freedmen's cabins approached it either. Delia Bright stopped going up after June 10. She said in her testimony that she felt on the morning of the eleventh that if she went up the road again, she would not come back this time.

What happened inside the church on the eighth, ninth, and tenth days can only be reconstructed through the testimony of a single surviving witness, and this witness never spoke publicly. He was a man named Josiah Kane, a white farmer from the far north of Yazoo County, who rode to Ashton Point on June 6 out of curiosity, having heard about the preacher from a traveling salesman at a crossroads. Kane entered the church and he came out of it. Kane, according to the doctor who examined him in Vicksburg on June 17, was physically sound, uninjured, able to eat, drink, and sign his name.

He was, however, unable to speak. He was not mute in the literal sense, and he was not deaf. He answered spoken questions by writing his answers in a hand his wife recognized on a slate the doctor placed in his lap. The answers he wrote during an examination that lasted one afternoon are preserved in the doctor's notebook, which was donated to the Mississippi State Medical Society in 1911 and is today in the archives of the University of Mississippi Medical Center in Jackson.

Kane's answers occupy four pages. They are, together, the only direct account of what went on inside the church during the last three days of the sermon, and they are, together, the reason the Ashton Point file was hidden. Kane wrote that the preacher, by the eighth day, had stopped speaking in any language at all, and began instead to emit, in his ordinary voice, a sequence of sounds Kane described on the slate as "sounds a room makes when it is being rearranged. " Kane wrote that the congregation, by the eighth day, had stopped swaying and began to produce a humming in unison, in a tone that was not among any known musical notes, and that this humming grew during the eighth day until it filled the inside of the church to such a degree that the wooden walls, according to Kane, began to visibly vibrate.

Kane wrote that on the ninth day the vibration extended to the floor, and that by the ninth day's noon, the floor was no longer a floor of wooden planks but appeared, when Kane looked down, as a floor of moving lines that reminded him of the surface of a river seen from a bridge. Kane wrote that on the tenth day, the inner circle of the formation on the packed earth in front of the church—the empty circle Delia Bright described—was no longer empty. Kane wrote that something was standing in it. He did not describe what it was.

He wrote on the slate, and the doctor recorded the sentence in a hand that was visibly shaking, "I will not describe its shape in words, because shape is a word. " Kane wrote that on the morning of the eleventh day, June 14, the preacher closed the book. According to Kane, the book closed itself under the preacher's hand. The preacher turned to the congregation.

He spoke in his original voice for the first time in six days. The preacher said one sentence. Kane refused to write the sentence on the slate. Instead, he drew a small mark, which the doctor described in the margin of his notebook as "resembling nothing so much as a door.

" Kane pointed to the mark and wrote beneath it, "This is the meaning. " Kane wrote that upon hearing the sentence, the congregation rose from their seats and walked in perfect order, without any verbal signal, out of the church and into the yard, where they arranged themselves inside the circles on the packed earth. Kane wrote that he rose with them, but that he was unable, for reasons he did not understand, to leave the church, and found himself standing alone in the aisle as the last of the congregation filed past him. Kane wrote that the preacher was the last to leave, and that the preacher passed him in the aisle.

The preacher looked at Kane once and said to him, in English, in a voice Kane described as, as he wrote, "the voice of a man I knew in Yazoo, who has been dead for eleven years. " Four words. Kane wrote the four words on the slate. The doctor recorded them in the case file.

The words read, as written, "You may go home. " Kane wrote that he walked out of the church and found the yard empty. The congregation was gone. The preacher was gone.

The three circles on the packed earth were still there, and the inner circle was empty again. Kane wrote that the ground inside the inner circle was "giving off a faint smoke, as if a fire had recently been put out in it, though there was no fire. " Though there was no fire. Kane wrote that he walked down the road, and that the road was clear this time, and that he reached Rain's Ferry by the evening of the fourteenth, ate a meal at the widow's house, and went to bed, and that when he woke on the morning of the fifteenth, he could not speak.

Kane never spoke again. He lived on his farm in Yazoo County for another thirty-one years. He died in 1897 of complications from a cold in the chest. His slate was buried with him at his request.

His wife wrote to the doctor who had examined him that in all those thirty-one years, Kane had never, as far as she knew, attempted to speak. She wrote that on quiet evenings he would sit on the porch and look toward Ashton Point, though the point itself was thirty miles south and had long been underwater, and that on those evenings his lips would move, forming the four words the preacher had said to him, without ever making a sound. The federal army detachment from Vicksburg reached Ashton Point on July 3, 1866. It had taken them three weeks to come north through the flooded country, and by the time they arrived, the church was already sealed.

The sealing was not done by the federal army. Someone had returned to the church between June 14 and July 3, closed the door, wrapped the door frame in an iron chain the Union officers estimated at eight feet in total length, and filled every crack in the door frame and the base of every wall with quicklime. No one in the surrounding area admitted to the act. No one in Rain's Ferry came out to see the officers.

The freedmen in the eastern cabins told the Union commander that the church's roof had been built in a single night during the third week of June, by unknown persons, and that they had heard, from a mile away, the sound of the chain being drawn tight and a sound they described as "singing that was not singing in the ordinary sense of the word" coming from around the church as the roof was built. The Union officer in charge of the detachment that reached Ashton Point on July 3 was a captain named Lyman Post. Post was a Vermonter, a Middlebury graduate, and a veteran of the Wilderness campaign. Before the war he had kept the books of a small woolen mill outside Rutland.

The accuracy of his bookkeeping is why we possess the measurements of the pulpit shelf. It is also why the sealed Ashton Point file contains, at its center, a report that is not the report the War Department wanted him to file. Post filed two reports. The first was the one his commander in Vicksburg requested: a routine survey of unregistered activity in the western Delta, filed on July 16, 1866.

As mentioned at the start of this story, it consisted of only three sentences. The report read in full: "The church on the rise at Ashton Point was found sealed upon arrival of the detachment. It was not entered. The ground is disturbed in three concentric rings before the church.

Recommendation is to leave the site as is and to strike the rise from all future federal survey work. " The word underlined at the bottom of that report was "buried. " Post wrote it in a hand that a later filing clerk described in a marginal note as "not the commander's usual hand, and apparently written under duress. " The second report was the one Post submitted on his own initiative three weeks later, in a private letter to a cousin in the War Department in Washington.

That letter is the document at the center of the drawer that was not opened until 1994. In it, Post describes what his detachment actually did during the four days they spent at Ashton Point. He describes the sealed church. He describes the three concentric rings on the packed earth.

He describes the way his horses refused to approach. He describes how his men, ordered to camp within sight of the church on the first night, requested and received permission to break camp and move a mile down the road before sunset. He describes, in a paragraph that has been published only twice in the historical literature, the sound the sentry reported hearing at approximately three in the morning of the second night, a sound the sentry described as "the sound of a very large book being opened very slowly, coming from the direction of the sealed church," although the church was empty and its door was chained shut. Post describes in his letter his decision to open the church.

He had been ordered to enter it. He was given a crowbar, a hammer, and a rope. He approached the door on the morning of July 5 with three of his men, and, as he wrote, took hold of the chain and then let it go. He did not describe what happened when he took hold of the chain, only what he did afterwards.

He returned to his horse, mounted, rode a hundred yards down the road, and then turned in the saddle and looked at the church. He wrote: "I understood at that moment that the door had not been sealed to keep anyone out, but to keep something in. And I understood that the man who had sealed it had done his work more skillfully than I could do it with a crowbar and a hammer, and that any attempt of mine to improve upon his work would be a foolishness that would destroy what remained. I therefore ordered the church left alone and I ordered it buried.

"

Post did not bury the church himself. He requested, by mail to Vicksburg on July 6, a work crew with digging equipment. The crew arrived on July 11, forty-two men, mostly contracted Freedmen's Bureau laborers, under the direction of a former enslaved man named Isaac Pruitt, who had been, before the war, an expert in levee construction on the Yazoo. Pruitt supervised the burial.

The church was not demolished; it was left standing. The crew built an earthen mound around and over the rise, approximately twenty-two feet high, using clay excavated from the two oxbow lakes surrounding the rise, and they packed the clay well, so well that the entire construction, as Pruitt described it in his report to the Bureau, was "ready for burial. " Pruitt's report survives, filed July 19. In it, Pruitt records that during the burial, his men reported hearing a faint knocking from inside the mound as it grew, at irregular intervals, which seemed to come from the direction of the sealed interior of the church.

Pruitt writes that he ordered his men not to speak of the knocking, to work faster, and under no circumstances to attempt to answer the knocking. He records that none of his forty-two men disobeyed this order. He writes in the last line of the report: "I do not know, and do not wish to know, what was behind that door, and I strongly recommend that no one be sent to find out. " The mound was completed on July 18.

The site was struck from federal survey on August 2. The state of Mississippi, when it conducted its own post-war survey in 1871, did not include the mound on any of its plats. When the railroad companies surveyed the Yazoo and Mississippi Valley line in 1882, they chose a route curving west around the site, a choice publicly criticized by engineers of the time as adding four miles of unnecessary track. The engineers were informed, in a memo from the railroad's chief surveyor, that the curve was to be built as designed, and that no discussion of the reasons was to be entertained with operating crews.

By 1874 the river changed course again, the two oxbow lakes merged into a single body of water whose level rose to lap at the base of the mound. By 1880 the new lake surrounded the mound on three sides, and the road that had once led to the church was impassable in any season. By 1900 the mound, from a distance, was indistinguishable from any of the low natural rises of the western Delta, and local memory of what lay beneath it was fading, as local memory does, into the category of things the old people warn about. Meanwhile, the papers had traveled far.

They left Vicksburg on July 29, 1866, in a canvas bag, with a mail courier who took the steamboat to St. Louis and then the train to Washington. They arrived at the War Department on August 14. The document was referred, within a week, to a sub-office of the War Department that no longer exists, and appears in the department's records only under a code identifier.

By the end of September, the document had settled into a locked drawer in the basement of that office. When the office was dissolved in 1912, its records, unopened, were transferred to the newly created agency that would become the National Archives. The drawer, still locked, was moved to a facility in Suitland, Maryland, where it remained for eighty-two years. In the spring of 1971, a survey team from the United States Geological Survey arrived in Sharkey County, Mississippi, under contract to the Army Corps of Engineers, to install a series of shallow groundwater monitoring wells along the lower Yazoo basin.

The team was five men. The team leader was a hydrologist named Dr. Emmet Warren, a federal veteran with seventeen years of field experience and no notable achievements. Warren appears in surviving photographs of the project as a thin man with a neat mustache, who seems to prefer solitude to anyone else.

The team's objective for the seventh well in the project, according to the contract site map, was a low rise on the west bank of a small oxbow lake, identified on modern Sharkey County topographic maps only as "unidentified water feature. " The rise was chosen because it sat on favorable aquifer elevation, and because the ground appeared dry and clear of vegetation in aerial photographs. This rise was Ashton Point. Warren insisted in his later writings about the project, for the rest of his life, that he had no knowledge of this at the time of selection.

He insisted he had never heard of the Ashton Point incident. He insisted no local warned him. He insisted that his selection of the site was, to his knowledge, a matter of pure hydrological convenience. The crew arrived at the rise on the morning of April 22, 1971.

They set up the rig. They began to drill. They reached about four feet without incident. At about six feet, the auger struck what the driller, a man named Tulio Sepulveda, described as "hard fill of unnatural consistency.

" Sepulveda asked Warren to come and look. Warren looked. Warren ordered the auger pulled and the drilling stopped. Warren wrote in his field notebook that evening that the auger had struck what he believed to be a layer of hand-packed clay of a type that does not occur naturally in river delta silt.

The layer, based on the auger's resistance, appeared to be at least fifteen feet thick. Warren, curious and competent, returned to his office in Vicksburg the next morning and asked the county clerk for any historical documents relating to the mound. The county clerk, a woman named Mrs. Halcomb, went into a back room and returned with a small file, and told Warren that to her knowledge, no one had opened that file in the recorder's office in forty-three years.

She allowed him to take the file for the afternoon. Warren sat in a diner across the street and read it. The file contained a copy of Isaac Pruitt's burial report from July 1866. It contained a copy of the 1871 state survey memo striking the mound from state plats.

It contained a copy of a private letter from a former Vicksburg Bureau agent to the county clerk in 1883, warning that the mound was not to be disturbed under any circumstances. And it contained, folded inside the back cover, a hand-drawn map of the burial mound as it was in 1866, showing the location of the sealed church inside it, marked on the map in a hand Warren did not recognize, with the words, "Do not open. This side up," with an arrow pointing to the surface. Warren described, in his written account of the project, submitted years later to a small journal called the Southeastern Geology Bulletin, his reaction upon reading the file: "I felt a chill run slowly up the back of my neck that lasted through the afternoon and had not fully subsided by the next morning.

" He wrote that he returned to the crew's motel that evening, gathered his four men, and explained the contents of the file to them. He wrote that he then proposed that the crew abandon the site, request court permission to relocate the well, and submit a report attributing the relocation to "adverse subsurface conditions. " He wrote that his four men unanimously agreed to this proposal without discussion. Warren wrote that on the morning of the next day, April 24, he went alone to the site before dawn to retrieve his instruments and dismantle the equipment before the crew arrived.

He wrote that as he approached the site in the faint light of dawn, he heard a sound coming from the ground that he could not immediately identify. It was low and constant, with a rhythm, as he wrote, unlike the rhythm of any natural process he knew. Warren wrote that the sound, in his professional estimation, was mechanical. It was not the sound of water moving underground.

It was not the sound of the earth settling. It was the sound of something working. He wrote that after three minutes he returned to his vehicle, drove back to Vicksburg without touching the equipment, and called the Corps of Engineers office in Memphis, reporting that the site was unsuitable for a monitoring well, and that a subcontractor would retrieve the equipment at a later date. Warren wrote that the equipment was never retrieved.

Warren also wrote in the same report that, on his own initiative and at his own expense, he returned to the mound twice during the summer of 1971, and on both occasions he brought with him a portable seismograph borrowed from a colleague in the geology department at Louisiana State University. He set the seismograph fifty yards from the mound. On the first visit he recorded a continuous low-frequency signal lasting the full two hours of observation. On the second visit he recorded the same signal, at the same frequency, with the same waveform, from the same source.

He wrote that when he later took the tapes to a colleague in the geology department and asked for a professional interpretation, the colleague listened to the tapes for about ten minutes, then removed them from the machine, handed them back to Warren, and said: "Emmett, please do not bring these tapes into this building again. " He refused to discuss the matter further. Warren kept the tapes for the rest of his life. He died in 1993 of pancreatic cancer at the age of seventy-one.

His widow, in accordance with his will, delivered the tapes and his notebooks from the 1971 project in a sealed box to the office of the Louisiana State Archaeological Survey in Baton Rouge on the morning after his funeral. The box was logged. The box was placed in a climate-controlled storage room. In October 1993, a note about the box, through a chain of inquiries that has never been fully traced, reached the desk of an archivist at the National Archives in Suitland, Maryland, who had been assigned three months earlier to catalog a sealed drawer which, according to transfer records, had not been opened since 1866.

The archivist's name was Adele Chen, age thirty-four, with a doctorate in American religious history from Yale. When the note about the Warren tapes reached her, she was about to open the drawer, though she did not yet know it. Adele Chen opened the drawer on the morning of March 14, 1994. She was alone in the reading room of the Suitland facility.

The drawer had been brought up from deep storage at her request the previous afternoon, and placed on a steel cart beside her workstation. The lock mechanism was original, from 1866, a brass keyway operated by a key already in the archives' possession, apparently held in the files for 128 years without ever being used. Chen turned the key. The drawer opened easily.

Inside she found a water-stained canvas bag, still tightly closed. Inside the bag, she found seven documents wrapped in a piece of waxed cloth, and a small object wrapped separately in a piece of black wool. She opened the documents first. She catalogued them in her work index.

She read them. She read Post's official three-sentence report. She read Post's private letter to his cousin. She read Pruitt's burial report.

She read a copy of Delia Bright's affidavit. She read a copy of Absalom Reed's testimony. She read Dr. Kane's records, including the four-sentence exchange on the slate and the small door-like drawing.

She read an undated memo in a hand she did not recognize, consisting of a single instruction: "This file is not to be opened except upon the occurrence of any disturbance at the site itself. " Then Chen unwrapped the small object from the black wool. She wrote in an incident log she submitted to her supervisor that afternoon that the object appeared to be "a piece of wood approximately three inches long, one inch wide, and half an inch thick, of a type I am not qualified to identify, with a surface that appears polished from use. " She wrote that the piece bore, on one side, a mark cut into the wood with a blade.

The mark she drew was the same mark Josiah Kane had drawn on his slate in 1866. It was the mark the doctor described as resembling a door. Chen wrote that the mark was warm in her hand as she held the piece, a sensation she could not attribute to her own body heat, and that after approximately five minutes of examination she re-wrapped the piece in the wool and returned it to the bag. Chen did not know what to do with the file.

She reported the opening to her supervisor. Her supervisor, Marcus Bell, a veteran archivist, requested a meeting with the Deputy Archivist of the United States. After reviewing Chen's summary, the Deputy Archivist formed a task force. The task force first met on March 22, 1994, in a conference room at the National Archives building on Pennsylvania Avenue.

The team consisted of Chen, Bell, Dr. Ilse Bergmann, a paleographer on loan from the Library of Congress, a chemist from the Smithsonian Institution, a historian of American religions from Georgetown University, and, at the special request of the Deputy Archivist, a Jesuit priest named Father Ambrose Rell, who had spent the previous nine years working as a consultant to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith at the Vatican on matters relating to the Index of Prohibited Books. Father Rell was not a public figure, and his name appears on no roster. His membership on the Ashton Point task force is confirmed only through the oral history Adele Chen gave to a Yale graduate student in 2008, three years before her death.

Chen told the student that Father Rell, when the documents from the bag and the piece of wood were shown to him, fell completely silent and asked to be left alone with them for an hour. She said that when she and the rest of the task force returned to the conference room, Father Rell was seated in the chair he had occupied initially, but the documents had been arranged neatly on the table, and the wool-wrapped piece of wood sat on top of the documents, and Father Rell said, in a voice Chen described as "quiet but very tired," three sentences. The first sentence, according to Chen, was "This is not a hoax. " The second was "This is not the first time, and it will not be the last.

" Chen said she would not repeat the third sentence, and asked the graduate student to stop the recording. The recording was stopped. When it resumed, the conversation had moved to another subject. Father Rell returned to Rome in April of 1994.

He died in a care facility outside Assisi in 2001. His personal papers were sealed after his death by order of his superior general, and remain sealed today. The task force issued a final memorandum in June 1994. The memorandum itself was classified at a level Chen described, in her oral history, as "above my security clearance and above my supervisor's," and it was returned to the drawer with the original bag and the wool-wrapped piece.

The drawer was closed again. The key was returned to its file. By administrative order, the task force was dissolved, and its members were forbidden from discussing the matter with anyone outside the team. The federal geologist mentioned at the outset of this story, who described the Ashton Point site as the most desecrated religious gathering in American history, was Dr.

Emmet Warren himself, and the phrase appears in a personal letter he wrote to his brother in 1989, four years before his death and five years before the drawer was opened. Warren wrote in that same letter that he had spent every year since 1971 trying to understand what he had heard in the ground on April 24 of that year, and that after two decades of reflection he had concluded that the sound was not made by anything he could identify as a machine, but by something he could only describe as "a reading in progress that has not yet ended. "

What is Ashton Point? What is the blank church no one remembered building?

What was Brother Ela, whom no witness could remember, whose voice contained tones no ear could account for, whose book turned its own pages, and by the fifth day was reading him? What closed the door in the third week of June 1866, and what was still knocking on the other side of it while forty-two men packed clay over the roof? What was still humming in the ground on April 24, 1971, when Emmet Warren stood on a delta road at dawn and realized he was listening to something working? There is a name for this pattern, and it is not a comfortable one.

It is the pattern that runs through every buried civilization the official record refuses to draw on its maps. Ashton Point is not an isolated incident. It is what happens when one of these buried things wakes up briefly enough to be witnessed, and is then hidden again with quicklime and river iron before it can complete what it began. The plank church was not a church.

It was a marker. It stood over something the official geology of the Delta refuses to describe. The iron anomaly the surveyors of the 1840s warned each other about is only the surface reading of what is actually there. Brother Ela was a keeper who came to open a door that had been closed at an earlier time by people who knew their work with terrible precision, and whose work was beginning to fade by June of 1866.

The eleven days were a reactivation. The book on the pulpit was instruction, written in a script that read top to bottom and right to left simultaneously. Folded, because the geometry it described was folded, and the sealed church on the head of Ashton is one of its folds. Because Ashton Point is still there.

The mound is still there. The river has covered part of it, but the top twelve feet remain above water, and can be reached by any determined group with a shovel and a boat in a single afternoon. The witnesses who could tell you why the earth at Ashton Point must never be turned over are in the earth themselves. And the door in the wooden church, beneath twenty-two feet of hand-packed Yazoo clay, was still closed the last time anyone verified it.

Whether it remains closed is a question history appears to have quietly left, without comment, for another century.
content_html:
In the summer of 1866, in a region of the Mississippi Delta so flooded that the maps of that era could not render it, a crowd gathered inside a wooden church whose name no one had ever written above its door. They came by wagon and they came on foot, from three neighboring counties, and some of them, according to a register a Union quartermaster later found nailed beneath the pulpit, came from places that appeared on no state survey after the war. They came to hear a preacher whose voice, by every surviving account, made grown men set their rifles aside and children gasp. They came for a service that lasted eleven continuous days.

By the morning of the twelfth day, the church was empty. The doors had been sealed from the outside with river iron and quicklime. The riverbank around it was covered with wagon tracks leading in and none leading out. Federal officers from Vicksburg, who reached the site three weeks later, filed a report so brief it was almost insulting.

Three sentences, one recommendation to leave the place alone, one word underlined at the bottom of the page. That word was buried, and the ground around the church was struck from every county map and every railroad map printed after 1867. The congregation, the preacher, the wagons, the eleven-day sermon, and the thing the report said the preacher had been reading from, all of it went into a sealed drawer in the National Archives that was not opened again until 1994. Yet what came out of that drawer in 1994 was not what the archivists expected.

This is not a story about a cult. It is not a story about a hoax. It is a story that suggests something entered the Sacramento River Delta after the war, took the form of a rural preacher, and read before a full hall for eleven days from a book that three witnesses swore was, by the fifth day, reading itself to him. It is a story about what the ground swallowed on the morning of the twelfth day.

And what a 1971 survey team found still resonates under six feet of Mississippi mud. To understand what happened in that wooden church, you must understand the Mississippi Delta of 1866. And to understand the Delta of 1866, you must accept an uncomfortable fact about the year the American Civil War ended. The war did not end in April of 1865.

That is what the textbooks say because that is what the surrender documents say. And the surrender documents are the polished version of history. What actually happened in the Deep South, and in the Mississippi Delta specifically, is that the war stopped and began to fade. Whole counties fell silent, a silence that was not supposed to exist.

Entire towns were emptied. Entire families left homes that were still furnished, still provisioned, still standing, and never returned. The post-war Mississippi Delta became a region the federal government lacked the manpower to patrol, the money to survey, or even the desire to visit. The Freedmen’s Bureau kept records, but those records were kept in Vicksburg, Natchez, and Jackson.

The country between those cities was, practically speaking, rumor. Rivers had changed course during the flood years of 1863 and 1864. Roads that existed on the 1860 militia maps were now submerged, or overgrown with kudzu, or gone entirely. The compilers of the 1870 census admitted in a margin almost no one read that entire census districts in the western Delta were, as the margin recorded, “not resolvable by any living inhabitant willing to speak of it.

”

That was the country where a church stood on a low rise between two oxbow lakes that appear on no modern map, because the river changed course again in 1874 and swallowed them. The freedmen who lived in a cluster of cabins about a mile east of the rise called it Ashton Point. The name came not from the elm trees, but from the shape of the land after a thunderstorm that swept across it every spring since time out of mind. The rise attracted lightning the way a metal rod attracts it.

Old survey markers from the 1840s noted the location as “an iron anomaly, to be avoided when using the compass. ” The men who set those markers were surveyors for the state land office, cautious men, and it is recorded that they feared this place. By the summer of 1866, Ashton Point held a small church. No one among the freedmen in the cabins a mile east remembered the church being built.

No one in the nearest white settlement, a small village called Rain’s Ferry about four miles south, remembered carpenters being hired. The wooden church simply existed one morning, a small rectangular building with one door, one window, and a roof of split cypress. It had a bell, but the bell had no clapper. It had a pulpit, but the pulpit held no Bible.

It had pews for perhaps forty people, and they sat empty through most of that spring, the way a theater set sits empty before the actors arrive. The first man to take notice of the church and record his observation was a Union quartermaster named Elias Rothven, attached to the occupation garrison at Vicksburg. Rothven was, by all accounts, a highly competent man. He kept lists and filed reports.

Before the war he had been an accountant in Cincinnati, and after the war he desperately wanted to return to being an accountant in Cincinnati. In June of 1866 his commander sent him upriver on a supply survey mission, after rumors reached the garrison of a gathering of unregistered people in the western Delta. The army wanted an accurate count before deciding whether to send troops. Rothven wrote a letter to his wife on the evening of June 18, 1866, from the porch of a widow’s house in Rain’s Ferry.

That letter survives. It is currently in a private collection in Charleston, reproduced in two academic publications, both long out of print. In the letter, Rothven describes the widow’s face when he asked her about the little church that seemed to have appeared out of nowhere. He wrote that she went pale, put her hand on the table, and told him in a voice he could barely hear that the church had been there since winter; that no one had built it; that a preacher had arrived in early June; and that the preacher had begun holding services on the first Sunday of that month.

She told Rothven she had not attended. She told him her son had attended, and that he had come home and not eaten for three days, and would not speak of what he had heard, and on the fourth day he left the house before dawn and went to the church and did not come back. Rothven noted, in the same letter, that while the widow spoke, a dog under the porch began to whine in a tone he had never heard before. He asked if the dog was injured.

The widow said, “That is what the dog does when the wind blows. ” Rothven checked his pocket watch, which held a small barometer, and noted that the wind that evening was, according to his instrument, perfectly still. He wrote to his wife: “I do not think I will sleep tonight, and I do not think I will write to you again from this county. ” He never wrote to her again from that county.

He wrote to her later, from a hospital in Memphis in September, and by then he could not hold a pen, so he dictated the letter to a nurse. The preacher arrived at Ashton Point on the morning of Sunday, June 3, 1866. That date is undisputed. It appears in the widow’s testimony, in an interview conducted by the Freedmen’s Bureau in October of that year with a laborer named Absalom Reed, and in a letter sent by a traveling Baptist preacher named Josiah Hemp to his bishop in Jackson, complaining that a stranger had begun preaching in his district without a letter of introduction, denominational affiliation, or any visible means of support.

Hemp’s letter was filed and forgotten. It was rediscovered in the 1980s when a graduate student at Ole Miss, reviewing parish records for a thesis on post-war religion in the American South, found it wedged between two pages of a hymnal, apparently used as a bookmark. Hemp writes that he first heard of the preacher on June 2 from a farmhand in Rain’s Ferry who claimed to have seen the stranger walking up the road from the river that morning. According to the farmhand, the man was tall and thin, wearing a black coat cut in a way no horseman had ever seen, with an unusually high collar and buttons in a single row on the side instead of the front.

The farmhand said the man carried no bag, no book, no cane, no rain coat, though a heavy rain had fallen the night before and the road was, in the farmhand’s words, as wet as any road in the state. The man’s boots were dry. Hemp wrote that he found the farmhand’s account strange but not alarming. What alarmed him was a second account from an elderly freedwoman named Delia Bright, who lived in one of the eastern cabins.

Delia told Hemp, when he went to her cabin on June 5 for his own inquiries, that she had seen the preacher pass her cabin on the morning of the third, and that he stopped at her gate and asked, in a voice “low and gentle as a well,” whether her family was well. Delia said she answered yes. The preacher then asked if the children of her family had been baptized. Delia said she answered yes to that too.

The preacher smiled, she said, and asked a third question, which she would not repeat at the time of Hemp’s visit. Two weeks later, in an interview with a Bureau agent who had come to inquire about something else, Delia was persuaded to repeat the question. According to the agent’s field notes, preserved in the Bureau archives in Vicksburg, the preacher asked Delia: “And were they baptized with the second water? ” Delia asked him what the second water was.

She said the preacher smiled again and told her, “You will know when you hear the bell. ” He continued walking up the road toward the rise. As established, the church bell had no clapper. It had not rung in living memory.

Delia would later swear, in an affidavit given in 1868 in a lawsuit that never went to trial, that on the evening of June 3, 1866, the bell at Ashton Point rang three times at intervals of approximately one minute, and that its sound was not, as she said, “the sound of a bell to be remembered. ” That is what she said, literally, and the affidavit was signed with her mark and witnessed by a lawyer named Cassius Pearl, who died within eighteen months under circumstances the Vicksburg coroner refused to specify. By sunset on June 3, the church at Ashton Point had a preacher, a ringing bell, and a congregation estimated at sixteen people, by Delia’s reckoning. By the following Sunday, June 10, the congregation numbered sixty-two, according to a note pinned to the back of the door and copied down by a Bureau agent.

By June 17, the congregation was too large for the church, and the preacher began holding service on the packed earth outside, the door open, and his voice, according to three separate witnesses, carrying downwind a distance no normal human voice should carry. The preacher identified himself, if he identified himself at all, as Brother Ela. He gave no surname. He gave no denomination.

When a visiting Methodist minister from Yazoo City, on the fourth Sunday, asked where he had been ordained, Brother Ela answered, according to two witnesses, “By a hand that has not finished writing me. ” The Methodist minister left before the service began. He wrote to his bishop the following week that he had been in the company of a man he did not believe to be a man, and that he would not return to the Mississippi Delta under any circumstances as long as the preacher holding the pulpit was still standing. No two people who saw Brother Ela gave matching physical descriptions.

He was tall in one account, medium height in another. His hair was dark in the widow’s memory, gray at the temples in Delia’s. His eyes were described, in every account, as light. Otherwise, no two witnesses agreed.

The horseman from Rain’s Ferry, when asked years later to describe the man, said only: “I do not remember his face, and I remember every face I have ever tied a horse to. ”

The strangest thing, however, is what Brother Ela did in his first evening at Ashton Point, in the last hour before he stood at the pulpit to deliver his first sermon. According to Absalom Reed, who was hired by the preacher himself that day to bring water for the church’s baptismal font, Brother Ela went out to the packed-earth yard at about five in the afternoon, knelt, and placed both hands flat on the ground. Reed said he remained that way for about half an hour, without moving, speaking, or appearing to breathe.

At the end of that half hour, the preacher rose, dusted his palms once, returned to the church, and rang the bell that had no clapper three times, in Reed’s words, “by pointing at it. ” Reed said he did not see the preacher touch the bell. He said the bell simply rang when the preacher pointed at it, and that the sound of the third ring hung in the air of the yard for a length of time Reed, a practical man and former plantation blacksmith, did not attempt to measure in seconds because he did not believe the seconds on his watch kept passing while the bell rang. That is the man who opened the eleven-day sermon on the evening of June 3, 1866.

The first sermon began at sunset and continued without interruption until sunrise on the fourth. The eleven days were not eleven days punctuated by rest periods. They were, according to two records preserved from inside the church itself, a single continuous sermon that paused only when the preacher himself paused, and his pauses over the eleven days totaled no more than four hours. This is physically impossible.

No human throat can produce continuous audible speech for eleven days. No human body can go without sleep for eleven days while maintaining the ability to speak. The Bureau agent who took the testimony of the musician Rubin Alt, hired to accompany the first four services on a small hand organ, wrote in the margin of Alt’s testimony: “The witness insists on the duration of eleven days. The witness refuses to amend his statement.

The witness produced a watch and a calendar to confirm the agent’s inability to explain. ” Alt’s testimony is the closest thing to an accurate record of what happened inside the church during the first three days. Alt was a free man of color from New Orleans, who had come across the river looking for work as a musician in one of the Vicksburg hotels, and had been recruited at the docks by a man he did not recognize, who paid him in advance, in silver, for four days of playing. Alt said he arrived at the church on the evening of June 2, a full day before the preacher arrived, and that the church was empty that evening.

The door was open, and the pump organ was already placed beside the pulpit. Alt said he did not know who brought the organ, that it was a make he did not recognize, and that the keys, as he said, were warm when he first touched them. He began playing at sunset on the third as ordered. He was given no hymns to play.

The preacher told him to play whatever the congregation asked for, and that he would know what they asked for. Alt said that in the first hour he played a slow melody in D minor he had never heard before and could not afterwards recall, and that the congregation, seated in the pews and standing in the aisle, listened to the melody without moving, without coughing, without shifting in their seats. At the end of the first hour, the preacher rose, went to the pulpit, opened a book that was lying on the pulpit shelf, and began to read. Alt did not see the book clearly that night.

He said it appeared to be a volume bound in black leather, with a cover free of any lettering, and pages, in his words, “thicker than any Bible page I have seen in my life, and yellower than any book with such a cover. ” He said the preacher read from the book through the entire first night, from sunset to sunrise, turning no more than about ten pages, and that the words the preacher spoke were English that night, although an English Alt did not recognize. When asked to give an example of what the preacher said, Alt refused. He said he could remember the sentences, but he had promised himself on the fourth day never to repeat them aloud.

The Bureau agent noted that Alt, when faced with this question, began to cry, in a manner the agent described as “silent and continuous, without any change in the witness’s expression. ” The agent did not press him further. The second night began at sunset on June 4. The congregation had grown to about forty people.

The preacher had not left the pulpit. He had not eaten, and he had not, as far as Alt knew, drunk any water. He preached through the entire day without pause, in a voice that did not grow hoarse, in a language that shifted, at some point during the daylight hours, from English into a language Alt did not recognize. Alt spoke French and some Spanish, and some Choctaw he had learned at the docks, but this was not a human language he knew.

The congregation did not seem to notice the change. They responded to the preacher’s words with faint affirmations—”yes,” “amen,” “let it be”—though the words they were affirming were in a language none of them had learned, as far as Alt knew. Alt said he asked the woman seated near him at the end of a pew what the preacher had just said. The woman turned to him and told him, in a voice Alt described as “gentle and somewhat puzzled,” that the preacher had just spoken the name of her mother, who had died in 1859, and that she had not heard her mother’s name spoken aloud in seven years, and that she was very happy to hear it now.

Alt said he did not sleep the second night. He said he was not sure afterwards whether anyone in the church had slept, or whether the congregation had felt the passage of night at all. He said the light of the second sunrise creeping through the church’s single window surprised him on the morning of the fifth, and that when he looked at his watch, he found it had stopped, and he could not remember when it had stopped, and the hands pointed to a time that was not any hour of the night he had lived. By the third day, June 6, the crowds had outgrown the walls of the church.

Word had reached Rain’s Ferry, and the freedmen’s cabins to the east, and also, through two riverboat pilots who had docked for wood at a landing four miles downstream, the town of Rolling Fork, twenty miles south. By the afternoon of June 6, wagons were arriving on the road to Ashton Point at the rate of one every quarter hour. The preacher had begun to step out of the church between passages of his reading, walk to the door, and call out into the yard the names of specific people who were arriving on the road at that very moment, before they appeared in sight. Rubin Alt said that at noon on June 6, the preacher went to the door and called out the name Cornelius Duval, and three minutes later a wagon appeared around a bend in the road, driven by a man named Cornelius Duval, and that Cornelius Duval had not met the preacher, spoken to him, or sent him any word, as far as anyone in the church later knew.

Alt said this happened forty-seven times over the course of June 6 alone.
