March 2019. Aurora, Illinois. The sky is flat and heavy, a dirty gray canopy that has parked itself over the region for days. A thin layer of slush covers the pavement, the kind of North Midwest afternoon where winter feels not like a season but a condition.

Outside the gates of a correctional facility, a 60-year-old man walks out into this dull, quiet cold. His hair has thinned and grayed. To anyone passing, he looks like just another name processed through the Illinois Department of Corrections. But for the families of eighteen missing and murdered women, this is the final living link to a period of unprecedented violence in the Chicago suburbs.

The man’s name is Thomas Kokoraleis. In the early 1980s, the group he ran with turned the Chicago suburbs into a place of genuine terror, a four-man crew that operated out of a red van and murdered women in a ritualized pattern of mutilation. For decades, the case was considered closed. One brother was executed.

The ringleader was sentenced to life. And Thomas, the man who gave police a detailed, gruesome confession, was locked away for what most assumed would be the rest of his life. Now, thanks to a sentencing law from a different era, Thomas Kokoraleis is walking free. This is the story of the Ripper Crew, and how a loophole in the law allowed a convicted killer to return to the very streets he once hunted.

In the spring of 1982, Elmhurst, Illinois presented itself as a picture of suburban stability. Located sixteen miles west of Chicago, it was a place where families moved to escape the city’s rising crime. For twenty-one-year-old Lorraine “Lori” Borowski, it was home, a place that felt entirely safe. She worked as a secretary at a real estate office on West Second Street, a responsible young woman with a reliable routine.

On the morning of May 15th, nothing about that routine was unusual. She parked her car, keys in hand, steps away from the office door. She never made it inside. When her boss arrived, he found the office dark and the door locked.

Strange in itself; Lori was never late. But on the sidewalk outside, he found a sight that shifted the morning from a missing person to a crime scene. Lori’s keys were scattered on the concrete. Her cosmetics had spilled out.

Most disturbingly, her shoes were sitting right there on the pavement. Elmhurst police realized they were looking at the aftermath of an incredibly fast struggle. It’s a detail that still haunts the case, the idea that she was pulled so forcefully out of her footwear that she didn’t even have time to scream. In broad daylight on a busy street, Lori Borowski had simply vanished.

The initial investigation was a procedural grind. Detectives went door to door, but 1982 offered no CCTV cameras or cell tower pings. There was only the pavement and a growing list of questions. For five months, Lori’s fourteen-year-old brother, Mark, watched as his parents’ lives centered around a telephone that wouldn’t ring.

Police found no motive, no evidence that she’d been targeted by someone she knew, and no sign of where she had been taken. The silence broke in October, when hunters in a Villa Park cemetery discovered skeletal remains. Dental records confirmed the nightmare. Lori Borowski was dead.

But the autopsy brought a new kind of horror. Lori hadn’t just been killed. She’d been subjected to a very specific type of violence, a pattern of surgical mutilation that suggested the killers weren’t just looking to end a life, but to perform a sadistic ritual. The wounds were precise, almost clinical.

As investigators tried to make sense of that, they soon realized Lori wasn’t an isolated tragedy. She was a data point in a much larger, darker pattern emerging across the Chicago area. While the Borowski family waited for answers, Chicago police were tracking a body count that didn’t make sense. Women were disappearing from street corners and bus stops across the city and its near west suburbs.

Linda Sutton had been found in May of 1981. Then Shari Mack. Then Sandra Delaware. Each bore the same ritualistic trauma.

The breakthrough finally came from a woman named Beverly Washington. On October 6th, 1982, she was found on a roadside, clinging to life after an ordeal that mirrored the other cases. From her hospital bed, she gave detectives the lead they’d been missing: a 1975 red Dodge van. She also remembered the driver, a man with an almost rehearsed, disarming demeanor.

That description led police to thirty-year-old Robin Gecht. Gecht wasn’t a social outcast. In fact, he was a contractor and a father of three. But his resume held a very dark connection.

He’d once worked as a carpenter for John Wayne Gacy, helping to build the very patio where some of Gacy’s victims were eventually discovered. Police put a twenty-four-hour surveillance detail on Gecht’s red van. During the stakeout, detectives noticed he wasn’t acting alone. He was often seen with three younger men: Edward Spreitzer, and two brothers, Andrew and Thomas Kokoraleis.

Thomas was only twenty-two, with a reputation for being slow and a soft face that didn’t fit the profile of a serial predator. On November 5th, police finally moved in. They picked up the entire crew and separated them into different interrogation rooms. Gecht remained a stone wall.

But the younger men began to crack under the pressure, and it was Thomas who talked first. He didn’t just admit to being in the van. He pointed police toward Gecht’s attic on North Paulina Street. He described a place of blacked-out windows and ritualistic tools, including a handcrafted box where Gecht allegedly kept trophies of the women they’d taken.

To investigators, it sounded like a nightmare. But Thomas provided the one thing they couldn’t ignore: the locations. He described the exact spot in the cemetery where they’d left Lori Borowski. The hunt for a red van had led the Chicago police into an attic of horrors.

Now they had the confessions and the vehicle. But they were about to enter a legal maze that would take decades to resolve. With the whole crew in custody, the investigation moved from the streets into the sterile environment of the interrogation rooms. Robin Gecht remained defiant and silent.

The dynamic among the younger men was shifting, though. The weight of multiple homicide charges was forcing them to look for a way out, and for Thomas Kokoraleis, that meant telling detectives exactly what they wanted to hear. Thomas wasn’t a criminal mastermind. He was in his early twenties, with an IQ that hovered around seventy-five, a fact that made him highly suggestible and easily led.

During hours of questioning, he began to paint a picture of the Ripper Crew that felt more like a dark cult than a street gang. He told police that Gecht was the architect of every move. He described how they would cruise the streets in the red van looking for women who were alone, and how Gecht would lead ceremonies once they returned to his home on North Paulina Street. The most disturbing part of the confession involved the attic.

Thomas described a room with blacked-out windows where Gecht acted as a sort of high priest. He detailed how Gecht would inflict precise, surgical cuts on the victims while they were still alive, and how he’d force the others to participate in what he called “sacraments. ”

But as Thomas spoke, detectives tried to separate fact from fantasy. Some of his descriptions were so extreme they seemed impossible.

Then he’d drop a detail that only a participant could know. He knew the specific locations where the remains of Linda Sutton and Sandra Delaware had been found. He knew the exact way Lori Borowski’s body had been positioned in the cemetery. While Thomas was talking, forensic teams were processing Robin Gecht’s home.

They found the attic just as Thomas had described it. They found evidence of blood and a physical struggle. Most notably, they found the small handcrafted box used to store the trophies taken from the women they targeted. The confessions from Thomas and Edward Spreitzer gave the state a narrative.

But they also created a legal problem. Robin Gecht hadn’t confessed. There was no DNA linking the men to the scenes, in an era before modern testing. The prosecution’s case rested almost entirely on the word of a man with borderline intellect describing ritualistic, cult-like behavior.

In 1985, the legal system had to decide if Thomas Kokoraleis was a monster or just a follower. He was convicted of the murder of Lori Borowski and sentenced to life in prison. At the time, it felt like the final word. But as the years passed, the world began to look back at Thomas’s confession with a more skeptical eye, and that doubt would eventually lead to the most controversial chapter of this entire story.

While Thomas Kokoraleis began his life sentence, the legal ground beneath him was already shifting. As the satanic panic of the early 1980s began to fade, legal experts started looking back at his confession with renewed skepticism. By the late 1980s, his defense team successfully argued that the initial conviction was fundamentally flawed, claiming Thomas was a suggestible subject who’d been fed details by investigators. In a move that stunned the Borowski family, the Illinois Appellate Court overturned the verdict and ordered a new trial.

The state was suddenly in a desperate position. Years had passed since Lori’s disappearance, and the physical evidence from the red van was tied more strongly to Robin Gecht than to Thomas Kokoraleis. Fearing they might lose a second trial and see him walk free immediately, prosecutors offered a deal. Thomas would plead to a single count of murder in exchange for a seventy-year sentence.

He took the deal. To the public, seventy years sounded like a definitive end. But there was a massive catch buried in the fine print of 1980s sentencing laws. Because the crime had occurred in 1982, Thomas fell under the system of “day-for-day good time credit.

” The math was cold and clinical. For every day he behaved himself in prison, he earned a day off his sentence. Essentially, his seventy-year term was actually a thirty-five-year term. While Thomas began his time at the Dixon Correctional Center, the rest of the crew faced different fates.

His brother, Andrew, was convicted of the same crimes but sentenced to death. On March 17th, 1999, Andrew Kokoraleis became the last person to be executed by the state of Illinois. Robin Gecht, the alleged ringleader, remained behind bars on a life sentence, never admitting to a single crime. Thomas, however, stayed quiet.

He wasn’t a problem inmate. He worked his assignments and slowly shaved decades off his life behind bars. He was a man who understood the calendar. By 2017, the clock Thomas had been watching for thirty years was nearing midnight.

The Illinois Department of Corrections notified the families that Thomas Kokoraleis had completed his time. Legally, the state had no grounds to hold him. He had served his debt according to the letter of the law written decades prior. The news hit the Chicago area like a cold front.

It wasn’t just that a convicted murderer was coming home. It was the type of crimes he’d been associated with. People wanted to know how a man who’d confessed to such ritualistic participation could ever be considered reformed. As the release date approached, the focus shifted from the past to the future.

Thomas was now sixty years old, stepping into a world that used technology he couldn’t imagine to track his every move. But the biggest question wasn’t where he would go. It was who he now claimed to be. When Thomas Kokoraleis finally walked through the gates of the Dixon Correctional Center in March 2019, he didn’t disappear into the shadows.

He couldn’t. His release triggered a wave of anxiety across the Chicago suburbs that reached all the way to the mayor’s office in Aurora. Because Thomas was a convicted murderer and a sexual predator, his living arrangements were strictly regulated. The only place willing to take him was Wayside Cross Ministries, a faith-based residential program in downtown Aurora.

Wayside is built on the philosophy of radical transformation, the idea that no one is beyond the reach of grace. The community wasn’t ready to test that theory on a member of the Ripper Crew. Protests erupted almost immediately. Neighbors worried about the ministry’s proximity to local schools and parks.

The mayor of Aurora publicly challenged the decision. The ministry stood its ground, arguing that if a man has served his time, he deserves a path toward a productive life. However, that path required one thing Thomas wasn’t willing to give: a confession. In June 2019, just months after his release, Thomas sat down for a televised interview with CBS Chicago.

It was the first time the public had seen him in decades. He didn’t look like the young, suggestible man from the 1980s. He looked like a frail, soft-spoken senior citizen. But the words coming out of his mouth were a total reversal of the narrative that had kept him imprisoned for thirty-five years.

“I was stuck doing the time for something I didn’t do. ”

“Lorraine’s murder, all of the other women that you were accused of being involved with their murders, you were not involved, that’s what you’re saying? ”

“Yes. Look in your eyes, I’m telling you, down to God’s truth, no.

I had no participation in none of these crimes. None. ”

When the interviewer pressed him on the detailed 1982 confession, the one that led police to Lori Borowski’s remains, Thomas had a new explanation. “Prosecutors said that you knew details that only someone would know if they had been there.

”

“No, what they told me. Like a dump pool, I repeat it right back to them. ”

“So, you feel you were coerced into saying that? ”

“Yes.

”

He alleged that detectives had fed him the details of the crimes, and that he simply repeated them back so they’d stop the questioning. The interview sent shockwaves through the community. For the Borowski family, it was a profound betrayal. Mark Borowski, Lori’s brother, watched with a sense of cold fury, pointing out the central flaw in Thomas’s new story.

If the police had fed him the details, how did he know exactly where Lori’s body was hidden? The police hadn’t found her yet. Thomas was the one who led them there. The recantation also created a crisis at Wayside Cross.

The program is built on the foundation of repentance. By claiming he was never guilty to begin with, Thomas was effectively telling his mentors that he had nothing to repent for. James Lukose, the director of the ministry, found himself defending a man who refused to admit to the very crimes that had brought him to their door. The tension in Aurora grew as residents realized that Thomas wasn’t just back in society.

He was actively trying to erase the legacy of the Ripper Crew. As the summer of 2019 faded, the community was left with a haunting question. If Thomas was telling the truth, one of the most brutal cases in Illinois history was essentially a lie. But if he was lying, it meant a man who had participated in ritualistic violence was walking their streets, unrepentant and free.

The story of the Ripper Crew didn’t end when the prison doors opened for Thomas Kokoraleis. Today, he remains a free man in the eyes of the state of Illinois, having satisfied every legal demand and sentencing requirement. But for the families left behind, “legal” is a hollow word. There’s a deep, lingering friction in the idea that a man once tied to such specific ritualistic violence now walks the same streets as a new generation of families.

Mark Borowski has spent forty years navigating that friction. He’s no longer the fourteen-year-old boy waiting for his sister to come home. He’s a man who’s watched Lori’s name become synonymous with a cult and a satanic chapel. To combat that dark legacy, the Borowski family established a butterfly garden in Lori’s name in Elmhurst.

In the quiet of that memorial, the focus remains where it belongs, on the victims. It’s a place of light that stands as a deliberate final contrast to the industrial alleys and the dark attic where this story began. The broader shadow of the Ripper Crew still hangs over the Chicago area. Robin Gecht, the alleged architect of the group, remains behind bars with no parole hearing until 2042.

He has never admitted to a single crime, never offered a word of truth, never wavered from his wall of silence. As recently as 2024, Thomas Kokoraleis was reportedly living at a ministry in Peoria. Some see him as a success story for rehabilitation. Others see a ticking clock.

The truth of 1982 may never be fully reconciled with the version of the story Thomas tells today. The state has taken its pound of flesh, and Thomas has taken back his words. The legal system might be finished with Thomas Kokoraleis.

But the people who remember the red van will never be finished with one of the darkest chapters in Chicago’s history.

“I was stuck doing the time for something I didn’t do. ”

“Lorraine’s murder, all of the other women that you were accused of being involved with their murders, you were not involved, that’s what you’re saying? ”

“Yes. Look in your eyes, I’m telling you, down to God’s truth, no.

I had no participation in none of these crimes. None. ”

When the interviewer pressed him on the detailed 1982 confession, the one that led police to Lori Borowski’s remains, Thomas had a new explanation. “Prosecutors said that you knew details that only someone would know if they had been there.

”

“No, what they told me. Like a dump pool, I repeat it right back to them. ”

“So, you feel you were coerced into saying that? ”

“Yes.

”

He alleged that detectives had fed him the details of the crimes, and that he simply repeated them back so they’d stop the questioning. The interview sent shockwaves through the community. For the Borowski family, it was a profound betrayal. Mark Borowski, Lori’s brother, watched with a sense of cold fury, pointing out the central flaw in Thomas’s new story.

If the police had fed him the details, how did he know exactly where Lori’s body was hidden? The police hadn’t found her yet. Thomas was the one who led them there. The recantation also created a crisis at Wayside Cross.

The program is built on the foundation of repentance. By claiming he was never guilty to begin with, Thomas was effectively telling his mentors that he had nothing to repent for. James Lukose, the director of the ministry, found himself defending a man who refused to admit to the very crimes that had brought him to their door. The tension in Aurora grew as residents realized that Thomas wasn’t just back in society.

He was actively trying to erase the legacy of the Ripper Crew. As the summer of 2019 faded, the community was left with a haunting question. If Thomas was telling the truth, one of the most brutal cases in Illinois history was essentially a lie. But if he was lying, it meant a man who had participated in ritualistic violence was walking their streets, unrepentant and free.

The story of the Ripper Crew didn’t end when the prison doors opened for Thomas Kokoraleis. Today, he remains a free man in the eyes of the state of Illinois, having satisfied every legal demand and sentencing requirement. But for the families left behind, “legal” is a hollow word. There’s a deep, lingering friction in the idea that a man once tied to such specific ritualistic violence now walks the same streets as a new generation of families.

Mark Borowski has spent forty years navigating that friction. He’s no longer the fourteen-year-old boy waiting for his sister to come home. He’s a man who’s watched Lori’s name become synonymous with a cult and a satanic chapel. To combat that dark legacy, the Borowski family established a butterfly garden in Lori’s name in Elmhurst.

In the quiet of that memorial, the focus remains where it belongs, on the victims. It’s a place of light that stands as a deliberate final contrast to the industrial alleys and the dark attic where this story began. The broader shadow of the Ripper Crew still hangs over the Chicago area. Robin Gecht, the alleged architect of the group, remains behind bars with no parole hearing until 2042.

He has never admitted to a single crime, never offered a word of truth, never wavered from his wall of silence. As recently as 2024, Thomas Kokoraleis was reportedly living at a ministry in Peoria. Some see him as a success story for rehabilitation. Others see a ticking clock.

The truth of 1982 may never be fully reconciled with the version of the story Thomas tells today. The state has taken its pound of flesh, and Thomas has taken back his words. The legal system might be finished with Thomas Kokoraleis.

But the people who remember the red van will never be finished with one of the darkest chapters in Chicago’s history.
