Silas McCready was chasing a wounded deer through the dense Missouri Ozarks in September 1873 when he stumbled onto the Eldridge property. The cabin appeared abandoned, and curiosity drew him deeper into the yard. Behind the main outbuilding he found a strange arrangement of stones, partly hidden beneath freshly disturbed soil. What he uncovered beneath those stones would eventually be described in official records only as evidence of wrongdoing sufficient to justify further investigation.

By the time authorities organized a formal search of the place, the Eldridge brothers had vanished. The case that came to be known as the Eldridge Brothers affair began years earlier, in 1869, when Isaiah and Jeremiah Eldridge arrived in Shannon County, Missouri, claiming to be Confederate war veterans seeking a quiet place to start over. They built a two-room cabin and several outbuildings on roughly forty acres of mostly wooded, rugged land about seven miles northeast of the small settlement of Eminence, accessible only by a winding dirt road that became nearly impassable during the frequent rains. Jeremiah, the elder brother at about thirty-five, was described in county records as a tall, thin man with a sharp, suspicious look that made people uncomfortable.

Isaiah, about three years younger, was said to be more sociable, though still reserved by local standards. Their background before arriving in Shannon County remained largely undocumented, though rumors suggested they had fled somewhere in Kentucky after unspecified trouble. Between 1869 and 1873, at least seven travelers disappeared while passing through the vicinity of the Eldridge property. Shannon County had no official sheriff during that period, and the isolated nature of the region meant travelers came and went without anyone noting their presence.

McCready’s discovery set off a chain of events that would expose something far darker than a simple case of robbery or murder. Under oath before a circuit judge who visited the county the following month, McCready described what he had found. His personal notes, later preserved in the Missouri Historical Society archives, described personal belongings of people who were not members of the Eldridge family, arranged in a way that suggested ritual significance rather than mere storage. The investigation, limited by the constraints of rural Missouri in 1873, uncovered several peculiarities.

The first was a detailed ledger hidden beneath a loose floorboard in the main cabin. Written in meticulous handwriting later attributed to Jeremiah Eldridge, the ledger contained entries dating back to 1866, three years before the brothers’ alleged arrival in Shannon County. Each entry followed a similar pattern: a date, a description of a person, usually a solitary traveler or sometimes a couple, and a series of cryptic symbols that included measurements, weights, and what appeared to be notes about quality and suitability. The final pages contained what one investigator described as recipes, though the listed ingredients were largely incomprehensible, identified only by initials or symbols.

Behind the cabin, partially hidden by a row of oak trees, investigators found a small meat smokehouse, a common structure for the era. But unlike the typical packed-earth or rough plank floors of such buildings, the Eldridge smokehouse featured a carefully constructed stone floor with unusual drainage channels leading to a covered pit nearly six feet deep. Interviews with the few neighbors who had any dealings with the brothers added another layer of suspicion. A woman named Martha Callaway, whose farm lay about three miles from the Eldridge property, told investigators she had on two occasions observed the brothers leading mules loaded with heavy burdens toward Eminence long after midnight.

When asked what they might have been carrying, Callaway reportedly answered only that whatever it was, they handled it with great care, as though it were precious to them, and covered it completely with cloth and rope. A storekeeper in Eminence named Jacob Thornton provided additional information. According to records he kept, the brothers regularly purchased unusual quantities of salt, black pepper, and a substance he recorded as preserving powder, most likely potassium nitrate, commonly used in meat preservation during that era. What made these purchases notable was not just their volume but their timing.

The brothers made these purchases regardless of season, whereas most locals preserved meat extensively only during the cool autumn months. The investigation might have ended there, with suspicious circumstances but no tangible evidence of wrongdoing beyond perhaps illegal whiskey production, had a man named Frederick Pearson not arrived in Eminence in November 1873. Pearson identified himself as an investigator for the Pinkerton agency in St. Louis, hired by the family of a missing businessman named Walter Hammond.

According to Pearson’s report, later partially published in the St. Louis Post-Dispatch, Hammond had been traveling through southern Missouri in August of that year, assessing timber opportunities for a St. Louis lumber company. His last known location was a small tavern in Van Buren, about thirty miles northeast of Eminence, where he told the owner of his intention to explore opportunities in Shannon County.

Pearson’s investigation led him to the abandoned Eldridge property, where he conducted a far more meticulous examination than local authorities had managed. What he discovered in the storage cellar beneath the main cabin prompted him to send a rider immediately to Eminence requesting additional investigators and proper digging tools. The findings of the Pinkerton investigators were documented in a report classified as confidential and sealed by order of the circuit judge, ostensibly to prevent public panic. According to court records, that report remained sealed until 1937, when a flood damaged parts of the Shannon County courthouse, prompting the transfer of many historical documents.

During this process, Pearson’s report was apparently misplaced. It was later discovered by a court clerk named Abigail Winters, who made a copy before returning the original to the court archives. Her copy eventually reached historian Gerald McKinney, who incorporated portions of it into his 1952 book Forgotten Crimes of the Ozarks. The book attracted little attention outside academic circles and went out of print after a single small printing.

In 1968, the remaining copies were purchased by an anonymous collector, making the text extremely rare today. According to portions of Pearson’s report quoted in McKinney’s book, the investigator found evidence that the Eldridge brothers had been involved in activities far more disturbing than moonshining or robbery. The storage cellar contained specialized tools, including custom-made knives with strangely shaped blades, and a set of butcher hooks modified for an unspecified purpose. More importantly, it contained a collection of personal effects: watches, rings, wallets, and other belongings that appeared to have been stripped from multiple people.

What transformed the case from a presumed series of robberies and possible murders into something far more sinister was the discovery Pearson and his team made when they expanded their search to the area surrounding the smokehouse. There, using information extracted from the ledger, they uncovered a series of systematic excavations arranged in an approximate semicircle around the building. The contents of these excavations were described in the report only as remains inconsistent with traditional burial practices, suggesting knowledge of body preservation techniques unfamiliar to that region. The most disturbing aspect of Pearson’s report, however, was not what was found on the Eldridge property, but what was discovered when investigators began tracing the brothers’ movements and connections.

Through interviews with merchants in Springfield, Missouri, Pearson confirmed that the Eldridges had been regularly transporting goods to that city, located about a hundred miles northwest of their Shannon County property. A butcher named William Gresham told investigators he had purchased what he believed to be venison and wild boar meat from the brothers on at least six occasions between 1870 and 1873. Gresham described the meat as of exceptional quality, though unusual in its cuts. He had paid premium prices for the products, which he then sold to several of the most exclusive restaurants and hotels in Springfield.

The investigation took a darker turn when Pearson traced financial records indicating the Eldridge brothers had opened an account at the Merchants Bank in Springfield in 1870 with an initial deposit of two thousand three dollars, a substantial sum for ostensibly poor farmers. By 1873, their account balance had exceeded three thousand dollars, with regular deposits following their trips to Springfield. The brothers’ possession of a significant bank account, combined with their regular purchases of preserving materials and the specialized tools found on their property, painted a picture that investigators were only beginning to understand. The path forward would lead through Springfield’s elite social circles, into the mountains of Kentucky, and eventually to questions that would remain unanswered for nearly a century and a half.

William Gresham’s testimony, recorded during an interview with Pearson in December 1873, included a disturbing observation: the meat he received from the Eldridge brothers was sold at the highest prices to his wealthiest customers. Clients specifically requested it. Gresham stated it had a flavor different from any game meat they had tasted before. Some claimed it gave them unusual vitality, like a tonic.

According to Pearson’s notes, at least three prominent Springfield citizens, a banker, a judge, and a physician, had standing orders for the brothers’ products, considering them a delicacy reserved for special occasions and important guests. The investigation became complicated by the social standing of those who had unknowingly consumed the brothers’ products. When Pearson began connecting the brothers to Springfield’s elite through their meat sales, he reportedly faced increasing pressure to handle the matter discreetly. According to a letter Pearson wrote to his Pinkerton supervisor in St.

Louis dated January 17, 1874, he had been approached by representatives of several influential Springfield families who urged him to consider the broader implications of his investigation. Pearson wrote that these gentlemen expressed concern not about the Eldridge brothers, whom they readily condemned, but about the reputations of those who had innocently consumed what might prove to be contaminated goods. They feared that public disclosure of the full circumstances would destroy respectable families and shake citizens’ confidence in the region’s commercial establishments. Whether because of this pressure or simply the challenges of investigating crimes decades old in a remote region, many aspects of the Eldridge case remained unresolved.

The total number of victims, for example, was never definitively established. Pearson’s report identified seven individuals who had disappeared in the vicinity of the Eldridge property between 1869 and 1873. But the ledger discovered in the cabin contained entries suggesting a far larger number, possibly dating back to the brothers’ time in Kentucky before their arrival in Missouri. The most comprehensive analysis of the case was conducted in 1967 by a University of Missouri graduate student named Rebecca Thornhill, who attempted in her master’s thesis in criminology to reconcile the various historical accounts and evidence.

Thornhill’s research, which included interviews with descendants of Shannon County residents from the 1870s and a review of previously unpublished court documents, suggested that the Eldridge brothers might have been responsible for the disappearance of up to twenty-one people over seven years. Thornhill’s thesis also explored a particularly disturbing aspect of the case that had received little attention: the possibility that the Eldridge brothers had not acted alone. Through analysis of local records and contemporary accounts, she identified at least three occasions when the brothers were seen in Eminence while smoke could simultaneously be seen rising from their cabin’s chimney miles away in the valley. This observation led Thornhill to theorize that the brothers may have had a partner, perhaps a family member or associate, who was never identified.

She noted several references in local accounts to a simple-minded cousin who occasionally visited the Eldridges, though no official record of such an individual existed in county documents. Thornhill’s proposal of a third participant gained additional credibility in 1968 when the sealed box discovered in the Shannon County courthouse was found to contain a daguerreotype showing the Eldridge cabin. In the background of the image, partially obscured by shadow, a third person could be seen standing near the smokehouse. The quality of the image made positive identification impossible, but the person appeared different in build and stance from either of the documented Eldridge brothers.

The question of what happened to this possible third participant added another layer of mystery to an already complex case. If such an individual existed, did he flee with the brothers when the property was abandoned in 1873? Or perhaps he remained in the area, potentially blending into the local community while retaining knowledge of the brothers’ activities. This possibility gained significance in light of an incident in Eminence in 1879, six years after the Eldridge brothers’ disappearance.

According to court records, a drifter named Thomas Leach was arrested after attempting to sell personal belongings belonging to a recently vanished traveler. During interrogation, Leach claimed he had learned his trade from masters of the craft, and referred to the valley where the smoke never stops. When investigators attempted to question Leach further about these statements, they found him dead in his cell, apparently having ended his life with a hidden razor blade. The incident was briefly investigated, then quickly dismissed as a desperate act by a common criminal seeking to make himself mysterious.

Thornhill and other researchers, however, later pointed out that Leach’s statements and subsequent death might represent a side link to the Eldridge case that authorities at the time overlooked. The potential geographic scope of the Eldridge brothers’ activities represented another unresolved aspect. While the original investigation focused on their Shannon County property, later research identified similar patterns of disappearances and unusual meat sales in other areas where men matching the brothers’ descriptions reportedly resided. Records from Harlan County, Kentucky, indicated that between 1864 and 1869, just before the brothers’ arrival in Missouri, at least four travelers had disappeared while passing through a remote area locally known as Still House Hollow.

During this same period, two brothers named Edward and John Smith operated a small meat smokehouse in the area, selling what they described as mountain venison to merchants in the larger town of Harlan. The resemblance to the Missouri Eldridge operation was striking, though no connection was ever made at the time between the Smith brothers of Kentucky and the Eldridges of Missouri. The potential link was not identified until 1963, when historian Patricia Donovan was researching disappearances in Appalachia during the post-Civil War period. Donovan discovered a record in the Harlan County courthouse indicating that Edward and John Smith had left the area suddenly in early 1869, after an incident described only as unwanted scrutiny from outside parties.

The timing aligned perfectly with the Eldridge brothers’ arrival in Shannon County, Missouri, later that same year. More compelling still, the physical description of Edward Smith in Harlan County records bore a striking resemblance to that of Jeremiah Eldridge in Missouri documents. Both men were described as tall and thin with a distinctive scar running from the left ear to the corner of the mouth. This precise detail had not been included in any published accounts of the Eldridge case, appearing only in original court documents, making the connection particularly compelling.

If Edward and John Smith were indeed Jeremiah and Isaiah Eldridge operating under assumed names, it suggested a pattern of systematic operation spanning multiple states, potentially involving dozens of victims over nearly a decade. The brothers would settle in a remote area, develop their operation over years, then move on when local suspicion or outside investigation threatened to expose them. This pattern might also explain the brothers’ ultimate fate after their disappearance from Shannon County in 1873. Rather than being captured or killed, they may simply have moved to another isolated region and resumed their activities under new identities.

The reports of individuals resembling the brothers in Louisiana in 1887 and Colorado in 1891 might represent later iterations of their operation, though neither was ever investigated thoroughly enough at the time to establish a definitive connection. One of the most disturbing possibilities raised by modern analysis of the Eldridge case was that the brothers may have been part of a larger network of like-minded individuals operating throughout America’s post-Civil War frontier regions. The years following the conflict were characterized by significant population movement, limited law enforcement in remote areas, and a general atmosphere of societal upheaval that might have provided cover for organized criminal activities. Dr.

Holbrook considered this possibility briefly in his 1955 analysis, noting that the sophistication of the Eldridge operation, particularly their ability to market and distribute their products through legitimate commercial channels, suggested a level of organization that might extend beyond two isolated individuals. He ultimately concluded, however, that the evidence was insufficient to support such a theory. The possibility of a broader network gained new significance in light of a discovery made in 1966 during renovation of a historic hotel in Springfield, Missouri. Workers removing a section of wall in what had once been the hotel kitchen discovered a small metal box containing a single sheet of paper.

The document, written in meticulous, cramped handwriting, listed twelve sets of initials, each followed by a location identified only by a combination of letters and numbers. Among the entries was J and IE or SC, which some researchers interpreted as referring to Jeremiah and Isaiah Eldridge in Shannon County. If this interpretation was correct, the document might represent a record of individuals engaged in similar activities throughout the region, with the letter and number combinations signifying territories or operational areas. The document was turned over to local authorities who, finding no evidence of recent criminal activity, eventually transferred it to the Missouri Historical Society.

There it remained largely forgotten until 1969, when researcher Martin Crayton encountered it while investigating another matter. Crayton immediately recognized the potential connection to the Eldridge case and attempted to analyze the other initials and location codes on the list. His efforts yielded only limited results, though he did identify two other sets of initials that possibly matched unsolved disappearances in Missouri and Arkansas during the same period. Before he could complete his analysis, Crayton suffered a severe stroke that prevented him from continuing his work.

His notes on the subject were said to be among materials donated to the University of Missouri archives upon his death in 1972, but have never been definitively located. The discovery of the list raised disturbing questions about the scope and organization of potential criminal networks in the post-Civil War frontier. If the Eldridge brothers were indeed part of a larger association of individuals engaged in similar activities, the implications for historical understanding of crime in that period would be significant. However, most researchers who have studied the case maintain that the evidence strongly supports the theory that the Eldridge brothers operated independently, developing their own methodology through trial and error rather than as part of an organized network.

The unique aspects of their operation, particularly the processing and sale of human remains as exotic meat, have few documented parallels in criminal history, suggesting an innovative approach rather than an established practice. The psychological profile of the Eldridge brothers represented another area of fascination and ongoing debate among researchers. Unlike many criminals of their era who left letters, confessions, or other direct expressions of their motives, the brothers maintained an almost complete documentary silence regarding the purpose or justification of their activities. The ledger found in their cabin, with its clinical observations and measurements, perhaps provided the only direct insight into their thinking.

The systematic nature of these records, with their focus on physical characteristics and quality assessments, suggested individuals who viewed their victims primarily as resources rather than as human beings. It was a perspective that criminologists identified as a form of extreme objectification common among the most dangerous types of serial offenders. Dr. Mayhew suggested in her 1964 analysis that this objectification might have roots in the brothers’ experiences during the Civil War.

If they had indeed served in the Confederate army as they claimed upon arriving in Shannon County, they would certainly have been exposed to mass casualties and the dehumanization inherent in that conflict. For individuals with certain psychological predispositions, such exposure might normalize violence and diminish the perceived value of human life. This theory gained additional support in 1965 when military historian Robert Canfield discovered records indicating that two brothers named Eldridge had served in the Confederate Fifth Kentucky Infantry during the war. The regiment had participated in some of the conflict’s bloodiest engagements, including the Battle of Shiloh, where casualties were particularly heavy.

More significantly, regimental records indicated that during the winter of 1863-1864, when supplies were critically low, several soldiers had been court-martialed for robbing the dead, and in at least one case for the illegal consumption of meat unfit for human consumption. Although the records did not mention the Eldridge brothers specifically in connection with these incidents, their presence in the regiment during that period suggested potential exposure to harsh survival situations that might have influenced their later behavior. The potential connection to wartime experiences provided one of the few plausible explanations for the brothers’ transformation from ostensibly ordinary soldiers to systematic killers and processors of human remains. The transition from the battlefield, where killing was sanctioned and corpses were familiar, to civilian life could be challenging even for psychologically healthy individuals.

For those predisposed to violence or sociopathy, the contrast between wartime and peacetime norms might create a context in which deviant behaviors could develop and escalate. This theory was supported by the apparent timeline of the brothers’ activities. If the connection to Edward and John Smith of Harlan County, Kentucky, was correct, their criminal operations had begun shortly after the Civil War ended, a period when they were transitioning from military to civilian life while also coping with the broader social upheaval of the post-war South. The evolution from their early activities in Kentucky to the more sophisticated operations in Missouri represented a development in both methodology and scale.

What may have begun as opportunistic predation on vulnerable travelers perhaps evolved into the systematic operation documented in Shannon County, with its specialized tools, record-keeping, and commercial distribution network. This developmental pattern aligned with modern understanding of serial offenders, who typically refine their methods through experience and repetition. The brothers’ apparent success in avoiding detection over years would have reinforced their behaviors while allowing them to perfect their techniques in killing, victim processing, and evidence concealment. The most disturbing aspect of the Eldridge case from a psychological perspective was the apparent absence of the emotional or sexual motives typically associated with serial killers.

Unlike most such offenders, who derive psychological or physical satisfaction from the act of killing itself, the evidence suggested that the Eldridges viewed killing primarily as a means to a financial end. This profit motive, combined with the systematic record-keeping documented in the ledger, placed the brothers in a rare category of offenders bridging the gap between serial killers and organized crime. Their operation, focused on resource extraction, from victims’ possessions and remains subsequently converted to money through legitimate commercial channels, represented a disturbing combination of predatory violence and business calculation. The long-term impact of the Eldridge case on the communities where they operated extended far beyond the immediate investigation and its inconclusive results.

In Shannon County, the legacy of the brothers’ activities manifested in a pervasive wariness of strangers that persisted for generations, a wariness that many researchers documented when they encountered significant resistance attempting to investigate the case. Martin Crayton described the reaction of local residents when he asked about the Eldridge brothers during his 1962 visit to the region: it was as though a curtain suddenly descended. People who had been speaking freely moments before about local history suddenly found urgent business elsewhere. Those who did respond offered only minimal acknowledgment of the brothers’ existence, usually followed by assurances that what happened was long ago and best forgotten.

This collective silence suggested a community response to trauma, a shared decision to distance themselves from events too disturbing to integrate into their communal identity. Similar patterns had been observed in other locations associated with heinous crimes, where populations often develop protective narratives that minimize the horror that occurred among them or attribute it to outsiders. In Springfield, Missouri, where unwitting consumers had purchased and eaten the brothers’ products, the response took a different form. Rather than collective silence, the community experienced what a contemporary observer described as a season of gastric hysteria when the nature of the Eldridge brothers’ work became known in early 1874.

According to Springfield Republic newspaper reports, local physicians were flooded with patients reporting mysterious ailments they attributed to consuming meat purchased from stores that had dealt with the Eldridge brothers. Although most of these complaints were likely psychosomatic responses to the disturbing revelation, the incident illustrated the profound psychological impact of the case on those who feared unwitting involvement in the brothers’ horrific trade. The site of the Eldridge home in Shannon County now lies within the boundaries of the Mark Twain National Forest, accessible only by a rarely used hiking trail that does not appear on most maps. The cabin and outbuildings have long since returned to the earth, leaving only slight depressions in the forest floor marking where they once stood.

Local residents occasionally report unusual experiences in the area, such as an oppressive stillness, as though the forest were holding its breath, or the faint smell of smoke while no fire burns. These reports, while impossible to verify objectively, contribute to the area’s reputation as a place best avoided, especially after dark. In 1975, a group of archaeology students from the University of Missouri attempted a systematic survey of the site as part of a broader study of nineteenth-century homesteads in the Ozarks. According to their field notes, the project was abandoned after three days due to equipment failures and adverse conditions.

One participant, speaking anonymously to a student newspaper after returning to campus, described an overwhelming feeling of being watched throughout their time at the site. Whether these accounts represented genuine paranormal phenomena, the power of suggestion affecting individuals who knew the site’s history, or simply the natural unease that can arise in remote places, they contributed to the enduring mystery surrounding the Eldridge case. The valley where the brothers lived had become a place where history and folklore intersected, where the documented horrors of the past blended seamlessly with the more intangible fears of the present. In 1982, a more meticulous archaeological investigation was organized by Dr.

Howard Mitchell of the Missouri State Archaeological Survey. With proper equipment and a team of experienced researchers, Mitchell hoped to resolve some of the outstanding questions about the physical evidence at the site. Over two weeks, the team conducted a systematic survey of approximately five acres surrounding the presumed location of the cabin. Their findings, detailed in a report published in the journal Historical Archaeology in 1983, included the stone foundation of the main cabin, remnants of the unusual drainage system associated with the smokehouse, and, most significantly, a series of small, regular depressions extending in an arc behind where the outbuildings would have stood, consistent with the systematic excavations mentioned in Pearson’s 1873 report.

Excavation of several of these depressions yielded bone fragments that Mitchell’s team initially identified as animal remains. However, subsequent laboratory analysis by forensic anthropologist Dr. Eleanor Wilkins revealed that at least some of the fragments were of human origin. Most disturbingly, Wilkins noted that many of the bones showed clear evidence of butchering with fine saw marks consistent with careful cutting rather than violent tearing.

Carbon dating of the remains placed them between 1865 and 1875, aligning perfectly with the period of the Eldridge brothers’ occupation of the site. This discovery provided the first scientifically proven physical evidence linking the brothers to the processing of human remains, confirming a central element of the historical accounts that some researchers had previously questioned. Mitchell’s team also recovered several small personal items from the site, including buttons, a pocket watch case, and a gold wedding ring engraved with the letters MLH to WH, 1868, potentially connecting it to Walter Hammond, the missing businessman whose disappearance had brought Pinkerton investigator Frederick Pearson to Shannon County in 1873. These findings, while significant, left many aspects of the case unresolved.

The total number of victims, the full extent of the brothers’ operations, and their ultimate fate remained matters of speculation rather than established fact. Mitchell concluded his report with the observation that the archaeological record, while confirming the disturbing reality at the heart of the Eldridge case, could only hint at the full scope of their activities. The personal backgrounds of the Eldridge brothers themselves represented another area where fact and speculation had often merged. The claim that they were Confederate veterans appeared supported by the military records discovered by historian Robert Canfield, but their lives before and after the war remained largely obscure.

In 1984, genealogist Margaret Holloway attempted to trace the brothers’ family connections through census records and other public documents. Her research, published in the American Genealogy Journal, identified Jeremiah and Isaiah Eldridge as having been born to a sharecropping family in eastern Tennessee in 1838 and 1841 respectively, ages consistent with the descriptions of the brothers in Shannon County. According to Holloway’s findings, the Eldridge family had moved to Harlan County, Kentucky, in the early 1850s, where the father worked as a butcher’s assistant before his death in 1858. This detail gained particular significance in light of the brothers’ later activities, suggesting they may have acquired their knowledge of meat processing through the family trade rather than independent experience.

Holloway’s research also revealed a significant gap in the documented history of the Eldridge brothers between their presumed enlistment in the Confederate army in 1861 and their appearance in Harlan County as Edward and John Smith in 1864. This period, coinciding with the most intense years of the Civil War, may have been crucial in the development of their particular pathology. Military historian James Donovan, building on Holloway’s work, suggested in a 1986 article that the brothers may have served not only in traditional combat roles but also in irregular units that operated behind enemy lines. These units operated with limited oversight, engaging in activities including sabotage, assassination, and terror tactics against civilians, practices found on both sides of the conflict.

Donovan noted that the Fifth Kentucky Infantry, in which soldiers named Eldridge were documented, had been temporarily attached to a command that included several such irregular units during the winter of 1863-1864. While no direct evidence linked the brothers to these units, Donovan suggested that exposure to their methods might have influenced the brothers’ later approach to violence, particularly their emphasis on secrecy, efficiency, and disposal of evidence. The commercial aspect of the Eldridge brothers’ operation remained one of its most distinctive and disturbing features. Unlike most killers who dispose of bodies to hide evidence, the brothers had apparently developed a system for processing and profiting from their victims’ remains, an innovation criminologists found particularly significant.

Forensic psychologist Dr. Rachel Simmons, in a 2011 analysis published in the Journal of Criminal Psychology, described this aspect of the case as representing a complete and unusual integration of homicidal motives and entrepreneurial spirit. According to Simmons, most profit-driven killers focused on stealing valuables, or in kidnapping cases, obtaining ransoms, regarding the victim’s body as mere waste to be disposed of. What distinguished the Eldridge case, Simmons wrote, was the apparent thoroughness of resource extraction from victims.

The brothers seemingly viewed their victims as sources of multiple forms of value: first, the traditional portable wealth of travelers such as money, watches, and other items; then, the commercial value of the human remains themselves. This comprehensive approach suggested a level of abstraction and commodification of human life that exceeded even what was typically seen among serial offenders. This commercial sophistication raised questions about how the brothers had developed and refined their methodology. If they had indeed operated in Kentucky as the Smith brothers and then in Missouri as the Eldridge brothers, the evolution of their methods over time represented a disturbing learning curve, one that may have continued after their disappearance from Shannon County in 1873.

The reports of individuals resembling the brothers in Louisiana in 1887 and Colorado in 1891 took on additional significance when viewed from this perspective. If these sightings represented the actual continuation of the Eldridge brothers’ activities in new locations, they would have had nearly two decades to perfect their methods since their first documented operations in Kentucky. The implications of such long-term, multi-state criminal activity, continuing largely beyond the awareness of authorities, were deeply troubling. The Eldridge case also raised questions about potential victims who might never have been identified or linked to the brothers’ activities.

The seven documented disappearances in Shannon County between 1869 and 1873 likely represented only a fraction of the total if the brothers had operated for years across multiple states. Historian Eliza Montgomery, in a 1992 study of mysterious disappearances in the post-Civil War era, identified thirty-four cases between 1865 and 1895 that shared characteristics potentially linking them to the Eldridge pattern: solitary male travelers, often carrying significant amounts of money, who disappeared while passing through remote areas where individuals matching the brothers’ descriptions had been reported. While acknowledging that many of these disappearances might have other explanations, from natural disasters to unrelated criminal activity, Montgomery argued that at least some represented undocumented victims of the Eldridges, or perhaps of others using similar methods. Her study highlighted the limitations of historical criminal investigation in an era predating unified record-keeping, forensic science, or effective interstate communication.

The question of whether others had adopted the Eldridge brothers’ particular methodology represented another troubling possibility. The case had received limited public attention at the time, with most newspaper coverage focusing on the disappearance and robbery aspects rather than the processing and sale of remains. However, those directly involved in the investigation were aware of the full details, creating the potential for imitation. Thomas Leach, the drifter arrested in Eminence in 1879 who claimed to have learned his trade from masters of the craft, represented a potential example of such imitation.

His apparent suicide before detailed interrogation prevented investigators from determining whether his statement specifically referenced the Eldridge brothers or whether he had actual knowledge of their methods. More broadly, the remote regions of the Ozarks and Appalachia, with their isolated valleys and limited law enforcement, continued to experience occasional disappearances into the twentieth century. While most of these cases likely had conventional explanations, the Eldridge case suggested the possibility of similar operations, perhaps on a smaller scale, in other locations. In 1956, a hunter in rural Oregon discovered an abandoned cabin containing equipment similar to that described in the Eldridge case: specialized cutting tools, a modified meat smokehouse, and a ledger containing entries with measurements and quality notes.

Local authorities, unaware of the historical Missouri case, investigated the site as a possible illegal hunting operation. By the time historian Gerald McKinney established the connection to the Eldridge pattern in 1963, the trail had gone completely cold. Similarly, in 1964, a hiker in Idaho’s Bitterroot Mountains reported finding a remote camp containing preserved human remains processed in a manner consistent with professional butchering. When authorities reached the site, it had been cleaned out, with only a few scattered tools remaining as evidence anyone had ever been there at all.

These incidents, while impossible to link conclusively to the Eldridge legacy, suggested the disturbing possibility that their methodology may have been adopted and adapted by others, whether through direct transmission of knowledge or through independent development of similar techniques. The isolated nature of such operations made their discovery unlikely, especially if practitioners maintained the apparent discipline of the brothers regarding victim selection and evidence disposal. Today, with improved forensic techniques, DNA analysis, and coordinated law enforcement databases, such operations would face greater challenges in avoiding detection. Yet remote areas still existed where determined individuals might operate beyond effective oversight, and the disappearance of hikers, travelers, and other vulnerable individuals continued at rates exceeding clear resolutions.

The cultural impact of the Eldridge case, despite its relatively limited prominence in mainstream historical narratives, had been significant in certain contexts. In the Missouri Ozarks, particularly in Shannon County, the story had achieved the status of a dark legend, a cautionary tale about the dangers that might lurk in seemingly peaceful rural settings. Local folklorist Dr. Samuel Hawkins documented numerous variations of the Eldridge story passed down through oral tradition in the region throughout the twentieth century.

In a 1997 article published in the Journal of American Folklore, Hawkins noted that these versions often incorporated supernatural elements absent from the historical record, describing the brothers as possessing unnatural power or the ability to draw travelers to them through hypnotic suggestion. These folkloric adaptations, Hawkins wrote, transformed the historical Eldridges from human criminals, however brutal, into something resembling demons or evil spirits, entities representing evil inherent in the landscape rather than mere human depravity. This transformation from historical figures to folkloric entities reflected a common pattern in cultural processing of traumatic events. By reimagining the brothers as supernatural beings rather than humans, the community created psychological distance from the disturbing reality that ordinary men had committed such acts among them.

The Eldridge case had also periodically attracted the attention of true crime authors and documentary filmmakers, though often with considerable embellishment or sensationalism. A 1976 book titled Butchers of the Ozarks presented a largely fictionalized account, introducing romantic subplots and graphic violence not present in the historical records. Similarly, a low-budget 1988 documentary titled American Monsters: The Eldridge Brothers featured dramatic reenactments focusing on the case’s most gruesome aspects while neglecting its historical context. A more academic treatment came in 2003 when historian Richard Patterson included a chapter on the Eldridge case in his book Forgotten Horrors: Criminal Episodes in American History.

Patterson’s account, based on extensive archival research, placed the brothers’ activities in the broader context of post-Civil War social upheaval and the limited law enforcement capabilities of frontier regions. The Eldridge case, Patterson wrote, represented not an aberration but an extreme manifestation of conditions existing throughout much of the American frontier during that period. The isolation that attracted settlers seeking independence also created spaces where predators could operate with minimal risk of detection or intervention. The legal legacy of the Eldridge case, while difficult to trace directly, included its potential influence on the development of more coordinated approaches to investigating disappearances across jurisdictional boundaries.

The difficulties authorities faced in attempting to track the brothers across state lines highlighted the limitations of local law enforcement in addressing mobile criminal operations. In 1874, partially in response to the Eldridge case and similar situations, the governors of Missouri, Arkansas, and Kentucky formalized an agreement to exchange information regarding missing persons and suspected criminals across state borders. While primitive by modern standards, this arrangement represented an early step toward the regional and national law enforcement coordination that would fully develop in the twentieth century. The medical implications of the Eldridge brothers’ activities had also attracted academic attention, particularly regarding potential consequences for those who had unknowingly consumed the meat the brothers sold.

Dr. Harold Winstead’s documentation of a cluster of neurological cases among Springfield’s elite in the 1890s, potentially linked to consumption of contaminated meat decades earlier, raised disturbing possibilities about the long-term public health impact of the brothers’ trade. Modern medical researchers noted that certain prion diseases, fatal brain disorders caused by misfolded proteins, could have incubation periods lasting many years or even decades. Neurologist Melissa Carpenter, reviewing Winstead’s accounts in a 2005 article for the Journal of Medical History, concluded that while definitive diagnosis based on limited historical descriptions was impossible, the pattern of symptoms described was consistent with what was now known as variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, which could be transmitted through consumption of contaminated neural tissue.

This medical dimension added another layer of horror to the Eldridge case: the possibility that the brothers’ crimes continued to claim victims years or even decades after the brothers themselves had disappeared, as those who had unknowingly consumed their products succumbed to slow-developing neurological conditions. One of the most disturbing aspects of the Eldridge case remained the possibility that the brothers, or others who used their methods, may have continued operating into the mid-twentieth century. The remote regions of the American interior, with their isolated expanses diminished but still substantial, could have provided cover for similar operations long after the original Eldridge brothers left the scene. Whether the brothers died shortly after their disappearance from Shannon County or continued their activities for decades in other locations, they represented a troubling chapter in American criminal history, one that challenged comfortable assumptions about the boundaries of human behavior and the safety of even the most seemingly peaceful rural settings.

Their legacy lived on not only in academic studies and Ozarks folklore but in the careful wariness that still characterized the region’s dealings with strangers, and in the persistent rumors surrounding certain remote valleys that local residents refused to venture into after dark. As one Shannon County resident told a researcher in 2012: some places hold memories that even the trees do not whisper. In the end, perhaps the most disturbing aspect of the Eldridge case was not what was known about the brothers and their activities, but what remained unknown: the questions that might never be fully answered about the extent of their crimes, the fate of all their victims, and whether their particular brand of systematic predation had truly ended with their disappearance, or had evolved and continued in ways not yet discovered. In the dark valleys of the American rural landscape, where isolation provided both refuge and opportunity, the conditions that allowed the Eldridge brothers to operate had never entirely disappeared.

As long as travelers continued to venture into remote areas, following winding dirt roads to destinations not easily reached by others, the threat of such predators remained a dark possibility etched into the terrain itself, as enduring as the ancient Ozark hills and as quietly persistent as the threads of mist that rose over their valleys on cold autumn mornings.

content_text:
On a Saturday afternoon in 1986, a teenager in suburban Ohio laced up her sneakers and asked her mother for a ride. There was no errand, no shopping list, nothing specific to buy. She simply wanted to go to the mall. That was the entire plan, and it was enough.

She would wander past neon signs, flip through cassette tapes, eat cheap pizza under fluorescent lights, try on clothes she could not afford, and run into half her school. The mall was not merely a place to shop. It was the town square, the playground, the living room, and the social center of an entire generation. Today, that same spot looks like something from a post-apocalyptic film.

Water-stained ceilings, shattered skylights, escalators frozen mid-step, dry fountains, a dark food court, and a parking lot cracked and overgrown with weeds. At their peak in the late 1980s, America had roughly 2,500 enclosed shopping malls. Today, fewer than 700 remain, and by some estimates, that number could fall to as few as 150 by the early 2030s. No new mega mall has been built in the United States since 2006.

Over the last decade, an average of 40 malls closed every year, and in 2025 alone, nearly 6,000 mall-based stores shut their doors, a 67 percent increase from the year before. The story of how this happened begins not with the internet, but with a socialist architect from Vienna named Victor Gruen. Born Victor David Grünbaum in 1903, Gruen was Jewish, an avant-garde architect, and a performer of satirical cabaret. When the Nazis annexed Austria in 1938, he fled to America with almost nothing.

He landed in New York, changed his name, and began designing storefronts on Fifth Avenue. But Gruen had a much larger vision. Looking at the new American suburbs built after the Second World War, he saw communities without centers, families isolated in identical ranch houses with no public gathering place. The GI Bill had given returning soldiers cheap mortgages and affordable education, and millions of families fled the cities for three-bedroom homes with two-car garages.

But moving thirty miles outside the city meant moving thirty miles away from restaurants, shops, theaters, and doctors. The suburbs had houses, but they did not have life. Gruen dreamed of something revolutionary: an enclosed, climate-controlled community hub that combined stores with gardens, art, medical facilities, schools, and public squares. He wanted to replicate the vibrant street life of Vienna in the middle of the American suburbs.

In 1952, the Dayton family, prominent department store merchants from Minneapolis, commissioned him to bring that vision to life. On October 8, 1956, the Southdale Center opened in Edina, Minnesota. It was the first fully enclosed, climate-controlled shopping mall in the United States, an 800,000-square-foot complex with 72 stores, 5,000 parking spots, and two anchor department stores placed at opposite ends to pull foot traffic past every smaller shop in between. The temperature inside was kept at a constant 75 degrees, a miracle for a region with brutal winters.

Gruen also engineered something subtler into the design, a psychological phenomenon later known as the Gruen transfer. The corridors curved, the sightlines shifted, and the lighting and music were all crafted to create a pleasant confusion that made shoppers forget what they came for and begin buying things they had not planned on. It was consumer psychology weaponized through architecture, and it worked. Life magazine called Southdale the splashiest shopping center in the country, and developers across America rushed to replicate the model.

By the mid-1970s, more than a thousand enclosed malls had been built. They followed an identical formula: two or three massive department stores as anchor tenants at opposite ends, a corridor of specialty shops between them, a food court near the center, a movie theater, an arcade, a fountain, and acres of free parking. The malls did not just change how Americans shopped. In suburbs with no downtown and no main street, the mall became the place for first dates, first jobs, ear piercings, and after-school hangouts.

For a long time, the arrangement worked beautifully for developers, retailers, and the millions of families who organized their weekends around it. But the model was not built to last. Through the 1970s and 1980s, the mall did not just grow; it metastasized. Developers realized malls were profit machines.

The formula was simple: buy cheap land on the suburban fringe, build the mall, watch the surrounding area explode with new housing and commercial development, and watch property values skyrocket. Anchor tenants signed long leases, smaller retailers paid premium rents for the foot traffic, and tax revenue poured into local governments. Everyone got rich, so they kept building. By 1986, America had roughly 25,000 retail malls and shopping centers.

Americans spent an average of twelve hours per month inside them. The country had accumulated nearly 24 square feet of retail space per person, ten to twenty times more than any other developed nation. Nobody stopped to ask whether that made sense. Each new mall required cheap land, so developers built further and further out.

New housing surrounded the new mall, families drifted away from older neighborhoods, and when an even larger, flashier mall was built even further out, the cycle repeated. The original mall lost its customer base, property values fell, retailers left, and the old mall deteriorated. This was the suburban sprawl death spiral, baked into the model from the very beginning. Every new mall was a ticking clock for the one that came before it.

Through the 1980s and 1990s, none of this mattered because the money was still flowing. The mall was the backdrop of American culture. Fast Times at Ridgemont High in 1982 was a love letter to mall culture. Tiffany performed her hit single on a mall tour in 1987.

The Mall of America opened in Bloomington, Minnesota, in 1992, a 5. 6-million-square-foot behemoth with an indoor amusement park, an aquarium, and over 500 stores. But beneath the surface, the foundation was already cracking. The entire economic model of the American mall rested on one pillar: the anchor tenant.

These massive department stores, names like Sears, JCPenney, Macy's, and Nordstrom, drew the foot traffic, paid for the advertising, and kept the smaller specialty shops alive. In return, they paid far lower rents than smaller tenants, often almost nothing, because their value was in the crowds. This arrangement worked as long as the anchors stayed healthy. Starting in the late 1990s and accelerating through the 2000s, the American department store began to die.

Sears, once one of the ten most valuable companies in America and an era-defining retailer that operated roughly 3,500 stores at its height, filed for bankruptcy in October 2018. By 2025, fewer than ten Sears stores remained. JCPenney followed a similar path, closing around 200 stores during its 2020 bankruptcy. Macy's announced plans in February 2024 to shutter 150 stores by 2026.

Lord and Taylor closed entirely, and Bon-Ton, a chain with 250 locations, liquidated in 2018. The impact on malls was catastrophic. When an anchor tenant closes, foot traffic to that mall drops by 20 to 25 percent almost immediately. But the damage goes further.

Most smaller tenants have co-tenancy clauses in their leases, meaning that if a major anchor leaves, they can renegotiate their rent downward or break their lease entirely. When Sears closed, the shoe store next to it started paying less rent, the clothing boutique triggered its exit clause, and the pretzel stand lost half its customers. The entire ecosystem collapsed inward like a building losing its load-bearing walls. The other major external force was the rise of e-commerce.

In 1994, Jeff Bezos founded a small online bookstore in his garage in Bellevue, Washington, called Amazon. Within a decade, it had expanded into almost everything. By 2017, a Business Insider analysis concluded that Amazon alone was generating more than 50 percent of all retail sales growth in the United States. E-commerce did not just compete with physical stores; it undermined the very reason people went to malls.

The mall's value proposition had been convenience, everything under one roof. But when you could find everything on a screen and have it delivered to your door the next day, that argument evaporated overnight. Then came March 2020 and the COVID-19 pandemic. Malls closed for weeks and sometimes months.

A record 12,000 stores closed in 2020 alone. JCPenney, J. Crew, Neiman Marcus, and Brooks Brothers all filed for bankruptcy. The pandemic permanently changed habits.

Shoppers who discovered they could get everything delivered, many never came back. Even by 2024, mall foot traffic remained 35 percent below pre-pandemic levels. But e-commerce and the pandemic were accelerants, not the root cause. The root cause was structural and had been building for decades.

America was grotesquely overbuilt in retail. The 24 square feet of retail space per person was eight times more than Spain, nine times more than Italy, eleven times more than Germany, and roughly 400 times more than India. Nobody on Earth needed that much retail, but developers kept building because the economics were irresistible in the short term, and the consequences were someone else's problem in the long term. Commercial real estate was incentivized by the tax code, cheap debt, and the ability to flip properties.

Local governments offered tax breaks and infrastructure subsidies to lure developers, hoping for sales tax revenue and jobs. But when three malls were built within twenty miles of each other, all competing for the same shoppers, the math stopped working. The pie did not get bigger; it just got sliced thinner. Not all malls are dying equally.

The industry is splitting in two. Premium class A malls in wealthy, high-traffic locations, like South Coast Plaza in California, the Galleria in Houston, and Tysons Corner Center in Virginia, have occupancy rates around 95 percent and have seen a 12 percent increase in foot traffic since the pandemic. They have reinvented themselves as luxury destinations where people go to dine, see art, and attend events. On the other end are class B, C, and D malls in smaller cities and declining suburbs.

An estimated 31 percent of all American malls fall into this lower tier, many of them zombie malls, technically still open but functionally dead, with vacancy rates 248 percent higher than the overall retail average. The average vacant mall sells at 43 percent below its original acquisition price, and once a mall goes dark, it stays dark for an average of nearly four years. What happens to dead malls turns out to be one of the more fascinating parts of the story. A dead shopping mall sitting on fifty acres of prime suburban land near a highway interchange is a redevelopment goldmine.

Nearly half of all mall redevelopments are mixed-use projects combining retail, residential, and commercial space. Thirty-one percent of vacant malls are reborn with new retail tenants. Nine percent become warehouses. Seven percent become residential housing.

Five percent become delivery and distribution centers, many of them serving the very e-commerce companies that helped kill the mall. Four percent become community colleges, medical facilities, or civic spaces. Landmark Mall in Alexandria, Virginia, closed in 2017, and the 51-acre site is now being redeveloped into a $2 billion mixed-use community with 4,400 apartments, a hospital, parks, and retail space. Amazon itself has partnered with Simon Property Group to convert former Sears and JCPenney spaces into fulfillment centers.

The company that did more than any other to destroy the American mall is now literally moving into the buildings it killed. Victor Gruen lived long enough to see what his creation became, and he hated it. By the 1970s, he had publicly disowned the suburban shopping mall, calling it a bastardization of his original vision. He had dreamed of a community center that happened to include shops.

America built a consumption machine that happened to have air conditioning. Gruen moved back to Vienna in 1968 and spent the last decade of his life advocating for walkable, mixed-use urban neighborhoods. He died in 1980, just as the mall was entering its most excessive and culturally dominant phase. He never saw the collapse, but the collapse was inevitable.

The American mall was built on assumptions that all turned out to be wrong: that suburbs would keep growing forever, that department stores would always anchor the model, that Americans would always prefer driving to a climate-controlled box over every other form of shopping and socializing, and that you could keep building retail space indefinitely without saturating the market. Every one of those assumptions shattered. The dead malls are not just a retail story. They are a mirror reflecting an entire way of thinking about growth, community, and public space.

The luxury malls will survive, and the ones that reinvent themselves as mixed-use hubs will survive too. The mall of the future, if it exists at all, will not be a shopping center. It will be a community center that happens to have some stores, which is exactly what Victor Gruen wanted in the first place.

Born Victor David Grünbaum in 1903, Gruen was Jewish, an avant-garde architect, and a performer of satirical cabaret. When the Nazis annexed Austria in 1938, he fled to America with almost nothing.

He landed in New York, changed his name, and began designing storefronts on Fifth Avenue. But Gruen had a much larger vision. Looking at the new American suburbs built after the Second World War, he saw communities without centers, families isolated in identical ranch houses with no public gathering place. The GI Bill had given returning soldiers cheap mortgages and affordable education, and millions of families fled the cities for three-bedroom homes with two-car garages.

But moving thirty miles outside the city meant moving thirty miles away from restaurants, shops, theaters, and doctors. The suburbs had houses, but they did not have life. Gruen dreamed of something revolutionary: an enclosed, climate-controlled community hub that combined stores with gardens, art, medical facilities, schools, and public squares. He wanted to replicate the vibrant street life of Vienna in the middle of the American suburbs.

In 1952, the Dayton family, prominent department store merchants from Minneapolis, commissioned him to bring that vision to life. On October 8, 1956, the Southdale Center opened in Edina, Minnesota. It was the first fully enclosed, climate-controlled shopping mall in the United States, an 800,000-square-foot complex with 72 stores, 5,000 parking spots, and two anchor department stores placed at opposite ends to pull foot traffic past every smaller shop in between. The temperature inside was kept at a constant 75 degrees, a miracle for a region with brutal winters.

Gruen also engineered something subtler into the design, a psychological phenomenon later known as the Gruen transfer. The corridors curved, the sightlines shifted, and the lighting and music were all crafted to create a pleasant confusion that made shoppers forget what they came for and begin buying things they had not planned on. It was consumer psychology weaponized through architecture, and it worked. Life magazine called Southdale the splashiest shopping center in the country, and developers across America rushed to replicate the model.

By the mid-1970s, more than a thousand enclosed malls had been built. They followed an identical formula: two or three massive department stores as anchor tenants at opposite ends, a corridor of specialty shops between them, a food court near the center, a movie theater, an arcade, a fountain, and acres of free parking. The malls did not just change how Americans shopped. In suburbs with no downtown and no main street, the mall became the place for first dates, first jobs, ear piercings, and after-school hangouts.

For a long time, the arrangement worked beautifully for developers, retailers, and the millions of families who organized their weekends around it. But the model was not built to last. Through the 1970s and 1980s, the mall did not just grow; it metastasized. Developers realized malls were profit machines.

The formula was simple: buy cheap land on the suburban fringe, build the mall, watch the surrounding area explode with new housing and commercial development, and watch property values skyrocket. Anchor tenants signed long leases, smaller retailers paid premium rents for the foot traffic, and tax revenue poured into local governments. Everyone got rich, so they kept building. By 1986, America had roughly 25,000 retail malls and shopping centers.

Americans spent an average of twelve hours per month inside them. The country had accumulated nearly 24 square feet of retail space per person, ten to twenty times more than any other developed nation. Nobody stopped to ask whether that made sense. Each new mall required cheap land, so developers built further and further out.

New housing surrounded the new mall, families drifted away from older neighborhoods, and when an even larger, flashier mall was built even further out, the cycle repeated. The original mall lost its customer base, property values fell, retailers left, and the old mall deteriorated. This was the suburban sprawl death spiral, baked into the model from the very beginning. Every new mall was a ticking clock for the one that came before it.

Through the 1980s and 1990s, none of this mattered because the money was still flowing. The mall was the backdrop of American culture. Fast Times at Ridgemont High in 1982 was a love letter to mall culture. Tiffany performed her hit single on a mall tour in 1987.

The Mall of America opened in Bloomington, Minnesota, in 1992, a 5. 6-million-square-foot behemoth with an indoor amusement park, an aquarium, and over 500 stores. But beneath the surface, the foundation was already cracking. The entire economic model of the American mall rested on one pillar: the anchor tenant.

These massive department stores, names like Sears, JCPenney, Macy’s, and Nordstrom, drew the foot traffic, paid for the advertising, and kept the smaller specialty shops alive. In return, they paid far lower rents than smaller tenants, often almost nothing, because their value was in the crowds. This arrangement worked as long as the anchors stayed healthy. Starting in the late 1990s and accelerating through the 2000s, the American department store began to die.

Sears, once one of the ten most valuable companies in America and an era-defining retailer that operated roughly 3,500 stores at its height, filed for bankruptcy in October 2018. By 2025, fewer than ten Sears stores remained. JCPenney followed a similar path, closing around 200 stores during its 2020 bankruptcy. Macy’s announced plans in February 2024 to shutter 150 stores by 2026.

Lord and Taylor closed entirely, and Bon-Ton, a chain with 250 locations, liquidated in 2018. The impact on malls was catastrophic. When an anchor tenant closes, foot traffic to that mall drops by 20 to 25 percent almost immediately. But the damage goes further.

Most smaller tenants have co-tenancy clauses in their leases, meaning that if a major anchor leaves, they can renegotiate their rent downward or break their lease entirely. When Sears closed, the shoe store next to it started paying less rent, the clothing boutique triggered its exit clause, and the pretzel stand lost half its customers. The entire ecosystem collapsed inward like a building losing its load-bearing walls. The other major external force was the rise of e-commerce.

In 1994, Jeff Bezos founded a small online bookstore in his garage in Bellevue, Washington, called Amazon. Within a decade, it had expanded into almost everything. By 2017, a Business Insider analysis concluded that Amazon alone was generating more than 50 percent of all retail sales growth in the United States. E-commerce did not just compete with physical stores; it undermined the very reason people went to malls.

The mall’s value proposition had been convenience, everything under one roof. But when you could find everything on a screen and have it delivered to your door the next day, that argument evaporated overnight. Then came March 2020 and the COVID-19 pandemic. Malls closed for weeks and sometimes months.

A record 12,000 stores closed in 2020 alone. JCPenney, J. Crew, Neiman Marcus, and Brooks Brothers all filed for bankruptcy. The pandemic permanently changed habits.

Shoppers who discovered they could get everything delivered, many never came back. Even by 2024, mall foot traffic remained 35 percent below pre-pandemic levels. But e-commerce and the pandemic were accelerants, not the root cause. The root cause was structural and had been building for decades.

America was grotesquely overbuilt in retail. The 24 square feet of retail space per person was eight times more than Spain, nine times more than Italy, eleven times more than Germany, and roughly 400 times more than India. Nobody on Earth needed that much retail, but developers kept building because the economics were irresistible in the short term, and the consequences were someone else’s problem in the long term. Commercial real estate was incentivized by the tax code, cheap debt, and the ability to flip properties.

Local governments offered tax breaks and infrastructure subsidies to lure developers, hoping for sales tax revenue and jobs. But when three malls were built within twenty miles of each other, all competing for the same shoppers, the math stopped working. The pie did not get bigger; it just got sliced thinner. Not all malls are dying equally.

The industry is splitting in two. Premium class A malls in wealthy, high-traffic locations, like South Coast Plaza in California, the Galleria in Houston, and Tysons Corner Center in Virginia, have occupancy rates around 95 percent and have seen a 12 percent increase in foot traffic since the pandemic. They have reinvented themselves as luxury destinations where people go to dine, see art, and attend events. On the other end are class B, C, and D malls in smaller cities and declining suburbs.

An estimated 31 percent of all American malls fall into this lower tier, many of them zombie malls, technically still open but functionally dead, with vacancy rates 248 percent higher than the overall retail average. The average vacant mall sells at 43 percent below its original acquisition price, and once a mall goes dark, it stays dark for an average of nearly four years. What happens to dead malls turns out to be one of the more fascinating parts of the story. A dead shopping mall sitting on fifty acres of prime suburban land near a highway interchange is a redevelopment goldmine.

Nearly half of all mall redevelopments are mixed-use projects combining retail, residential, and commercial space. Thirty-one percent of vacant malls are reborn with new retail tenants. Nine percent become warehouses. Seven percent become residential housing.

Five percent become delivery and distribution centers, many of them serving the very e-commerce companies that helped kill the mall. Four percent become community colleges, medical facilities, or civic spaces. Landmark Mall in Alexandria, Virginia, closed in 2017, and the 51-acre site is now being redeveloped into a $2 billion mixed-use community with 4,400 apartments, a hospital, parks, and retail space. Amazon itself has partnered with Simon Property Group to convert former Sears and JCPenney spaces into fulfillment centers.

The company that did more than any other to destroy the American mall is now literally moving into the buildings it killed. Victor Gruen lived long enough to see what his creation became, and he hated it. By the 1970s, he had publicly disowned the suburban shopping mall, calling it a bastardization of his original vision. He had dreamed of a community center that happened to include shops.

America built a consumption machine that happened to have air conditioning. Gruen moved back to Vienna in 1968 and spent the last decade of his life advocating for walkable, mixed-use urban neighborhoods. He died in 1980, just as the mall was entering its most excessive and culturally dominant phase. He never saw the collapse, but the collapse was inevitable.

The American mall was built on assumptions that all turned out to be wrong: that suburbs would keep growing forever, that department stores would always anchor the model, that Americans would always prefer driving to a climate-controlled box over every other form of shopping and socializing, and that you could keep building retail space indefinitely without saturating the market. Every one of those assumptions shattered. The dead malls are not just a retail story. They are a mirror reflecting an entire way of thinking about growth, community, and public space.

The luxury malls will survive, and the ones that reinvent themselves as mixed-use hubs will survive too. The mall of the future, if it exists at all, will not be a shopping center. It will be a community center that happens to have some stores, which is exactly what Victor Gruen wanted in the first place.
