content_text:
In June of 1968, a platoon of soldiers was sent to carve a bomb shelter into the slopes of Mount Lingshan in China. They were not archaeologists. They were not looking for anything but solid rock to dig into. But as they broke through a massive stone wall, they found themselves staring into an ancient burial chamber.

It was intact. It was untouched. And it would turn out to be one of the most important archaeological discoveries in Chinese history. Word of the find reached Beijing quickly.

An emergency team from the Academy of Sciences was dispatched to the site, and they confirmed what the soldiers had stumbled upon. This was a tomb from the Han Dynasty—an imperial family tomb. A second burial chamber was soon found nearby. The tombs belonged to Liu Sheng, Prince of Zhongshan, and his wife, Dou Wan.

They had been sealed for more than two thousand years. This was a discovery that seemed almost impossible. The tombs had survived grave robbers, which was rare for any elite burial from the Han Dynasty. Most had been looted long ago.

But these tombs, cut deep into the eastern slope of the mountain, had been hidden so effectively that they remained untouched. By the end of the summer, the excavation was complete, and the Mancheng Han tombs became a symbol of China’s cultural achievements. The discovery came during the Cultural Revolution, a violent campaign launched by Mao Zedong against the intellectuals he called bourgeois elements. It was a dark era.

But Mao allowed the archaeological work to continue, because it made for excellent propaganda. Inside the tombs, the archaeologists found a subterranean palace. The chambers were designed to mirror the earthly home of the prince and his wife. This reflected a belief held by the Han elite: the tomb was an eternal residence, and it needed to be comfortable.

It needed to be filled with treasures. The tombs held a wealth of artifacts from the second century BC. There were bronze ritual vessels, silver objects, wooden carvings, and figurines meant to recreate the pleasures of earthly life in the afterlife. But the most stunning items were the jade burial suits.

Jade had long been associated with immortality and the heavens in Chinese culture. It was used in funerary rites long before the emperors. The Han rulers, having seen their predecessors die from drinking mercury potions in pursuit of eternal life, placed their faith in jade instead. They believed the stone had a mystical power to stop decay and fix the soul in place forever.

Historians and archaeologists had known about these suits from ancient texts, but no one had ever found a real one. Not until the Mancheng discovery. Liu Sheng’s suit was made of 2,498 individual pieces of jade, stitched together with more than two pounds of pure gold wire. It took an estimated ten years of master craftsmanship to complete.

It was a full suit of armor designed to protect the prince in the afterlife and prevent his body from decaying. But time won in the end. When archaeologists opened the suit after more than two thousand years, Liu Sheng’s body had long since turned to dust. All that remained was his gleaming jade armor.

In 1952, archaeologists in Mexico broke into an ancient tomb and found a lost king in perfect condition. It had taken four full years to clear the rubble from the stairway leading to the tomb of Pacal the Great. Technically, Alberto Ruz Lhuillier had discovered the resting place of the great Mayan ruler in 1948, but he could not actually reach the burial chamber until 1952. When Alberto entered the inner room, he was stunned.

In the center of the chamber was a massive stone sarcophagus, something out of an adventure film. Inside that enormous coffin was a skeleton still wearing a traditional funerary mask of jade. It was also covered with beaded necklaces and surrounded by carvings and inscriptions, most of which showed Pacal ascending from a mortal man to a divine figure. This king believed he would become a god after death.

This was K’inich Janaab Pakal I, the Ajaw of the city of Palenque. Everyone likes to call him King Pacal the Great, but the truth is that king was not his title. He was an Ajaw, which means lord in the Mayan language. He ruled Palenque, but he was not a king of the Maya.

This was an important distinction. Every city, from Palenque to Chichen Itza, had its own ruler. The Maya operated as independent states that attacked their neighbors. Pacal was born during a very tense period in Palenque’s history.

The city, located in the jungles of present-day Chiapas, had recently been invaded and sacked by the more powerful Mayan city of Calakmul. Four years before Pacal was born, Palenque suffered a disastrous attack, followed by another attack during Pacal’s childhood in 611. These attacks were orchestrated by the Ajaw of Calakmul, known only as Scroll Serpent. During this turbulent period, Palenque’s leader was killed along with his heir.

These two deaths led to a succession crisis, which eventually resulted in Pacal taking the throne at the age of twelve, in July of 615. From an early age, Pacal had an expansionist mentality. He expanded Palenque’s power by reaching into neighboring territories. In 628, when one of his officials was captured, Pacal retaliated by kidnapping the Ajaw of Santa Elena and bringing him to Palenque, then making Santa Elena a tributary of Palenque.

Mayan civilization was like a high-stakes game of risk, with territory endlessly taken and lost. He married a woman from the ruling lineage of the nearby settlement of Uxte’k’uh, bringing more neighbors under his sway. During their marriage, Pacal and his wife, Lady Tz’akbu Ajaw, had at least two sons, and possibly a third. Pacal was expansionist, but he was also a patron of the fine arts.

He began a building program in the capital that produced some of the finest art and architecture in the entire kingdom. By turning Palenque into a center of arts and culture, he elevated his city’s status and made it a shining jewel in Maya life. He would go on to rule for 68 years, the fifth longest reign of any monarch in human history, and the longest of any ruler in the Americas. The four longer-reigning monarchs were Louis XIV of France, who reigned for 72 years; Queen Elizabeth II, who reigned for 70 years and 214 days; Rama IX of Thailand, 70 years and 126 days; and Johann II, Prince of Liechtenstein, 70 years and 91 days.

Pacal the Great held the throne for 68 years and 33 days. Near the end of his life, his loved ones began to die around him, one by one. His wife, with whom he had lived for 47 years, died in November of 672. Eight years later, his third son died.

Then, in August of 683, at the age of eighty, Pacal followed his wife and sons to the afterlife. He had sat on the throne for so long that he was already a god-king to the people of Palenque. He must have seemed nearly immortal, living more than three-quarters of a century while most people barely reached the age of thirty-five. Naturally, he was deified after his death.

Pacal was consecrated and buried in a massive stone sarcophagus deep within the city’s largest pyramid, known as the House of the Nine Sharpened Spears. Archaeologists today call it the Temple of Inscriptions. In the early twentieth century, archaeologists began digging into the ruins of Palenque. They knew the great ruler was buried somewhere in the city, but they could not find the secret entrance to his tomb.

They did not realize it was closed off by a massive stone slab, with the stairway completely blocked by rubble. After Alberto Ruz Lhuillier’s miraculous discovery of the secret entrance, followed by four years of clearing debris, the world finally got its first look at the divine king of Palenque. Based on the bones, scientists estimated Pacal’s height at about 5 feet 2 inches, average for a Mesoamerican man from 1,400 years ago. The most interesting aspect was his skull, which showed clear cranial deformation—elongated and tilted backward.

As an infant, Pacal had undergone head-binding techniques, with his head pressed between cloth and wooden boards to completely reshape his cranium. The result of this modification was that his face grew forward and outward, almost like a dog’s. It pushed his facial features outward, making him look somewhat frightening, at least to modern eyes. With his filed teeth and flat incisors, he would have looked rather beastly.

But behind that fierce appearance, Pacal was not a tyrant. By all historical accounts, he was actually one of the most stable and effective Mayan leaders ever. He ruled peacefully alongside his wife for nearly 50 years, ushering in a golden age of art and prosperity. For years after his death, Pacal remained a beloved figure in Palenque society.

They continued to make works of art depicting him decades after his burial. Today, the only real mystery still surrounding Pacal is his carved sarcophagus lid, which has become a subject of great controversy. The massive stone coffin lid is a unique piece of Maya art. Around the edges of the lid is a frame of cosmic symbols.

Those large borders, with all their seemingly random geometric shapes, are actually signs for the sun, the moon, and various stars. Each rectangular section has its own distinct meaning. But it is the central image that gets everyone talking. In 1968, when ancient astronaut theorist Erich von Däniken published his book Chariots of the Gods, he pointed to this lid.

He claimed the central image shows Pacal piloting a spacecraft. Von Däniken argued that the sarcophagus lid shows Pacal sitting inside a rocket-powered vehicle, with Mayan symbols surrounding the ruler representing technological components. Pacal’s hands were allegedly on controls, with a breathing apparatus near his face. According to the archaeologists and historians who have devoted their lives to studying Maya history and culture, none of that is accurate.

The symbols represent cosmic signs. The central image is not a spacecraft. It is a cross-shaped World Tree. Beneath Pacal is one of the heads of a celestial double-headed serpent.

The Ajaw and the serpent head are framed within the open jaws of a massive funerary serpent, indicating the entrance to the underworld. Pacal’s strange posture inside the serpent’s mouth is a representation of resurrection. Looking at the image closely, noticing all these small details, it becomes clear it could not be a spaceship. It is simply not realistic.

Furthermore, Pacal was an eighty-year-old man when he died. If he had plans to move to a new world, would he not have done it a little earlier? On the other side of the world, rulers in ancient China were buried in full suits of jade, as if locked inside an iron jade coffin. For years, jade burial suits were just a rumor, an interesting legend that Chinese archaeologists dreamed of.

Then in 1968, soldiers accidentally found the imperial family tombs of a prince and princess of the Han Dynasty. More than 2,000 years ago, a small army of builders began carving into the rock of the eastern slope of the mountain. After removing thousands of tons of rock, workers dug out a complex of tombs dedicated to preserving the remains of Liu Sheng and Dou Wan. Liu Sheng was the Prince of Zhongshan, and Dou Wan was his wife.

His father was Jing Di, the sixth emperor of the Han Dynasty. The Han Dynasty was the second dynasty of the empire, after the legendary Qin Shi Huang, the ruler who first unified China under the Qin. The Han ruled from 206 BC to 220 AD. When a major rebellion broke out in 154 BC, Emperor Jing sent his son Liu Sheng to take control of Zhongshan, a border region known for its instability in the fledgling empire.

Historians suspect construction of the tombs began shortly after Liu Sheng took power. They were so massive that they took decades to complete, requiring a colossal number of workers who labored without pause. It would have been a devastating financial burden. But when you are a prince, you get to choose how to spend your money.

By the time of Liu Sheng’s death in 113 BC, and then his wife’s death in 104 BC, their tombs were complete and filled with a variety of funerary goods. Once the lady was buried with the goods inside the tomb, both tunnels leading to the tombs were sealed with brick walls, filled with cast iron, and hidden. While many other elite Han Dynasty tombs were looted by grave robbers, the sealing measures of the Mancheng tombs proved surprisingly effective. It took the brutal force of dictator Mao Zedong to force the mountain to reveal its treasures.

In Sardinia, a giant’s tomb was found by chance. It is so massive that hardly anyone believes it was built 4,000 years ago. This tomb is not entirely unique in Sardinia. Researchers who found it claim it is part of a much larger group of mysterious funerary complexes called Giants’ Tombs.

The reason for the name is self-evident. The tombs are large enough to hold the bodies of giants, and who knows, perhaps some of them really did. The tomb was discovered when two surveyors were digging at a completely different archaeological site in the same location. They moved some vegetation and suddenly found themselves in front of the weathered stone of a massive grave.

The grave had simply been hidden by some overgrown weeds. Although there are many Giants’ Tombs, researchers are very excited about this one because it appears to be of strategic importance. The Italian science team suspects, due to its position on the southern slope of Monte Cresia with a wide view over the Macomer plain down to the Gulf of Oristano, that a figure of great importance was buried here. The most prominent features are a pair of large stone platforms, a sacred well, a residential quarter, and a vast burial area.

That is a lot of features for a tomb built shortly after the construction of Stonehenge. Unfortunately, someone appears to have already excavated the tomb illegally. A large part of the structure is damaged, not just by time and weather. It seems someone found the tomb and dug into it, probably to loot valuables.

All the team found inside were ceramic remains that were perhaps not important enough to steal. This massive tomb was built by the Nuragic civilization. These people dominated the island of Sardinia from the Bronze Age through the Iron Age. Not much is known about them today.

Unlike the Egyptians or Sumerians, the Nuragic people left no written records. What they left behind are 7,000 nuraghi towers and many other stone tombs. The towers are undoubtedly the most famous Nuragic structures. Although 7,000 towers remain, archaeologists believe there may have been up to 30,000 before the civilization disappeared.

Each tower is round in shape with a flat, truncated top. The tower has a cylindrical interior with a diameter of up to about 40 feet. The oldest known examples date to the 18th century BC. The problem is that no one knows what these towers were used for.

Some nuraghi reach heights of 90 feet, while others are only a few feet high. Some have complex dwellings inside, while others house wells or storage areas. The purpose of these structures is one of the most debated topics in archaeology today. Were they grain silos?

Defensive forts? Astronomical observatories or temples? Artifacts found inside the towers suggest they were homes. Archaeologists have found stone tools, cooking pots, and hearths inside these towers—everything needed for a prehistoric home.

But since thousands of stone houses have also been found in Sardinia, usually surrounding the famous stone towers, they were not homes for everyone. Perhaps they were for the elite. The Giants’ Tombs are scattered across Sardinia almost as much as the towers, though often found in the center of the island and usually filled with dozens or hundreds of bodies. Archaeologists believe the Nuragic people cared a great deal not only about burying their dead respectfully, but also about keeping them close to their villages.

Perhaps there was some kind of ancestor worship, with the Nuragic people believing in some form of afterlife. But they left no written records, so there is no way to know what they thought happened specifically after death. After centuries in Sardinia without much competition or external threats, Carthage began its conquest. The Carthaginians spread from North Africa to dominate the Balearic Islands, Malta, Iberia, and Sardinia.

By the time Rome defeated Carthage a few centuries later, the Nuragic civilization had virtually died out. The Epic of Gilgamesh predates almost everything known in ancient literature. Written in the cradle of ancient Mesopotamia thousands of years before the Greeks appeared on the map, it is the first recorded epic in the world, following the most ambitious legendary ruler in history. He was the king of Uruk, two-thirds god and one-third human, named Gilgamesh.

The epic takes the reader on Gilgamesh’s great journey in search of immortality and meaning. The story has endured for nearly 5,000 years because Gilgamesh sought the same thing we all seek in our lives: meaning. Historians today argue about whether Odysseus, the hero of the Odyssey, was a real king of Ithaca, just as they argue about whether Gilgamesh really ruled the city of Uruk in Mesopotamia. In 2003, archaeologists may have found his tomb.

Twenty-three years earlier—that is, in 2003—an announcement of a groundbreaking discovery shocked the archaeological community. A team of German scientists was excavating near the ruins of Uruk in southern Iraq. During their work, they found a massive funerary complex. This site was unlike any burial complex ever found before.

It was huge, with an imposing entrance, multi-layered chambers, and a massive tomb fit for a demigod. Experts in Mesopotamian literature were quick to notice the similarities between the tomb discovered in Iraq and the one described in the Epic of Gilgamesh. Could this actually be the tomb of the legendary ruler? When the news first spread, there was excitement and denial.

Some archaeologists hailed it as the greatest discovery in Iraqi history. Others argued there was not enough evidence to link the tomb to Gilgamesh. There were no inscriptions bearing Gilgamesh’s name, no artifacts associated with his reign, no information about who was buried there. The tomb was fit for a king, but if it was for Gilgamesh, there was no definitive proof.

However, there was some compelling evidence hinting at a possible link. The location of the tomb, found on an ancient channel of the Euphrates River, matches exactly the description of Gilgamesh’s burial in the epic. According to the ancient tale, believed to have been written about 4,200 years ago, Gilgamesh was buried under the Euphrates. The story says the people of Uruk grieved Gilgamesh’s death so much that they diverted the course of the Euphrates to build his tomb in the riverbed.

That was one way to protect the tomb from looters. They diverted the river, built the tomb, placed Gilgamesh inside, then allowed the river to return to its course over the burial chamber, sealing it forever—or at least until the river dried up. The Euphrates is no longer the great river it once was. The river’s flow has decreased by more than 60% over the past hundred years.

Severe drought and climate change have made it a sad stream compared to the life-giving flow of the past. This is why, in 2003, archaeologists found the tomb in the heart of the site where the river once flowed. Perhaps someone else was buried under the Euphrates, but who could that be? Looking at the list of ancient kings of Uruk, there is no one else said to have been buried beneath that river.

Gilgamesh was the only one worth diverting the river’s waters for. It was a massive project rivaling the building of the Great Pyramid. Another piece of evidence that the tomb belonged to Gilgamesh was the architecture, which reflected the lavish palaces and stepped pyramids associated with the ancient kings of Uruk. The style, design, and architecture were what archaeologists would expect from Gilgamesh’s tomb.

This put archaeologists at a crossroads. There was no real evidence inside the tomb, but the situation was too similar to the ancient epic to ignore. The artifacts found inside the tomb made things even more complicated. There were clay tablets inscribed with cuneiform telling stories of epic deeds and legendary journeys, but without any explicit mention of Gilgamesh.

Perhaps these clay tablets were similar to the hieroglyphic inscriptions found inside Egyptian royal tombs, which describe the titles and deeds of the deceased. This meant that whoever was buried in this massive tomb was boasting of adventures similar to those in the Epic of Gilgamesh. The broken clay tablets were enough to keep the mystery alive. That mystery persists to this day, with no modern archaeologists willing to accept that the tomb belonged to Gilgamesh.

Despite the striking coincidence of its location, the tomb of Gilgamesh seems to have been hidden and ignored.

In June of 1968, a platoon of soldiers was sent to carve a bomb shelter into the slopes of Mount Lingshan in China. They were not archaeologists. They were not looking for anything but solid rock to dig into. But as they broke through a massive stone wall, they found themselves staring into an ancient burial chamber.

It was intact. It was untouched. And it would turn out to be one of the most important archaeological discoveries in Chinese history. Word of the find reached Beijing quickly.

An emergency team from the Academy of Sciences was dispatched to the site, and they confirmed what the soldiers had stumbled upon. This was a tomb from the Han Dynasty—an imperial family tomb. A second burial chamber was soon found nearby. The tombs belonged to Liu Sheng, Prince of Zhongshan, and his wife, Dou Wan.

They had been sealed for more than two thousand years. This was a discovery that seemed almost impossible. The tombs had survived grave robbers, which was rare for any elite burial from the Han Dynasty. Most had been looted long ago.

But these tombs, cut deep into the eastern slope of the mountain, had been hidden so effectively that they remained untouched. By the end of the summer, the excavation was complete, and the Mancheng Han tombs became a symbol of China’s cultural achievements. The discovery came during the Cultural Revolution, a violent campaign launched by Mao Zedong against the intellectuals he called bourgeois elements. It was a dark era.

But Mao allowed the archaeological work to continue, because it made for excellent propaganda. Inside the tombs, the archaeologists found a subterranean palace. The chambers were designed to mirror the earthly home of the prince and his wife. This reflected a belief held by the Han elite: the tomb was an eternal residence, and it needed to be comfortable.

It needed to be filled with treasures. The tombs held a wealth of artifacts from the second century BC. There were bronze ritual vessels, silver objects, wooden carvings, and figurines meant to recreate the pleasures of earthly life in the afterlife. But the most stunning items were the jade burial suits.

Jade had long been associated with immortality and the heavens in Chinese culture. It was used in funerary rites long before the emperors. The Han rulers, having seen their predecessors die from drinking mercury potions in pursuit of eternal life, placed their faith in jade instead. They believed the stone had a mystical power to stop decay and fix the soul in place forever.

Historians and archaeologists had known about these suits from ancient texts, but no one had ever found a real one. Not until the Mancheng discovery. Liu Sheng’s suit was made of 2,498 individual pieces of jade, stitched together with more than two pounds of pure gold wire. It took an estimated ten years of master craftsmanship to complete.

It was a full suit of armor designed to protect the prince in the afterlife and prevent his body from decaying. But time won in the end. When archaeologists opened the suit after more than two thousand years, Liu Sheng’s body had long since turned to dust. All that remained was his gleaming jade armor.

In 1952, archaeologists in Mexico broke into an ancient tomb and found a lost king in perfect condition. It had taken four full years to clear the rubble from the stairway leading to the tomb of Pacal the Great. Technically, Alberto Ruz Lhuillier had discovered the resting place of the great Mayan ruler in 1948, but he could not actually reach the burial chamber until 1952. When Alberto entered the inner room, he was stunned.

In the center of the chamber was a massive stone sarcophagus, something out of an adventure film. Inside that enormous coffin was a skeleton still wearing a traditional funerary mask of jade. It was also covered with beaded necklaces and surrounded by carvings and inscriptions, most of which showed Pacal ascending from a mortal man to a divine figure. This king believed he would become a god after death.

This was K’inich Janaab Pakal I, the Ajaw of the city of Palenque. Everyone likes to call him King Pacal the Great, but the truth is that king was not his title. He was an Ajaw, which means lord in the Mayan language. He ruled Palenque, but he was not a king of the Maya.

This was an important distinction. Every city, from Palenque to Chichen Itza, had its own ruler. The Maya operated as independent states that attacked their neighbors. Pacal was born during a very tense period in Palenque’s history.

The city, located in the jungles of present-day Chiapas, had recently been invaded and sacked by the more powerful Mayan city of Calakmul. Four years before Pacal was born, Palenque suffered a disastrous attack, followed by another attack during Pacal’s childhood in 611. These attacks were orchestrated by the Ajaw of Calakmul, known only as Scroll Serpent. During this turbulent period, Palenque’s leader was killed along with his heir.

These two deaths led to a succession crisis, which eventually resulted in Pacal taking the throne at the age of twelve, in July of 615. From an early age, Pacal had an expansionist mentality. He expanded Palenque’s power by reaching into neighboring territories. In 628, when one of his officials was captured, Pacal retaliated by kidnapping the Ajaw of Santa Elena and bringing him to Palenque, then making Santa Elena a tributary of Palenque.

Mayan civilization was like a high-stakes game of risk, with territory endlessly taken and lost. He married a woman from the ruling lineage of the nearby settlement of Uxte’k’uh, bringing more neighbors under his sway. During their marriage, Pacal and his wife, Lady Tz’akbu Ajaw, had at least two sons, and possibly a third. Pacal was expansionist, but he was also a patron of the fine arts.

He began a building program in the capital that produced some of the finest art and architecture in the entire kingdom. By turning Palenque into a center of arts and culture, he elevated his city’s status and made it a shining jewel in Maya life. He would go on to rule for 68 years, the fifth longest reign of any monarch in human history, and the longest of any ruler in the Americas. The four longer-reigning monarchs were Louis XIV of France, who reigned for 72 years; Queen Elizabeth II, who reigned for 70 years and 214 days; Rama IX of Thailand, 70 years and 126 days; and Johann II, Prince of Liechtenstein, 70 years and 91 days.

Pacal the Great held the throne for 68 years and 33 days. Near the end of his life, his loved ones began to die around him, one by one. His wife, with whom he had lived for 47 years, died in November of 672. Eight years later, his third son died.

Then, in August of 683, at the age of eighty, Pacal followed his wife and sons to the afterlife. He had sat on the throne for so long that he was already a god-king to the people of Palenque. He must have seemed nearly immortal, living more than three-quarters of a century while most people barely reached the age of thirty-five. Naturally, he was deified after his death.

Pacal was consecrated and buried in a massive stone sarcophagus deep within the city’s largest pyramid, known as the House of the Nine Sharpened Spears. Archaeologists today call it the Temple of Inscriptions. In the early twentieth century, archaeologists began digging into the ruins of Palenque. They knew the great ruler was buried somewhere in the city, but they could not find the secret entrance to his tomb.

They did not realize it was closed off by a massive stone slab, with the stairway completely blocked by rubble. After Alberto Ruz Lhuillier’s miraculous discovery of the secret entrance, followed by four years of clearing debris, the world finally got its first look at the divine king of Palenque. Based on the bones, scientists estimated Pacal’s height at about 5 feet 2 inches, average for a Mesoamerican man from 1,400 years ago. The most interesting aspect was his skull, which showed clear cranial deformation—elongated and tilted backward.

As an infant, Pacal had undergone head-binding techniques, with his head pressed between cloth and wooden boards to completely reshape his cranium. The result of this modification was that his face grew forward and outward, almost like a dog’s. It pushed his facial features outward, making him look somewhat frightening, at least to modern eyes. With his filed teeth and flat incisors, he would have looked rather beastly.

But behind that fierce appearance, Pacal was not a tyrant. By all historical accounts, he was actually one of the most stable and effective Mayan leaders ever. He ruled peacefully alongside his wife for nearly 50 years, ushering in a golden age of art and prosperity. For years after his death, Pacal remained a beloved figure in Palenque society.

They continued to make works of art depicting him decades after his burial. Today, the only real mystery still surrounding Pacal is his carved sarcophagus lid, which has become a subject of great controversy. The massive stone coffin lid is a unique piece of Maya art. Around the edges of the lid is a frame of cosmic symbols.

Those large borders, with all their seemingly random geometric shapes, are actually signs for the sun, the moon, and various stars. Each rectangular section has its own distinct meaning. But it is the central image that gets everyone talking. In 1968, when ancient astronaut theorist Erich von Däniken published his book Chariots of the Gods, he pointed to this lid.

He claimed the central image shows Pacal piloting a spacecraft. Von Däniken argued that the sarcophagus lid shows Pacal sitting inside a rocket-powered vehicle, with Mayan symbols surrounding the ruler representing technological components. Pacal’s hands were allegedly on controls, with a breathing apparatus near his face. According to the archaeologists and historians who have devoted their lives to studying Maya history and culture, none of that is accurate.

The symbols represent cosmic signs. The central image is not a spacecraft. It is a cross-shaped World Tree. Beneath Pacal is one of the heads of a celestial double-headed serpent.

The Ajaw and the serpent head are framed within the open jaws of a massive funerary serpent, indicating the entrance to the underworld. Pacal’s strange posture inside the serpent’s mouth is a representation of resurrection. Looking at the image closely, noticing all these small details, it becomes clear it could not be a spaceship. It is simply not realistic.

Furthermore, Pacal was an eighty-year-old man when he died. If he had plans to move to a new world, would he not have done it a little earlier? On the other side of the world, rulers in ancient China were buried in full suits of jade, as if locked inside an iron jade coffin. For years, jade burial suits were just a rumor, an interesting legend that Chinese archaeologists dreamed of.

Then in 1968, soldiers accidentally found the imperial family tombs of a prince and princess of the Han Dynasty. More than 2,000 years ago, a small army of builders began carving into the rock of the eastern slope of the mountain. After removing thousands of tons of rock, workers dug out a complex of tombs dedicated to preserving the remains of Liu Sheng and Dou Wan. Liu Sheng was the Prince of Zhongshan, and Dou Wan was his wife.

His father was Jing Di, the sixth emperor of the Han Dynasty. The Han Dynasty was the second dynasty of the empire, after the legendary Qin Shi Huang, the ruler who first unified China under the Qin. The Han ruled from 206 BC to 220 AD. When a major rebellion broke out in 154 BC, Emperor Jing sent his son Liu Sheng to take control of Zhongshan, a border region known for its instability in the fledgling empire.

Historians suspect construction of the tombs began shortly after Liu Sheng took power. They were so massive that they took decades to complete, requiring a colossal number of workers who labored without pause. It would have been a devastating financial burden. But when you are a prince, you get to choose how to spend your money.

By the time of Liu Sheng’s death in 113 BC, and then his wife’s death in 104 BC, their tombs were complete and filled with a variety of funerary goods. Once the lady was buried with the goods inside the tomb, both tunnels leading to the tombs were sealed with brick walls, filled with cast iron, and hidden. While many other elite Han Dynasty tombs were looted by grave robbers, the sealing measures of the Mancheng tombs proved surprisingly effective. It took the brutal force of dictator Mao Zedong to force the mountain to reveal its treasures.

In Sardinia, a giant’s tomb was found by chance. It is so massive that hardly anyone believes it was built 4,000 years ago. This tomb is not entirely unique in Sardinia. Researchers who found it claim it is part of a much larger group of mysterious funerary complexes called Giants’ Tombs.

The reason for the name is self-evident. The tombs are large enough to hold the bodies of giants, and who knows, perhaps some of them really did. The tomb was discovered when two surveyors were digging at a completely different archaeological site in the same location. They moved some vegetation and suddenly found themselves in front of the weathered stone of a massive grave.

The grave had simply been hidden by some overgrown weeds. Although there are many Giants’ Tombs, researchers are very excited about this one because it appears to be of strategic importance. The Italian science team suspects, due to its position on the southern slope of Monte Cresia with a wide view over the Macomer plain down to the Gulf of Oristano, that a figure of great importance was buried here. The most prominent features are a pair of large stone platforms, a sacred well, a residential quarter, and a vast burial area.

That is a lot of features for a tomb built shortly after the construction of Stonehenge. Unfortunately, someone appears to have already excavated the tomb illegally. A large part of the structure is damaged, not just by time and weather. It seems someone found the tomb and dug into it, probably to loot valuables.

All the team found inside were ceramic remains that were perhaps not important enough to steal. This massive tomb was built by the Nuragic civilization. These people dominated the island of Sardinia from the Bronze Age through the Iron Age. Not much is known about them today.

Unlike the Egyptians or Sumerians, the Nuragic people left no written records. What they left behind are 7,000 nuraghi towers and many other stone tombs. The towers are undoubtedly the most famous Nuragic structures. Although 7,000 towers remain, archaeologists believe there may have been up to 30,000 before the civilization disappeared.

Each tower is round in shape with a flat, truncated top. The tower has a cylindrical interior with a diameter of up to about 40 feet. The oldest known examples date to the 18th century BC. The problem is that no one knows what these towers were used for.

Some nuraghi reach heights of 90 feet, while others are only a few feet high. Some have complex dwellings inside, while others house wells or storage areas. The purpose of these structures is one of the most debated topics in archaeology today. Were they grain silos?

Defensive forts? Astronomical observatories or temples? Artifacts found inside the towers suggest they were homes. Archaeologists have found stone tools, cooking pots, and hearths inside these towers—everything needed for a prehistoric home.

But since thousands of stone houses have also been found in Sardinia, usually surrounding the famous stone towers, they were not homes for everyone. Perhaps they were for the elite. The Giants’ Tombs are scattered across Sardinia almost as much as the towers, though often found in the center of the island and usually filled with dozens or hundreds of bodies. Archaeologists believe the Nuragic people cared a great deal not only about burying their dead respectfully, but also about keeping them close to their villages.

Perhaps there was some kind of ancestor worship, with the Nuragic people believing in some form of afterlife. But they left no written records, so there is no way to know what they thought happened specifically after death. After centuries in Sardinia without much competition or external threats, Carthage began its conquest. The Carthaginians spread from North Africa to dominate the Balearic Islands, Malta, Iberia, and Sardinia.

By the time Rome defeated Carthage a few centuries later, the Nuragic civilization had virtually died out. The Epic of Gilgamesh predates almost everything known in ancient literature. Written in the cradle of ancient Mesopotamia thousands of years before the Greeks appeared on the map, it is the first recorded epic in the world, following the most ambitious legendary ruler in history. He was the king of Uruk, two-thirds god and one-third human, named Gilgamesh.

The epic takes the reader on Gilgamesh’s great journey in search of immortality and meaning. The story has endured for nearly 5,000 years because Gilgamesh sought the same thing we all seek in our lives: meaning. Historians today argue about whether Odysseus, the hero of the Odyssey, was a real king of Ithaca, just as they argue about whether Gilgamesh really ruled the city of Uruk in Mesopotamia. In 2003, archaeologists may have found his tomb.

Twenty-three years earlier—that is, in 2003—an announcement of a groundbreaking discovery shocked the archaeological community. A team of German scientists was excavating near the ruins of Uruk in southern Iraq. During their work, they found a massive funerary complex. This site was unlike any burial complex ever found before.

It was huge, with an imposing entrance, multi-layered chambers, and a massive tomb fit for a demigod. content_text:
On a crisp November evening in 1930, as the Great Depression ravaged the nation, New York City’s elite converged upon the Ritz-Carlton Hotel to celebrate the eighteenth birthday of Barbara Hutton, heiress to the monumental Woolworth store fortune. Upon arrival, the guests—hailing from the most illustrious families of the age, such as the Astors, Vanderbilts, Whitneys, and Rockefellers—were greeted by Maurice Chevalier, the renowned French entertainer, whimsically costumed as Santa Claus. Inside, the grand ballroom was a vision of a winter wonderland, adorned with extravagant decorations and a sea of flowers that alone bore a price tag of fifty thousand dollars, equal to nearly one million dollars in today’s currency. The atmosphere was alive with melodies from four orchestras, and the echoes of champagne cork pops filled the air as the night unfolded, with two thousand bottles of champagne served by a contingent of two hundred waiters.

As midnight approached, the revelry did not wane; instead, it escalated with the serving of seventeen-course suppers. As the night stretched into the early hours, one thousand breakfasts were laid out for those who had danced through the night. The pièce de résistance of the evening, however, was the party favors bestowed upon the guests: each attendee received a small jewelry case filled with unmounted diamonds, emeralds, rubies, and sapphires—a lavish token that left the crowd in awe of the hostess’s generosity. The celebration, which reportedly cost a staggering sixty thousand dollars, equivalent to over one million today, was capped off by Barbara Hutton herself.

As the radiant centerpiece of the evening, clad in a stunning debutante gown, she embodied the "poor little rich girl," a nickname that would cling to her through varied fortunes. That night at the Ritz-Carlton was more than just a lavish party; it was the heralding of Barbara Hutton’s entrance into the world of high society and the public eye. As one attendee poignantly observed, this was the moment when "Bobby became Barbara Hutton, debutante, glamour queen, playgirl of the Western World. " Little did they know this splendid introduction foreshadowed a tragic life of glamour, heartache, and the eternal pursuit of happiness amidst the glittering yet often unforgiving world of the rich and famous.

Barbara Hutton, an emblem of wealth from infancy, found herself at the center of a vortex of fortune and scrutiny as early as twelve years old. With the death of her grandmother, Jennie Katherine Woolworth, in 1924, Barbara was left a staggering inheritance that rivaled the tales of fairy-tale princesses: twenty-six million dollars, a sum that would inflate to almost five hundred million dollars in today’s currency. Even further, her mother’s estate cushioned this with an additional 2. 1 million dollars in stocks, managed by her father, Franklin Laws Hutton.

This trust bloomed to a monumental forty-two million dollars by the time Barbara reached twenty-one, crowning her one of the richest women globally during an era marked deeply by the Great Depression. Her father, Franklin, a titan in the financial realm and co-founder of the renowned E. F. Hutton and Company, was a master of his craft.

His financial moves, particularly his timely divestment before the 1929 market crash, significantly safeguarded and multiplied Barbara’s inheritance. Yet while Franklin navigated the financial storms with acumen, his personal life brewed with scandal. The mysterious death of Barbara’s mother, Edna Woolworth, in 1917—believed to be a self-inflicted end linked to Franklin’s infidelities—left a young Barbara to stumble upon her mother’s lifeless body, an image that haunted her throughout her life. In the wake of her mother’s death, Franklin’s subsequent marriage to Irene Bodt only deepened Barbara’s emotional isolation.

Regarded widely as an opportunistic stepmother, Irene’s presence ensured that Barbara’s upbringing was shuffled among various relatives, leaving her often in the hands of governesses rather than family. Despite these early traumas, Barbara’s entry into society was nothing short of spectacular, and her aforementioned debutante ball was absolutely legendary. Barbara Hutton’s personal life at its peak unfolded like a carefully choreographed ballet of opulence. She owned sumptuous estates across the globe, from the Japanese-inspired Suwama in Mexico to the regal Cidi Hosne in Tangier.

Each home was not merely a residence but a testament to her wealth and her impeccable taste for the exotic and the beautiful. But her passion for luxury was not confined to real estate. Hutton was also known for her incredible collection of jewelry, including the famed Vladimir Tiara, and her wardrobe was a parade of haute couture from legends like Cristóbal Balenciaga and Oleg Cassini. And it was Cassini, commissioned by Cary Grant, who attempted to navigate the tumultuous waters of their marriage through style.

Socially, Barbara was a magnet for high-profile gatherings, her debutante ball in New York being particularly notable for its extravagance. Despite the allure, this display of wealth was not without its critics, especially given the harsh economic climate of the Great Depression. Her visibility and lifestyle choices made her a constant subject of media fascination and public critique. By 1934, Barbara’s life had inspired both film and song, capturing the public imagination and solidifying her status as a cultural icon, albeit one often viewed through a lens of scorn and envy.

This public narrative portrayed her as the "poor little rich girl," a moniker that underscored the complex interplay of wealth, privilege, and personal adversity that defined her life. To understand how someone could go from a million-dollar debutante party to poverty, one must roll back the clock and begin with a psychological profile rooted in her uniquely difficult youth. Born into opulence on the fourteenth of November 1912 in New York City, Barbara Woolworth Hutton emerged as the sole child of Edna Woolworth of the retail empire and Franklin Laws Hutton, a founder of the E. F.

Hutton and Company investment firm, making her an instant heiress to one of America’s grandest fortunes. Yet the wealth that defined her birthright would also shape a life marred by emotional turmoil. Barbara’s upbringing was steeped in material wealth but plagued by emotional neglect. Her father, Franklin, notorious for his infidelities, was a distant figure, while her mother, Edna, ensnared in loneliness, sought comfort in an affair with Bud Bouvier, Jacqueline Kennedy’s future uncle.

This chaotic household environment left Barbara profoundly isolated, craving the affection that her fractured family could not provide. Tragedy struck with brutal force at the tender age of five when Barbara discovered her mother lifeless, an image that would haunt her for decades. Officially, Edna’s death was attributed to complications from mastoiditis, but whispers of a self-inflicted end persisted, some suggesting the family might have influenced city officials to avoid probing too deeply into the actual cause. Reeling from this loss, Barbara’s subsequent childhood was a relentless shifting of guardians as she moved from one relative’s home to another.

She spent significant periods at her maternal grandparents’ luxurious sixty-room Long Island mansion, a place where material excess was abundant but emotional warmth was scarce. Her grandmother, Jennie Katherine Woolworth, was consumed by dementia, and her once-doting grandfather, Frank Woolworth, was ailing. He affectionately called her "princess," but his failing health meant he could not provide the stable affection she so desperately needed. After her grandfather’s death in 1919, Barbara’s father moved her frequently, each relocation eroding her sense of stability further.

Described as a "wistful, imaginative, lonely child" by those who knew her, Barbara harbored complex feelings for her father, intertwining threads of fear and a yearning for his approval. Throughout these formative years, Barbara’s cousin Jimmy Donahue was a kindred spirit, and he too knew the cold embrace of wealth coupled with familial neglect. This bond, forged in shared experience, became a rare constant in her early life. Barbara’s education was reflective of her status, with stints at prestigious schools like Miss Hutch’s Classes and Miss Porter’s School for Girls.

However, the luxury of her educational background did little to heal the deep emotional wounds inflicted by her turbulent upbringing. The imprint of such a fraught childhood left an indelible mark on Barbara Hutton as she matured; her life became a quest fraught with troubled relationships and a continuous search for the love and stability that her youth had so cruelly denied her. Barbara Hutton’s quest for love was as storied as it was heartbreaking, beginning with her first marriage to Prince Alexis Mdivani in 1933. Barbara first met Alexis through a calculated encounter orchestrated by Alexis’s sister, Roussie, known as Rusi.

The Mdivanis, a family of social climbers, were known for marrying into wealth, which they often flaunted in high society. Roussie thus arranged for her brother to meet Barbara under the pretense of social gatherings, exploiting Barbara’s vulnerability and immense wealth. Their initial encounter led to a scandalous affair while Alexis was still married to his first wife, Louise Van Allen. This affair culminated in a hasty marriage to Barbara after Alexis’s quick divorce from Louise.

At the young age of twenty, the Woolworth heiress married the self-proclaimed Georgian prince in a grand ceremony in Paris, dressed in a white gown with dramatic shoulders and a sweeping veil. She hoped for a fairy-tale ending, yet the reality was far from it. Mdivani, infamous as one of the "marrying Mdivanis," quickly set about spending Hutton’s vast inheritance on a luxurious home, polo ponies, lavish attire, and men’s jewelry. Their marriage dissolved in March 1935, not even two full years after they had exchanged vows.

But her divorce from Mdivani did little to deter Hutton’s marital pursuits. In May 1935, she entered into marriage with Count Kurt Heinrich Erdmann Georg von Haugwitz-Hardenberg-Reventlow. This relationship brought her only child, Lance Reventlow, into the world in 1936. However, like her first, this marriage crumbled by 1941.

Barbara Hutton’s third marriage, to the charismatic Hollywood icon Cary Grant, began just a year later in 1942. content_text:
In November 1960, eight-year-old Gloria Kowalczyk left her home on Chicago’s South Side to attend Mass at St. Mary of Mount Carmel Church. The church stood about three blocks away, less than half a mile from her back door. She never arrived.

Before noon, a laundry truck driver passing through Palos Park, a southwestern suburb of Cook County, stopped along 104th Street beside a wooded area. There he found Gloria. She had been shot. Investigators determined she was still alive when she was brought to those woods.

Less than half a mile from her home, her world had been small and close. By midday, she lay dead more than fifteen miles away. Using a metal detector, police found a single spent bullet casing in the ground. Her shoe and her purse were found a few feet from her body.

Her coat was missing and later discovered several miles away, apart from everything else. On the strap of her purse, investigators found fingerprints. They also found prints on her Bible. For detectives in 1960, this was promising.

A fingerprint belonged to only one person. But evidence only becomes an answer when it can be matched to someone. The problem was the nature of fingerprint files at the time. Records were kept on paper cards and searched by hand.

Trained examiners compared ridge patterns card by card. Those files were organized around complete sets of ten fingerprints taken at a police station or office. A single print lifted from a purse strap was far harder to search against thousands of cards. When detectives had a suspect, the task was simple: pull his card and compare.

When they had none, the print sat in the file waiting for a name. The empty casing carried the same limitation. Without the weapon, it could point to nothing by itself. The detectives had a crime scene, a timeline measured in hours, a casing, and fingerprints.

They did not have a single name to compare any of it against. That same day, Edward Kowalczyk identified his daughter near the place where she was found. The investigation that followed was extensive. Police interviewed more than 1,300 people.

Her clothing was displayed on a mannequin for press photographs, and the story spread beyond Chicago. Within days, detectives had another case to consider. On the evening of November 13, fourteen-year-old Nancy Eagleson was walking home from a movie theater in Boulding, Ohio, with her five-year-old sister. A man in a car forced her inside and drove away.

Her body was found the next day in a wooded area about eight miles away. Police investigated whether the cases were connected, but no link was ever established. Nancy’s case remains unsolved today. On November 16, 1960, Gloria’s funeral was held at the same church she had been walking toward four days earlier.

More than a thousand people attended. Six of her third-grade classmates served as pallbearers. She was buried in Mount Carmel Catholic Cemetery in Hillside, Illinois. The same day, a newspaper in Hammond, Indiana, reported that police could find no strong evidence identifying the person responsible.

Weeks turned into months. Tips came in and were checked. A Tribune report later described the search as overwhelmed by tips, dead-end investigations, and arrests that led nowhere. By the spring of 1961, about six months after Gloria’s death, the investigation had lost its momentum.

The evidence collected on November 12 remained in storage: the bullet casing, the clothing, the fingerprints on her purse strap. The man police now name as a suspect continued his career. Thomas Francis McInerney was a United States Army veteran. In 1960, he was a patrol officer on Chicago’s West Side.

In 1964, he was promoted to detective. Over the years that followed, his assignments took him across the city investigating robberies, vice, and gangs on the South Side. At one point, he worked as a homicide detective. Public records do not indicate he ever worked on Gloria’s case.

He remained on the Chicago Police Department until 1987 and died in Las Vegas in 2006. For forty-six years after Gloria’s murder, he lived without his name being publicly connected to it. Meanwhile, science changed. DNA analysis made it possible to link biological traces to a single person, and testing became sensitive enough to work on older, smaller samples.

Gloria’s clothing was still in storage. In July 2010, nearly fifty years after her death, the Chicago Police Department used grant funding to send her dress to a DNA laboratory. The fingerprints from her purse strap and Bible were also sent for examination. It was the first time the 1960 evidence had been examined with modern forensic tools.

Five months later, the lab reported a result. According to Lieutenant Marc Kearns of the department’s Area 1 detectives, the test revealed a male DNA profile from biological evidence on Gloria’s dress. For the first time, investigators had a genetic profile of the man linked to the evidence. The profile was entered into CODIS, the FBI’s national database of DNA profiles collected by law enforcement agencies across the United States.

If the man’s profile was already in the system, a search might yield a name. If his data had never been entered, no search of CODIS could find him directly. Kearns said several new suspects were developed, not one name but several. Each had to be examined, and each had to be confirmed or eliminated.

At the end of that process, the case remained open. Investigators now had what they lacked in 1960, a profile of the man they were looking for, but still no name. For years after 2010, the profile had no match. Then in 2024, the department used another federal grant to send a second piece of evidence, Gloria’s coat, to the FBI.

This time, the method was different. Investigative genetic genealogy, which became widely used after a notable case in California in 2018, does not depend on the suspect being in a criminal database. Instead, investigators compare the unknown DNA profile to people who have voluntarily submitted their DNA to family tree websites. These people are not suspects.

They may be distant relatives. By building family trees from those matches, genealogists can narrow the search toward one family and eventually one person. This method was designed for the problem Gloria’s case had faced since 2010: investigators had a profile but no name, and the man who matched it did not need a criminal record to be found. There is an important limit to this technique.

A match in a family tree is a lead, not proof. Federal Department of Justice policy requires confirming a genetic lead through direct DNA comparison before treating it as an identification. Earlier in 2026, according to the Tribune, the FBI’s genealogy work gave the case new momentum, pointing toward a specific name. In July 2026, according to Lieutenant Kearns, Thomas McInerney was definitively identified as the source of the DNA extracted from Gloria’s dress.

The name belonged to a man who, in November 1960, had been a Chicago police officer. The DNA identification was not the end of the investigation. Detectives turned to evidence unrelated to DNA. McInerney’s 1959 application to the Chicago Police Department included the fingerprints he had submitted to join the force.

Investigators compared those prints to the fingerprint taken from Gloria’s purse strap in 1960. According to investigators, they matched. That fingerprint had been part of the case from the first day. It had been lifted, logged, and stored.

In 2010, it had been sent for examination again. For sixty-five years, it had waited for a name and a set of prints that, according to investigators, matched. They had been inside the department’s own records since before Gloria was killed. The evidence had never been missing.

The connection had been. The fingerprint mattered for another reason. It was entirely separate from the DNA. It came from a different purpose, was collected in a different era, and was compared by a different method.

Police say both pointed to the same man. There was also the firearm evidence. According to a Tribune report, McInerney owned three Colt pistols, the same type of weapon used to fire the bullet found in Gloria’s case. This proves he owned weapons of the same type.

It does not equal matching a specific gun to the bullet, and no such match has been announced. Combined, the DNA evidence, the fingerprint comparison, and the firearm formed the basis of the department’s conclusion. The Tribune described that conclusion as the result of a series of ballistics tests, fingerprint comparisons, and DNA tests conducted over several years. Each line of evidence came from a different moment in the case.

The bullet casing and fingerprint were collected on the first day in 1960. The DNA profile came from 2010 testing. The name came from genealogy work that began in 2024. They were only assembled together in 2026.

But the evidence answered only part of what investigators needed to know. Cold case detectives say there was no known connection between McInerney and Gloria before her death. Census records cited by the Tribune show that in 1950, ten years before the murder, McInerney’s parents lived on South Lawndale Street, about three-quarters of a mile east of where the Kowalczyk family lived. His father was a correctional officer at the Cook County Jail.

Those records place his family in the same part of the city, but they do not prove any connection to Gloria. The reason an eight-year-old girl on her way to Mass was targeted remains unknown. The case now has a name. It still lacks a motive.

Because McInerney had died twenty years earlier, criminal prosecution was no longer possible. When a suspect is identified, an investigation normally moves into a new phase: arrest, formal charges, review by prosecutors, the test of the courtroom. None of those steps could happen. McInerney was never charged in Gloria’s death.

He never stood trial. No court ever ruled on the evidence against him. What the Chicago Police Department reached was an investigative conclusion. Cold case detectives identified the person they believe killed Gloria based on DNA, fingerprints, and firearm evidence.

That is not a conviction, and it was never tested in court. Police also say McInerney is not a suspect in any other crimes. This distinction is not merely technical. A trial is where evidence is challenged.

The defense could question how samples were stored for six decades, how comparisons were made, and what the results could and could not show. In this case, that process never happened and never can. The department could only close the file. According to police data reported by the Chicago Tribune, Gloria’s murder case is one of the oldest closed by Chicago police detectives in nearly a decade.

The findings were made public on October 11, 2026. For Adam Kowalczyk, the news came months earlier. He had been an infant when his sister was killed. Earlier in 2026, cold case detectives called to tell him what they had found.

He told the newspaper the call lifted a heavy weight from him. Learning that the identified man had been a Chicago police officer came as a shock. He praised the investigators who closed the case, but he also said he was troubled that McInerney faced no accountability for his sister’s death. The family still wonders why Gloria was targeted.

The file was closed, but one question remained inside it unanswered. The documented answer to why this took so long is this: the fingerprint alone did not show a name. DNA did. The 2010 profile gave investigators the man’s genetic fingerprint.

The genealogy work that followed in 2024 led them to his identity. Only then did investigators have reason to pull a sixty-seven-year-old job application and compare the two sets of prints side by side. The public record does not clarify whether that comparison could have been made earlier or why it was not. The report does not state whether the purse strap print was entered into automated fingerprint systems once they came into use.

Without that information, any answer is speculation. What the record does show is the order in which the pieces came together: evidence collected in 1960, a profile developed in 2010, a name emerging in 2026, and a fingerprint match confirming it. The evidence collected on November 12, 1960, survived across the decades, waiting until science could read it.

At Mount Carmel Catholic Cemetery in Hillside, Illinois, a headstone marks Gloria Kowalczyk, 1951 to 1960.

In November 1960, eight-year-old Gloria Kowalczyk left her home on Chicago’s South Side to attend Mass at St. Mary of Mount Carmel Church. The church stood about three blocks away, less than half a mile from her back door. She never arrived.

Before noon, a laundry truck driver passing through Palos Park, a southwestern suburb of Cook County, stopped along 104th Street beside a wooded area. There he found Gloria. She had been shot. Investigators determined she was still alive when she was brought to those woods.

Less than half a mile from her home, her world had been small and close. By midday, she lay dead more than fifteen miles away. Using a metal detector, police found a single spent bullet casing in the ground. Her shoe and her purse were found a few feet from her body.

Her coat was missing and later discovered several miles away, apart from everything else. On the strap of her purse, investigators found fingerprints. They also found prints on her Bible. For detectives in 1960, this was promising.

A fingerprint belonged to only one person. But evidence only becomes an answer when it can be matched to someone. The problem was the nature of fingerprint files at the time. Records were kept on paper cards and searched by hand.

Trained examiners compared ridge patterns card by card. Those files were organized around complete sets of ten fingerprints taken at a police station or office. A single print lifted from a purse strap was far harder to search against thousands of cards. When detectives had a suspect, the task was simple: pull his card and compare.

When they had none, the print sat in the file waiting for a name. The empty casing carried the same limitation. Without the weapon, it could point to nothing by itself. The detectives had a crime scene, a timeline measured in hours, a casing, and fingerprints.

They did not have a single name to compare any of it against. That same day, Edward Kowalczyk identified his daughter near the place where she was found. The investigation that followed was extensive. Police interviewed more than 1,300 people.

Her clothing was displayed on a mannequin for press photographs, and the story spread beyond Chicago. Within days, detectives had another case to consider. On the evening of November 13, fourteen-year-old Nancy Eagleson was walking home from a movie theater in Boulding, Ohio, with her five-year-old sister. A man in a car forced her inside and drove away.

Her body was found the next day in a wooded area about eight miles away. Police investigated whether the cases were connected, but no link was ever established. Nancy’s case remains unsolved today. On November 16, 1960, Gloria’s funeral was held at the same church she had been walking toward four days earlier.

More than a thousand people attended. Six of her third-grade classmates served as pallbearers. She was buried in Mount Carmel Catholic Cemetery in Hillside, Illinois. The same day, a newspaper in Hammond, Indiana, reported that police could find no strong evidence identifying the person responsible.

Weeks turned into months. Tips came in and were checked. A Tribune report later described the search as overwhelmed by tips, dead-end investigations, and arrests that led nowhere. By the spring of 1961, about six months after Gloria’s death, the investigation had lost its momentum.

The evidence collected on November 12 remained in storage: the bullet casing, the clothing, the fingerprints on her purse strap. The man police now name as a suspect continued his career. Thomas Francis McInerney was a United States Army veteran. In 1960, he was a patrol officer on Chicago’s West Side.

In 1964, he was promoted to detective. Over the years that followed, his assignments took him across the city investigating robberies, vice, and gangs on the South Side. At one point, he worked as a homicide detective. Public records do not indicate he ever worked on Gloria’s case.

He remained on the Chicago Police Department until 1987 and died in Las Vegas in 2006. For forty-six years after Gloria’s murder, he lived without his name being publicly connected to it. Meanwhile, science changed. DNA analysis made it possible to link biological traces to a single person, and testing became sensitive enough to work on older, smaller samples.

Gloria’s clothing was still in storage. In July 2010, nearly fifty years after her death, the Chicago Police Department used grant funding to send her dress to a DNA laboratory. The fingerprints from her purse strap and Bible were also sent for examination. It was the first time the 1960 evidence had been examined with modern forensic tools.

Five months later, the lab reported a result. According to Lieutenant Marc Kearns of the department’s Area 1 detectives, the test revealed a male DNA profile from biological evidence on Gloria’s dress. For the first time, investigators had a genetic profile of the man linked to the evidence. The profile was entered into CODIS, the FBI’s national database of DNA profiles collected by law enforcement agencies across the United States.

If the man’s profile was already in the system, a search might yield a name. If his data had never been entered, no search of CODIS could find him directly. Kearns said several new suspects were developed, not one name but several. Each had to be examined, and each had to be confirmed or eliminated.

At the end of that process, the case remained open. Investigators now had what they lacked in 1960, a profile of the man they were looking for, but still no name. For years after 2010, the profile had no match. Then in 2024, the department used another federal grant to send a second piece of evidence, Gloria’s coat, to the FBI.

This time, the method was different. Investigative genetic genealogy, which became widely used after a notable case in California in 2018, does not depend on the suspect being in a criminal database. Instead, investigators compare the unknown DNA profile to people who have voluntarily submitted their DNA to family tree websites. These people are not suspects.

They may be distant relatives. By building family trees from those matches, genealogists can narrow the search toward one family and eventually one person. This method was designed for the problem Gloria’s case had faced since 2010: investigators had a profile but no name, and the man who matched it did not need a criminal record to be found. There is an important limit to this technique.

A match in a family tree is a lead, not proof. Federal Department of Justice policy requires confirming a genetic lead through direct DNA comparison before treating it as an identification. Earlier in 2026, according to the Tribune, the FBI’s genealogy work gave the case new momentum, pointing toward a specific name. In July 2026, according to Lieutenant Kearns, Thomas McInerney was definitively identified as the source of the DNA extracted from Gloria’s dress.

The name belonged to a man who, in November 1960, had been a Chicago police officer. The DNA identification was not the end of the investigation. Detectives turned to evidence unrelated to DNA. McInerney’s 1959 application to the Chicago Police Department included the fingerprints he had submitted to join the force.

Investigators compared those prints to the fingerprint taken from Gloria’s purse strap in 1960. According to investigators, they matched. That fingerprint had been part of the case from the first day. It had been lifted, logged, and stored.

In 2010, it had been sent for examination again. For sixty-five years, it had waited for a name and a set of prints that, according to investigators, matched. They had been inside the department’s own records since before Gloria was killed. The evidence had never been missing.

The connection had been. The fingerprint mattered for another reason. It was entirely separate from the DNA. It came from a different purpose, was collected in a different era, and was compared by a different method.

Police say both pointed to the same man. There was also the firearm evidence. According to a Tribune report, McInerney owned three Colt pistols, the same type of weapon used to fire the bullet found in Gloria’s case. This proves he owned weapons of the same type.

It does not equal matching a specific gun to the bullet, and no such match has been announced. Combined, the DNA evidence, the fingerprint comparison, and the firearm formed the basis of the department’s conclusion. The Tribune described that conclusion as the result of a series of ballistics tests, fingerprint comparisons, and DNA tests conducted over several years. Each line of evidence came from a different moment in the case.

The bullet casing and fingerprint were collected on the first day in 1960. The DNA profile came from 2010 testing. The name came from genealogy work that began in 2024. They were only assembled together in 2026.

But the evidence answered only part of what investigators needed to know. Cold case detectives say there was no known connection between McInerney and Gloria before her death. Census records cited by the Tribune show that in 1950, ten years before the murder, McInerney’s parents lived on South Lawndale Street, about three-quarters of a mile east of where the Kowalczyk family lived. His father was a correctional officer at the Cook County Jail.

Those records place his family in the same part of the city, but they do not prove any connection to Gloria. The reason an eight-year-old girl on her way to Mass was targeted remains unknown. The case now has a name. It still lacks a motive.

Because McInerney had died twenty years earlier, criminal prosecution was no longer possible. When a suspect is identified, an investigation normally moves into a new phase: arrest, formal charges, review by prosecutors, the test of the courtroom. None of those steps could happen. McInerney was never charged in Gloria’s death.

He never stood trial. No court ever ruled on the evidence against him. What the Chicago Police Department reached was an investigative conclusion. Cold case detectives identified the person they believe killed Gloria based on DNA, fingerprints, and firearm evidence.

That is not a conviction, and it was never tested in court. Police also say McInerney is not a suspect in any other crimes. This distinction is not merely technical. A trial is where evidence is challenged.

The defense could question how samples were stored for six decades, how comparisons were made, and what the results could and could not show. In this case, that process never happened and never can. The department could only close the file. According to police data reported by the Chicago Tribune, Gloria’s murder case is one of the oldest closed by Chicago police detectives in nearly a decade.

The findings were made public on October 11, 2026. For Adam Kowalczyk, the news came months earlier. He had been an infant when his sister was killed. Earlier in 2026, cold case detectives called to tell him what they had found.

He told the newspaper the call lifted a heavy weight from him. Learning that the identified man had been a Chicago police officer came as a shock. He praised the investigators who closed the case, but he also said he was troubled that McInerney faced no accountability for his sister’s death. The family still wonders why Gloria was targeted.

The file was closed, but one question remained inside it unanswered. The documented answer to why this took so long is this: the fingerprint alone did not show a name. DNA did. The 2010 profile gave investigators the man’s genetic fingerprint.

The genealogy work that followed in 2024 led them to his identity. Only then did investigators have reason to pull a sixty-seven-year-old job application and compare the two sets of prints side by side. The public record does not clarify whether that comparison could have been made earlier or why it was not. The report does not state whether the purse strap print was entered into automated fingerprint systems once they came into use.

Without that information, any answer is speculation. What the record does show is the order in which the pieces came together: evidence collected in 1960, a profile developed in 2010, a name emerging in 2026, and a fingerprint match confirming it. The evidence collected on November 12, 1960, survived across the decades, waiting until science could read it.

At Mount Carmel Catholic Cemetery in Hillside, Illinois, a headstone marks Gloria Kowalczyk, 1951 to 1960.
